**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 1 (part 1 of 2)**

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Surat al-Anfal is Medinan, and it is Badri (concerning the Battle of Badr), according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Jabir and 'Ata'. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Medinan except for seven verses, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [8:30] to the end of the seven verses. [[See p. 395 of this volume.]]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, set right the relations among yourselves, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers﴾ [8:1].

There are six issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to Badr, and they met the enemy. When Allah routed them, a group of the Muslims pursued them, killing them. Another group surrounded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and another group took possession of the camp and the plunder. When Allah had repelled the enemy and those who had pursued them returned, they said: "The *nafl* (extra share) is ours, for we are the ones who pursued the enemy, and it was through us that Allah repelled them and defeated them." Those who had surrounded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You have no more right to it than we do. Rather, it is ours, for we surrounded the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that the enemy would not reach him unawares." And those who had taken possession of the camp and the plunder said: "You have no more right to it than we do. It is ours, for we gathered it and took control of it." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger. So fear Allah, set right the relations among yourselves, and obey Allah and His Messenger, if you are believers﴾. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided it among them equally, without delay.

Abu 'Umar said: The people of knowledge in the Arabic language said: *istalawu* means they surrounded and encompassed. It is said: "Death encompasses the servants" (*al-mawtu mustalin 'ala al-'ibad*). As for His saying, "*fa-qasamahu 'an fuwaq*" (he divided it without delay), it means "quickly." They said: *al-fuwaq* is the interval between two milkings of a she-camel. It is said: "He waited for him a *fuwaq* of a she-camel," meaning this amount of time. It is pronounced both *fuwaq* and *fawaq*. This occurred before the revelation of: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils of war, a fifth of it belongs to Allah﴾ [8:41].

The meaning according to the scholars is: the ruling concerning them and the handling of them belongs to Allah and to the Messenger, in a manner that brings one closer to Allah, Exalted is He.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith and others of our companions told me, on the authority of Sulayman ibn Musa al-Ashdaq, on the authority of Makhul, on the authority of Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: I asked 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit about the *anfal*. He said: It was revealed concerning us, the company of those at Badr, when we disputed over the *nafl* and our characters were corrupted regarding it. So Allah took it out of our hands and placed it with the Messenger, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided it *'an bawa'*, meaning equally." So that was the fear of Allah, obedience to His Messenger, and the setting right of relations among them.

It is related in the Sahih, on the authority of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seized a great spoil, and among it there was a sword. I took it and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Grant me this sword as a *nafl*, for you know my condition." He said: "Return it to where you took it." So I went off, and when I was about to throw it into the *qabad* (the pile of collected spoils before division), my soul reproached me. So I went back to him and said: "Give it to me." He then raised his voice at me: "Return it to where you took it!" So I went off again, and when I was about to throw it into the *qabad*, my soul reproached me. I returned to him and said: "Give it to me." He raised his voice at me: "Return it to where you took it!" Then Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾. This is the wording of Muslim.

The narrations are numerous, and what we have mentioned is sufficient. And Allah is the Granter of success to guidance.

**The second issue:** *Al-anfal* is the plural of *nafal*, with the *fa'* vowelled with a fatha. The poet said:

*Indeed, the fear of our Lord is the best of *nafal*,
and by the leave of Allah are my delay and my haste.*

That is, the best spoil. *Al-nafl* also means an oath, and from it comes the hadith: "*fa-tubarri'ukum Yahud bi-nafli khamsin minhum*" (then the Jews will clear you by swearing fifty oaths). *Al-nafl* also means disclaiming (*intifa'*), and from it comes the hadith: "*fa-intafala min waladiha*" (so he disclaimed her child). *Al-nafal* is also a well-known plant. *Al-nafl* means an addition beyond what is obligatory, which is voluntary worship (*tatawwu'*). A grandchild is called *nafilah* because he is an addition beyond the child. Spoils are called *nafilah* because they are an addition to what Allah has made lawful for this community that had been forbidden to others. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been favoured over the prophets in six ways, and among them: the spoils have been made lawful for me."

*Al-anfal* also means the spoils themselves. 'Antarah said:

*Indeed, when the battle reddens, we quench our spears with blood,
and we abstain at the division of the *anfal*, that is, the spoils.*

**The third issue:** The scholars differed about where the *anfal* is to be placed, in four opinions:

The first: their place is in what is seized from the unbelievers by the Muslims, or what is taken without fighting.

The second: their place is the one-fifth (*khums*).

The third: the one-fifth of the one-fifth.

The fourth: the head of the spoils, according to what the Imam sees fit.

The school of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that the *anfal* are gifts of the Imam from the one-fifth, according to what he sees fit by way of personal reasoning (*ijtihad*). There is no *nafl* in the four-fifths. He did not regard the *nafl* as coming from the head of the spoils because its recipients are specified, namely those who made the effort (*al-mujaffun*), and the one-fifth is returned, its division left to the Imam's reasoning, and its recipients are not specified. [Note: *al-mujaffun* are those who gather with horses and riders; *al-ijaf* is rapid movement.] The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have no share of what Allah has bestowed (*afa'a*) upon you except the one-fifth, and the one-fifth is returned to you." Therefore, after this, it is not possible for the *nafl* to be from anyone's right, but it comes from the right of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which is the one-fifth. This is the well-known position of his school, though it has been related from him that it is from the one-fifth of the one-fifth. This is the view of Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah.

The cause of the disagreement is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, which Malik related: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment (*sariyyah*) toward Najd, and they seized many camels. Their shares were twelve camels, or eleven camels, and they were given a camel each as a *nafl*. Thus Malik related it with doubt in the transmission of Yahya from him, and the group of transmitters of the Muwatta' followed him in this, except al-Walid ibn Muslim, who related it from Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, and he said in it: "Their shares were twelve camels, and they were given a camel each as a *nafl*," and he did not express doubt. Al-Walid ibn Muslim and al-Hakam ibn Nafi' also mentioned, on the authority of Shu'ayb ibn Abi Hamzah, on the authority of Nafi', on the authority of Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us in an army toward Najd (in al-Walid's narration: four thousand men), and a detachment broke off from the army (in al-Walid's narration: "I was among those who went out with it"). So the shares of the army were twelve camels, twelve camels, and the people of the detachment were given a camel each as a *nafl*, so their shares were thirteen camels. Abu Dawud mentioned it.

Those who say that the *nafl* is only from the total of the one-fifth argue by this. Its explanation is that if this detachment were supposed to have been ten men, for example, and had obtained a spoil of one hundred and fifty, its one-fifth, thirty, would be removed, and there would remain one hundred and twenty, which is divided among ten, so each one is due twelve camels, twelve camels. Then the men were given a camel each from the one-fifth, because the one-fifth of thirty cannot contain ten camels. Once you know the rule for ten, you know the rule for a hundred, a thousand and more.

Those who say that this was from the one-fifth of the one-fifth argue that it is possible that there were garments being sold and goods other than camels, so the one who did not reach a camel was given the value of a camel from those goods. Something that supports this is what Muslim related in some chains of this hadith: "We obtained camels and sheep," and so on.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq mentioned in this hadith that the commander gave them the *nafl* before the division, and this requires that the *nafl* be from the head of the spoils, which is contrary to the view of Malik. But the view of the one who narrated the opposite is preferable, because they were memorizers (*huffaz*), as Abu 'Umar, may Allah have mercy on him, said.

Makhul and al-Awza'i said: one should not give a *nafl* exceeding one-third. This is the view of the majority of the scholars. Al-Awza'i said: If he gives them more, he should fulfil it for them and make that from the one-fifth. Al-Shafi'i said: There is no limit in the *nafl* that the Imam may not exceed.

**The fourth issue:** The hadith of Ibn 'Umar indicates, as al-Walid and al-Hakam related from Shu'ayb from Nafi', that when a detachment goes out from the army and seizes spoils, the army are their partners. This is a matter and a ruling that none of the transmitters mentioned in the hadith other than Shu'ayb on the authority of Nafi' related, and the scholars have not differed concerning it, praise be to Allah.

**The fifth issue:** The scholars differed concerning an Imam who says before the fighting: "Whoever demolishes such-and-such part of the fortress shall have such-and-such; whoever reaches such-and-such place shall have such-and-such; whoever brings a head shall have such-and-such; whoever brings a captive shall have such-and-such," thereby inciting them (*yudarrihim*). [Note: *al-tadriyah* is incitement.] It is related from Malik that he disliked it, and said: "This is fighting for worldly gain," and he did not permit it. Al-Thawri said: That is permissible and there is no harm in it. I say: This meaning has also come in a raised (*marfu'*) hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: On the day of Badr the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever kills a slain enemy, he shall have such-and-such, and whoever takes a captive, he shall have such-and-such." The hadith in full. And in the narration of 'Ikrimah from him, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does such-and-such and goes to such-and-such place, he shall have such-and-such." So the young men hastened, and the elders remained with the banners. When victory was granted to them, the young men came seeking what had been promised to them. The elders said to them: "Do not take it without us, for we were a reserve for you." So Allah revealed: ﴿and set right the relations among yourselves﴾. Ismail ibn Ishaq also mentioned this.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said to Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali when he came to him with his people, intending to go to Syria: "Would you like to come to Kufa, and for you will be a third after the one-fifth from every land and captive?" This was the view of a group of the jurists of Syria: al-Awza'i, Makhul, Ibn Hayawah and others. They regarded the one-fifth as part of the total spoils, and the *nafl* after the one-fifth, and then the spoils are divided among the people of the army. This was also the view of Ishaq, Ahmad and Abu 'Ubayd. Abu 'Ubayd said: "And people today hold that there is no *nafl* from the spoils until it has been divided into fifths."

Malik said: It is not permissible for the Imam to say to a detachment: "Whatever you take, one-third of it is yours." Sahnun said: He means at the outset. If it occurs (*nazal*), it proceeds, and they have their shares in the remainder. Sahnun also said: If the Imam says to a detachment, "Whatever you take, there is no one-fifth due from you on it," this is not permissible; if it occurs, I would reverse it, because this is an aberrant ruling that is not permissible and is not to be enforced.

**The sixth issue:** Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, preferred that the Imam give only what is visible, such as a turban, a horse, or a sword. Some scholars prohibited the Imam from giving gold, silver, pearls and the like. Others said: the *nafl* is permissible from anything. This is the sound view, in accordance with the saying of 'Umar and the implication of the verse, and Allah knows best.

**The seventh issue:** His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So fear Allah and set right the relations among yourselves﴾ is a command to piety and reconciliation, that is: be united upon the command of Allah. In supplication one says: "O Allah, set right *dhat al-bayn*," that is, the state in which unity takes place. This indicates the explicit statement that there had arisen among them disagreement, or that souls had inclined toward rivalry, as is stated in the hadith. The meaning of piety has already been mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 161.]]; that is: fear Allah in your words and your deeds, and set right the relations among yourselves.

(And obey Allah and His Messenger) in regard to the spoils of war and the like.

(If you are believers) meaning: indeed, the way of the believer is to comply with what we have mentioned. It has also been said that "in" (inna) here means "since" (idh).

**Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 8, verses 2–4:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely.﴾ On this there are three issues.

The first: The scholars said: This verse is an exhortation to hold firmly to obedience to the Messenger ﷺ in what he commanded concerning the division of that spoil of war. *Al-wajal* (trembling, fear) means *al-khawf* (fear). In its imperfect form (*mustaqbal*) there are four dialects: *wajila yawjalu*, *yajalu*, *yayjalu*, and *yayjilu*, as transmitted by Sibawayh. The verbal noun is *wajalan*, *wajalan* and *mu'jalatan* (with a fatha). The adjective is *mu'jilah* (with a kasra), for the place and for the noun. Whoever says *yajalu* in the imperfect makes the waw an alif because of the fatha before it. The language of the Qur'an is the waw form: ﴿They said, "Do not fear" [qalu la tawjal]﴾. [See vol. 10, p. 34.] Whoever says *yayjilu* with a kasra on the ya' follows the dialect of the Banu Asad, for they say: *ana ijilu*, *nahnu nijilu*, *anta tijilu*, all with a kasra. Whoever says *yayjalu* forms it on this dialect but opens the ya', as they open it in *ya'lamu*; the ya' is not given a kasra in *ya'lamu* because they find a kasra on a ya' burdensome. In *yayjilu* it is given a kasra in order to strengthen one of the two ya's by the other. The imperative from it is *ijal*, and the waw became a ya' because of the kasra before it. You say: "Indeed I am *awjal* (more fearful) regarding it." For the feminine one does not say *wajla'*, but *wajilah*.

Sufyan narrated from al-Suddi concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾, that he said: When a man intends to commit an injustice, it is said to him: "Fear Allah," and his heart trembles.

The second: Allah the Exalted described the believers in this verse with fear and trembling at the mention of Him. That is due to the strength of their faith and their watchfulness over their Lord, as though they were standing before Him. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿And give good tidings to the humble (al-mukhbitin), those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾. [See vol. 12, p. 58 and following.] And He said: ﴿Their hearts are at rest through the remembrance of Allah﴾. [See vol. 9, p. 314 and following.] This refers to the perfection of knowledge (*al-ma'rifah*) and the confidence of the heart. *Al-wajal* is dread of the punishment of Allah, so there is no contradiction. Allah has combined the two meanings in His saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent and repeating; the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it, then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾. [See vol. 15, p. 248.] That is, their souls become tranquil, in terms of certainty, towards Allah, even though they fear Allah. This is the state of those who know Allah, who fear His might and His punishment. It is not like what the ignorant common folk and the base innovators do, of shouting, roaring, and braying like the braying of donkeys. It is said to whoever engages in that and claims that it is ecstasy and humble submission: "You have not attained to equal the state of the Messenger nor the state of his Companions in knowledge of Allah, in fear of Him, and in glorifying His majesty. Yet despite that, their state at admonitions was understanding from Allah and weeping out of fear of Allah." For this reason Allah described the states of those who have knowledge when His remembrance is heard and His Book is recited, saying: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized. They say: "Our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses."﴾ [See vol. 6, p. 258.] This is a description of their state and a recounting of their words. Whoever is not like this is not upon their guidance nor their path. Whoever would follow a model, let him follow it. Whoever engages in the states of the madmen and the insane, he is among the lowest of them in condition, and madness has many kinds.

Muslim narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the people questioned the Prophet ﷺ until they pressed him (*ahfawhu*), meaning they persisted greatly in their questioning. He went out one day, ascended the pulpit, and said: "Ask me, you will not ask me about anything except that I will make it clear to you as long as I am in this place." When the people heard that, they fell silent (*arammu*) and feared that some matter had come close. Anas said: "I began looking to the right and to the left, and every person had his head covered in his garment, weeping." And he mentioned the hadith.

At-Tirmidhi narrated and authenticated from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ admonished us with an eloquent admonition, from which the eyes overflowed and the hearts trembled. [He mentioned] the hadith. He did not say: "We shouted, nor did we dance, nor did we clap (*zafan*), nor did we stand up."

The third: His saying: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾, meaning in affirmation (*tasdiq*). The faith of this moment is an increase over the faith of yesterday; whoever affirms a second and third time, his affirmation is an increase relative to what preceded. It was also said: it is an increase in the expansion of the breast (*inshirah al-sadr*) through the abundance of signs and proofs. This meaning has already passed in the commentary on Surah Al 'Imran. [See vol. 4, pp. 280 and 189.]

﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾: The meaning of *tawakkul* has already been discussed in Surah Al 'Imran as well. [See vol. 4, pp. 280 and 189.]

﴿Who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾: This has been discussed at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 164.]

﴿Those are the true believers (*haqqan*)﴾: That is, those whose outward and inward are equal in faith. This indicates that every truth has a reality (*haqiqah*). The Prophet ﷺ said to Harithah: "Every truth has a reality, so what is the reality of your faith?" [He mentioned] the hadith. A man asked al-Hasan: "O Abu Sa'id, are you a believer?" He said to him: "Faith is of two kinds. If you are asking me about faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, Paradise, Hellfire, resurrection, and reckoning, then I am a believer in it. But if you are asking me about the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾ up to His saying ﴿Those are the true believers﴾, then by Allah, I do not know whether I am among them or not." Abu Bakr al-Wasiti said: Whoever says "I am a believer in Allah in truth," it is said to him: "Reality indicates elevation, awareness, and comprehensiveness; whoever lacks it, his claim in it is void." He means by this what the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) said: the true believer is the one who is judged to be in Paradise. Whoever does not know that from the secret of His wisdom, the Exalted, then his claim to be a true believer is invalid.

Whoever does not know that from the secret of His wisdom, the Exalted, then his claim to be a true believer is invalid.

**Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 8, verses 2–4:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely.﴾ On this there are three issues.

The first: The scholars said: This verse is an exhortation to hold firmly to obedience to the Messenger ﷺ in what he commanded concerning the division of that spoil of war. *Al-wajal* (trembling, fear) means *al-khawf* (fear). In its imperfect form (*mustaqbal*) there are four dialects: *wajila yawjalu*, *yajalu*, *yayjalu*, and *yayjilu*, as transmitted by Sibawayh. The verbal noun is *wajalan*, *wajalan* and *mu'jalatan* (with a fatha). The adjective is *mu'jilah* (with a kasra), for the place and for the noun. Whoever says *yajalu* in the imperfect makes the waw an alif because of the fatha before it. The language of the Qur'an is the waw form: ﴿They said, "Do not fear" [qalu la tawjal]﴾. [See vol. 10, p. 34.] Whoever says *yayjilu* with a kasra on the ya' follows the dialect of the Banu Asad, for they say: *ana ijilu*, *nahnu nijilu*, *anta tijilu*, all with a kasra. Whoever says *yayjalu* forms it on this dialect but opens the ya', as they open it in *ya'lamu*; the ya' is not given a kasra in *ya'lamu* because they find a kasra on a ya' burdensome. In *yayjilu* it is given a kasra in order to strengthen one of the two ya's by the other. The imperative from it is *ijal*, and the waw became a ya' because of the kasra before it. You say: "Indeed I am *awjal* (more fearful) regarding it." For the feminine one does not say *wajla'*, but *wajilah*.

Sufyan narrated from al-Suddi concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾, that he said: When a man intends to commit an injustice, it is said to him: "Fear Allah," and his heart trembles.

The second: Allah the Exalted described the believers in this verse with fear and trembling at the mention of Him. That is due to the strength of their faith and their watchfulness over their Lord, as though they were standing before Him. A parallel to this verse is: ﴿And give good tidings to the humble (al-mukhbitin), those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾. [See vol. 12, p. 58 and following.] And He said: ﴿Their hearts are at rest through the remembrance of Allah﴾. [See vol. 9, p. 314 and following.] This refers to the perfection of knowledge (*al-ma'rifah*) and the confidence of the heart. *Al-wajal* is dread of the punishment of Allah, so there is no contradiction. Allah has combined the two meanings in His saying: ﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent and repeating; the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it, then their skins and hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾. [See vol. 15, p. 248.] That is, their souls become tranquil, in terms of certainty, towards Allah, even though they fear Allah. This is the state of those who know Allah, who fear His might and His punishment. It is not like what the ignorant common folk and the base innovators do, of shouting, roaring, and braying like the braying of donkeys. It is said to whoever engages in that and claims that it is ecstasy and humble submission: "You have not attained to equal the state of the Messenger nor the state of his Companions in knowledge of Allah, in fear of Him, and in glorifying His majesty. Yet despite that, their state at admonitions was understanding from Allah and weeping out of fear of Allah." For this reason Allah described the states of those who have knowledge when His remembrance is heard and His Book is recited, saying: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized. They say: "Our Lord, we have believed, so record us among the witnesses."﴾ [See vol. 6, p. 258.] This is a description of their state and a recounting of their words. Whoever is not like this is not upon their guidance nor their path. Whoever would follow a model, let him follow it. Whoever engages in the states of the madmen and the insane, he is among the lowest of them in condition, and madness has many kinds.

Muslim narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the people questioned the Prophet ﷺ until they pressed him (*ahfawhu*), meaning they persisted greatly in their questioning. He went out one day, ascended the pulpit, and said: "Ask me, you will not ask me about anything except that I will make it clear to you as long as I am in this place." When the people heard that, they fell silent (*arammu*) and feared that some matter had come close. Anas said: "I began looking to the right and to the left, and every person had his head covered in his garment, weeping." And he mentioned the hadith.

At-Tirmidhi narrated and authenticated from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ admonished us with an eloquent admonition, from which the eyes overflowed and the hearts trembled. [He mentioned] the hadith. He did not say: "We shouted, nor did we dance, nor did we clap (*zafan*), nor did we stand up."

The third: His saying: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾, meaning in affirmation (*tasdiq*). The faith of this moment is an increase over the faith of yesterday; whoever affirms a second and third time, his affirmation is an increase relative to what preceded. It was also said: it is an increase in the expansion of the breast (*inshirah al-sadr*) through the abundance of signs and proofs. This meaning has already passed in the commentary on Surah Al 'Imran. [See vol. 4, pp. 280 and 189.]

﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾: The meaning of *tawakkul* has already been discussed in Surah Al 'Imran as well. [See vol. 4, pp. 280 and 189.]

﴿Who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾: This has been discussed at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. [See vol. 1, p. 164.]

﴿Those are the true believers (*haqqan*)﴾: That is, those whose outward and inward are equal in faith. This indicates that every truth has a reality (*haqiqah*). The Prophet ﷺ said to Harithah: "Every truth has a reality, so what is the reality of your faith?" [He mentioned] the hadith. A man asked al-Hasan: "O Abu Sa'id, are you a believer?" He said to him: "Faith is of two kinds. If you are asking me about faith in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, Paradise, Hellfire, resurrection, and reckoning, then I am a believer in it. But if you are asking me about the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾ up to His saying ﴿Those are the true believers﴾, then by Allah, I do not know whether I am among them or not." Abu Bakr al-Wasiti said: Whoever says "I am a believer in Allah in truth," it is said to him: "Reality indicates elevation, awareness, and comprehensiveness; whoever lacks it, his claim in it is void." He means by this what the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) said: the true believer is the one who is judged to be in Paradise. Whoever does not know that from the secret of His wisdom, the Exalted, then his claim to be a true believer is invalid.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The kaf (ka, "as") is in the accusative position, meaning: the spoils belong to you just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth, that is, like your Lord bringing you forth from your house in truth. The meaning is: proceed with your command concerning the spoils, and grant extra shares (nafl) to whomever you wish, even if they dislike it, because some of the Companions said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he gave something to everyone who brought in a captive: "Most people will be left with nothing." So the position of the kaf in "kama" is accusative, as we have mentioned. Al-Farra' also said the same. Abu 'Ubayda said: It is an oath, meaning: "By the One who brought you forth," so the kaf carries the meaning of the waw, and ma carries the meaning of alladhi (who). Sa'id ibn Mas'ada said: The meaning is: "Those are the believers in truth, just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth." He said: Some scholars said: "Just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth" [means] "so fear Allah and set right your affairs among yourselves." Ikrimah said: The meaning is: "Obey Allah and His Messenger, just as He brought you forth." It was also said: "Just as He brought you forth" is connected to His saying "For them are degrees [of rank]." The meaning: for them are degrees with their Lord, and forgiveness and generous provision. That is, this promise to the believers is true in the Hereafter, just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth, the truth that was due to Him, so He fulfilled His promise to you and granted you victory over your enemy and fulfilled it for you, because He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And [recall] when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾. Just as He fulfilled this promise in this world, so He will fulfill for you what He has promised you in the Hereafter. This is a good view, mentioned and preferred by al-Nahhas. It was also said: The kaf in "kama" is the kaf of comparison, and its explanation is by way of recompense, like the saying of a man to his slave: "Just as I directed you against my enemies and you were weakened, and you asked for reinforcement so I reinforced you, strengthened you and removed your affliction, now take them and punish them with such-and-such. And just as I clothed you and provided you with sustenance, do such-and-such. And just as I have done good to you, thank Me for it." So He said: ﴿Just as your Lord brought you forth from your house in truth, and He covered you with drowsiness as security from Him﴾ — meaning by it Himself and those with him — ﴿and sent down water from the sky to purify you by it, and sent down upon you from the sky angels following one another. So strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip﴾. It is as if He is saying: "I have removed your afflictions, and I have reinforced you with the angels, so strike these places of them, which are the vital points, so that you may attain Allah's aim of establishing the truth and nullifying falsehood." And Allah knows best.

(And indeed a group of the believers were certainly averse) — that is, they were averse to leaving Makkah, and to leaving their wealth and their homes.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 6:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They dispute with you concerning the truth after it has become clear﴾. Their disputing (mujadalatuhum) was their saying, when he urged them toward the caravan (al-'ir) and the caravan escaped, and he commanded them to fight while they did not have much in the way of equipment (uhbah), and that was hard on them, and they said: "If you had informed us of the fighting, we would have taken the necessary provisions." And the meaning of "concerning the truth" is: concerning the fighting. "After it has become clear" to them that you do not command anything except by the permission of Allah. It was also said: after it had become clear to them that Allah had promised them one of two things, either victory over the caravan or over the people of Makkah, and when the caravan had escaped, there was no alternative but the people of Makkah and victory over them. So the meaning of the statement is a denunciation of their disputing.

﴿As if they were being driven to death﴾, out of aversion to meeting the people.

﴿while they are looking on﴾, that is, knowing that this is bound to befall them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾, meaning: will know.

[[See vol. 19, p. 183.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 7–8:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Allah promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾. "Iḥdā" (one of) is in the accusative position as the second object. "Annahā lakum" (that it would be yours) is also in the accusative position, as a substitute (badal) for "iḥdā". "Watawaddūna" means "you love" (tuḥibbūna), "anna ghayra dhāti al-shawkati takūnu lakum" (that the one without the thorn [i.e., without armed strength] would be yours). Abu 'Ubayda said: that is, the one without edge (ghayr dhāti al-ḥadd). And al-shawka means weapons, and al-shawk means the plant that has a thorn, and from it comes the expression rajulun shā'ikun al-silāḥ, meaning a man with sharp weapons, that is, with keen arms. Then it is inverted and it is said shākī al-silāḥ (armed with weapons). That is, you wished to overcome the group that had no weapons and in which there was no fighting. This is related from al-Zajjaj.

﴿And Allah intends to establish the truth by His words﴾: that is, to make Islam manifest. The truth is always truth, but its manifestation is a confirmation of it, inasmuch as if it does not become manifest, it resembles falsehood. "By His words" means by His promise, for He promised His Prophet that in the sura "al-Dukhan," when He said: ﴿On the day We seize with the greatest seizure; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [see vol. 16, p. 133], that is, from Abu Jahl and his companions. And He said: ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [see vol. 8, p. 121 and what follows]. It has also been said: "by His words" means by His command to you, not to fight them.

﴿And to cut off the trailing end of the disbelievers﴾: that is, to uproot them by destruction.

﴿That He may establish the truth﴾: that is, He makes the religion of Islam manifest [in C: the religion of Allah] and honours it.

﴿And nullify falsehood﴾: that is, disbelief. Its nullification is its annihilation, just as establishing the truth is making it manifest: ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 277].

﴿Although the criminals dislike it﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verses 9–10:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord﴾. Al-istighathah (seeking relief) is asking for help and victory. It is said: "ghawwatha al-rajul" when a man cries out, "Wa ghawthah!" (Oh, relief!). The noun is al-ghawth, al-ghuwath and al-ghawath. "Istaghatha-ni fulan, fa-aghathtuhu" (someone sought relief from me, so I gave him relief), and the noun is al-ghiyath [[The waw has become a ya because of the kasrah before it.]], from al-Jawhari.

Muslim narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: When the day of Badr came, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the polytheists, who were a thousand, while his companions were three hundred and seventeen [[What is in Sahih Muslim is: "... nineteen ..." The well-known figure is three hundred and thirteen, as will come.]] men. The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) turned to the qiblah, then stretched out his hands, and began to call upon his Lord: "O Allah, fulfil for me what You have promised me. O Allah, bring me what You have promised me. O Allah, if this small band of the people of Islam perishes, You will not be worshipped on the earth." He continued calling upon his Lord with his hands outstretched, facing the qiblah, until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr came to him, took his cloak, placed it back upon his shoulders, then embraced him from behind and said: "O Prophet of Allah, your pleading with your Lord is enough, for He will surely fulfil for you what He has promised you." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you: "I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another"﴾. So Allah reinforced him with the angels. And he mentioned the hadith.

(Murdifin) with a fatha on the dal is the reading of Nafi'. The rest read it with a kasrah as an active participle, meaning "following one another," one group coming after another, and that is more awe-inspiring to the eyes. "Murdafin" with a fatha on the dal is in the passive form, because the people who fought on the day of Badr were "uridfu" (given a following) with a thousand angels, meaning they were sent down to them to help them against the disbelievers. So "murdafin" with a fatha on the dal is an adjective (na't) of "alf" (a thousand). It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the accusative in "mumiddukum," meaning "He reinforces you while you are being followed by a thousand angels," and this is the view of Mujahid. Abu 'Ubaydah related that "radifani" and "ardafani" have the same meaning. Abu 'Ubayd denied that "ardafa" means "radifa," saying: the words of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, "followed by the following (al-radifah)," do not say "al-murdifah." Al-Nahhas, Makki and others said: the reading with a kasrah on the dal is preferable, because the commentators on this reading interpret it as "some of them followed others," and because it carries the meaning of "opening" according to what Abu 'Ubaydah related, and because most of the readers follow it. Sibawayh said: Some read "murridifin" with a fatha on the ra' and a shaddah on the dal, some read "muridifin" with a kasrah on the ra', and some read "muriddifin" with a dammah on the ra'. The dal is kasrah and shaddah in all three readings. The first reading, according to Sibawayh, is originally "murtadifin," then the ta' was assimilated into the dal, and its vowel was moved onto the ra' so that two unvowelled consonants would not meet. In the second, the ra' was given a kasrah to avoid the meeting of two unvowelled consonants. In the third, the ra' was given a dammah to match the dammah of the mim, as you say: "radda, wa-rudda, wa-ridda" (O man). Ja'far ibn Muhammad and 'Asim al-Jahdari read "bi-alf" (in the plural), as the plural of "alf," like "fals" and "afluS." It is also related from both of them: "bi-alf" (singular). The mention of the descent of the angels, their marks and their fighting has already passed in Surat Al 'Imran. The statement concerning the meaning of His words "And Allah did not make it except as glad tidings" has also been discussed earlier there. What is meant here is reinforcement (al-imdad), and it is permissible that it be "al-irdaf" (following).

(And victory is only from Allah) He draws attention to the fact that victory is from Him, the Mighty and Majestic, not from the angels; that is, were it not for His help, no benefit would be gained from the large number of angels. Victory from Allah may come by the sword, and it may come by proof.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 11 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: (When He covers you with drowsiness) [[This is the reading of Nafi'.]] is two objects. It is the reading of the people of Medina, and it is good because the verb is attributed to Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, given the earlier mention of Him in His saying: "And victory is only from Allah."

And because after it comes "and He sends down upon you," so the verb is attributed to Allah, may He be mighty and majestic. Likewise, the covering is attributed to Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, so that the speech is consistent. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "yaghshakumu al-nu'as" (it covers you, drowsiness being the subject), attributing the verb to the drowsiness. Its evidence is "security, drowsiness that covers" [[See vol. 4, p. 241.]] in the reading of one who reads with the ya or with the ta, attributing the verb to the drowsiness or to the security. Security is drowsiness, so He informed that drowsiness is what covers the people. The rest read "yughashshikum" (with a fatha on the ghayn and a shadda on the shin), "al-nu'as" in the accusative, in the sense of Nafi''s reading. They are two dialects with the same meaning: ghashsha and aghsha. Allah, may He be exalted, said: "So We covered them" [[See vol. 15, p. 9.]]. And He said: "Then there covered them that which covered" [[See vol. 17, p. 118.]]. And He said: "As if their faces had been covered" [[See vol. 8, p. 332.]] [10:27].

Makki said: The preferred reading is with a damma on the ya and a shadda, and the accusative of "al-nu'as," because after it is "security from Him," and the pronoun in "minhu" [[60]] refers to Allah. So it is He who covers them with drowsiness, and because most readers follow it. It was also said: "security from the enemy," and "amanatan" is an object of purpose or a verbal noun. It is said: amina amanatan, amnan, and amanan, all are the same. Drowsiness is the state of one who is secure and fears nothing. This drowsiness occurred on the night before the battle, so sleep was remarkable given the important matter before them, but Allah steadied their hearts.

It is related from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "There was no horseman among us on the day of Badr except al-Miqdad on a piebald horse. We saw ourselves, and none of us was awake except the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was beneath a tree praying and weeping until morning." Al-Bayhaqi related it. [[In K and Ya: and al-Mawardi.]] Al-Mawardi said: Regarding Allah's favour upon them with sleep on this night, there are two aspects. First: that He strengthened them through rest for the fighting on the following day. Second: that He gave them security by removing terror from their hearts, as it is said: "Security causes sleep, and fear causes wakefulness." It was also said: He covered them at the time the two lines met. A similar matter was already discussed regarding the Day of Uhud in "Al 'Imran."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He sends down upon you water from the sky to purify you thereby and remove from you the defilement of Satan and to strengthen your hearts and plant firmly thereby the feet﴾. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that the drowsiness was before the rain. Ibn Abi Najih said: the rain was before the drowsiness. Al-Zajjaj related that the disbelievers on the day of Badr got to the water of Badr before the believers and camped by it, while the believers were left without water. Their souls were struck with fear, they became thirsty and needed ritual purification, and they prayed in that state. Some of them said to themselves, through Satan's insinuation: "We claim that we are the friends of Allah, and the Messenger is among us, and our state is this while the polytheists are at the water." So Allah sent down rain on the night of Badr, the seventeenth of Ramadan, until the valleys flowed. They drank, purified themselves, watered the camels, and the sabkha [[Sabkha (with a vowel): land with salt and brine. Here it means the ground in which feet sink.]] between them and the polytheists became packed so that the feet of the Muslims were firm during the fighting. It has been said that these conditions were before their arrival at Badr, and this is more sound, and it is what Ibn Ishaq mentioned in his Sira and others. Here is its summary: Ibn 'Abbas said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was informed about Abu Sufyan, that he was coming from Syria, he called the Muslims to them and said: "This is the caravan of Quraysh, carrying the wealth. Go out to them, perhaps Allah will grant you it as spoils." He said: Those who were light-hearted set out with him, and some were burdened and disliked going out. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ hastened, not turning toward those who were excused, nor waiting for those who had fallen behind. He marched with three hundred and thirteen of his companions, from the Emigrants and the Helpers.

In al-Bukhari, on the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: The Emigrants on the day of Badr were a little over eighty, and the Helpers were a little over two hundred and forty. He also related from him, who said: We used to say that the companions of Muhammad ﷺ were three hundred and a few more, equal to the number of the companions of Talut who crossed the river with him, and none crossed with him except a believer. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned on the authority of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who said: We went out, meaning to Badr, and when we had travelled a day or two, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered us to count ourselves, so we did, and we were three hundred and thirteen men. We informed the Prophet ﷺ of our number, and he was pleased, praised Allah, and said: "The number of the companions of Talut." Ibn Ishaq said: All the people had thought that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would not face battle, so their preparation was not great. Abu Sufyan, when he drew near the Hijaz, was spying for news and questioning whoever he met of the riders, out of fear for the people's wealth, until he obtained news from some riders that Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, had called the people to march against you. He became wary at that, and hired Damdam ibn 'Amr al-Ghifari and sent him to Makkah, ordering him to come to Quraysh, calling them to defend their wealth and informing them that Muhammad ﷺ had set upon it with his companions. Damdam did so. The people of Makkah went out, about a thousand men or so, and the Prophet ﷺ went out with his companions. News came to him of Quraysh's departure to protect their caravan, so the Prophet ﷺ consulted the people. Abu Bakr stood and spoke well, and 'Umar stood and spoke well. Then al-Miqdad ibn 'Amr stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah, proceed as Allah has commanded you, for we are with you. By Allah, we will not say as the Children of Israel said: 'So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here' [5:24]. Rather, go, you and your Lord, and fight, and we are fighting with you. By the One who sent you with the truth, if you were to travel to Bark al-Ghimad, meaning the city of Abyssinia, we would fight alongside you against whatever is before it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pleased with that and supplicated for him with good. Then he said: "Advise me, O people," meaning the Helpers, for they were the majority of the people. When they pledged to him at al-'Aqaba they had said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are free of your covenant until you reach our homes. When you arrive among us, you are under our protection, and we will protect you from what we protect ourselves, our sons and our women." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ feared that the Helpers might think their support was owed only in Medina, and that they were not obliged to march him against an enemy outside their lands. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh spoke, though it was said it was Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, and it is possible that both spoke that day. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, do you mean us, the group of the Helpers?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Yes." He said: "We have believed in you and followed you, so proceed as Allah has commanded you. By the One who sent you with the truth, if you were to lead us into this sea and plunge into it, we would plunge with you." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Proceed in the blessing of Allah, for I seem to see the places where the people will fall." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ proceeded and got ahead of Quraysh to the water of Badr. A great rain sent down on them by Allah prevented Quraysh from reaching it first, and it did not befall the Muslims except enough to firm the sand of the valley and help them march. The dahs is soft sand in which feet sink. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stopped at the nearest water to Medina among the waters of Badr. Al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh advised him otherwise and said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me, is this a station that Allah has brought you to, so that we may not advance beyond it or fall back from it, or is it opinion, war and strategy?" He said, peace be upon him: "Rather, it is opinion, war and strategy." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is not a station for you. Move us to the nearest water to the enemy, and let us stop there and block up the wells behind it [[To block the springs of water is to bury and seal them.]], then build a basin over it, fill it, and drink while they do not drink." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ approved of this opinion and did it. Then they met, and Allah gave victory to His Prophet and the Muslims. He killed seventy of the polytheists and took seventy prisoners, and He avenged the believers upon them, and Allah healed the chests of His Messenger, peace be upon him, and the chests of his companions from their rage. Concerning that, Hassan said:

I recognised the dwellings of Zaynab at the sand-hill, like the writing of revelation on fresh parchment [[Al-wahy: writing. Al-qashib: new.]]
The winds have passed over them, and every dark cloud of the spring rain, pouring and abundant.
Its dwellings became ruins, and its open lands became waste after its beloved inhabitant.
So leave off remembering every day, and turn back the heat of the grieving breast [[Al-ka'ib: sorrowful.]].
And tell of what has no fault in it, truthfully, not the report of a liar.
Of what God did on the morning of Badr, for us, of the share against the polytheists.
A morning when Hira seemed to gather them, its pillars showing at the edge of sunset [[Al-Jawb: the surface of the earth.]].
We met them from among us with a host like lions of the thicket, young and old.
In front of Muhammad, they supported him against the enemies in the heat of wars.
In their hands were keen swords, and every experienced one, thick of joints.
The noble Aws, who supported them, and the Banu al-Najjar in the firm religion.
So we left Abu Jahl fallen, and 'Utba, whom we left on the face of the earth.
And Shayba whom we left among men of lineage, who, when named, are honoured.
The Messenger of Allah called to them when we flung them, in heaps, into the well.
Did you not find my words to be true, and the command of Allah that takes hold of hearts?
They did not speak, and had they spoken they would have said: you were right, and you were a man of sound opinion.

Here there are three issues.

The first: Malik said, "It has reached me that Jibril (peace be upon him) said to the Prophet (ﷺ), 'How do you regard the people of Badr among you?' He said, 'They are our best.' He said, 'They are likewise among us.'" This indicates that the nobility of created beings lies not in their essences but in their deeds. The angels have their noble deeds, such as their constant glorification of God (tasbih). We have our deeds, through sincere obedience. Acts of obedience differ in excellence according to the excellence assigned to them by the Law (shar'). The best of them is jihad (struggle in the way of God), and the best jihad was the day of Badr, because the foundation of Islam was built upon it.

The second: The Prophet's (ﷺ) going out to intercept the caravan indicates the permissibility of going forth (nafir) for booty (ghanimah), because it is lawful earning. This refutes what Malik disliked of that, when he said, "That is fighting for worldly gain." What has come, that whoever fights so that the word of God is supreme is in the way of God, in contrast to one who fights for booty, is to be understood as referring to a case where his intention is for that alone and the religion has no share in it.

Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) finished with Badr, they said to him, "Pursue the caravan; nothing stands between you and it." Al-Abbas, who was among the captives, called out, "This is not appropriate." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "Why?" He said, "Because God promised you one of the two groups, and God has given you what He promised you." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "You have spoken truly." Al-Abbas knew this from the narrations of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and from what had occurred concerning Badr, so he heard this in the course of the account.

The third: Muslim narrated from Anas ibn Malik that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) left the slain of Badr for three days, then stood over them and called out to them, saying: "O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham! O Umayyah ibn Khalaf! O Utbah ibn Rabi'ah! O Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah! Have you not found what your Lord promised to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true." Umar heard the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, "O Messenger of God, how can they hear, and how can they answer, when they have decayed?" He said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, you are no more able to hear what I say than they are, but they are not able to answer." Then he gave orders concerning them, and they were dragged and thrown into the well (al-qalib), the well of Badr.

"Jayyafu" with a fatha on the jim and the ya means that they became putrid and turned into carrion (jiyaf). Umar's saying "How can they hear?" expresses astonishment at what is customary. The Prophet (ﷺ) answered him that they hear as the living hear. In this there is an indication that death is not pure non-existence or mere annihilation, but rather the severing of the soul's attachment to the body and its separation from it, a barrier between the two, a change of state and a transfer from one abode to another. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, when the deceased is placed in his grave and his companions turn away from him, he surely hears the sound of their sandals," and the hadith (continues). It was narrated by the Sahih.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that He may make firm the feet thereby﴾. The pronoun in "thereby" refers to the water which firmed the sand of the valley, as has been mentioned. It was also said that it refers to the binding of hearts, so that making the feet firm is an expression for victory and support in the place of battle.

In the Qur'an's words, ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "Indeed I am with you"﴾. The element that governs "idh" (when) is "yuthabbit" (He makes firm), meaning: He makes the feet firm by it at that time. It is also said that the governing element is "liyarbit" (so that He may bind), meaning: and so that He may bind [the hearts] at the time He revealed. It may also be that the implied sense is: "Remember when your Lord revealed to the angels, 'Indeed I am with you'," in a position of accusative (naṣb), and the meaning is: "that I am with you," i.e., with victory and help. "Ma'akum" (with you) with a fatha on the ʿayn is an adverb of place (ẓarf); whoever reads it with a sukun considers it a particle (ḥarf).

﴿So make firm those who believe﴾: that is, give them good news of victory, or of fighting alongside them, or of being present with them without fighting. The angel would walk in front of the row in the form of a man and say: "Advance, for Allah is your helper." The Muslims would think he was one of them. It has already been mentioned in the commentary on Āl ʿImrān [[See vol. 4, pp. 190, 232.]] that the angels fought on that day. They would see heads falling from necks without any striker being seen. Some of them heard a speaker whose voice was heard but whose person was not seen say: "Advance, Ḥayzūm!" [[Ḥayzūm: the name of a horse among the horses of the angels.]] It is also said that this "making firm" was the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informing the believers of the descent of the angels as reinforcement.

﴿I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾: its explanation has already been given in Āl ʿImrān.

﴿So strike above the necks﴾: this command is addressed to the angels. It is also said it is addressed to the believers, meaning "strike the necks," and "above" (fawq) is superfluous; this was said by al-Akhfash, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and ʿAṭiyya. Al-Mas'ūdī narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was not sent to punish with the punishment of Allah, but I was sent to strike necks and to tighten bonds." Muḥammad ibn Yazīd said: this is an error, because "fawq" conveys a meaning, so it cannot be superfluous; rather the meaning is that they were permitted to strike the faces and what is near them. Ibn ʿAbbās said: every skull and cranium. It is also said: that is, what is above the necks, which is the heads, as ʿIkrima said. Striking the head is more forceful, because the slightest blow affects the brain. Some of this meaning has already passed in "al-Nisā'" and that "fawq" is not superfluous, at the words: "above two" [[See vol. 5, p. 63.]].

﴿And strike from them every fingertip﴾. Al-Zajjāj said: the singular of "banān" is "bananah," and here it means the fingers and other limbs. "Banān" is derived from the expression "abana al-rajul bi-al-makān," meaning when a man settled in a place. So the "banān" is that by which one performs what is needed for settling and life. It is also said: what is meant here by "banān" is the tips of the fingers of the hands and feet. It is a metaphor for steadfastness in war and the place of striking; when the banān of the one struck is struck, fighting is disabled for him, unlike other limbs. ʿAntara said:

*And the hero of the battle who protects its honour / and strikes at the moment of distress every banān*

Among what shows that "banān" means fingers is also ʿAntara's saying:

*And death is subservient to my hand when / I join its banān with the Hindi sword*

This usage is common in Arabic poetry. Al-Banān means the fingers. Ibn Fāris said: al-banān is the fingers, and it is also said: the extremities. Some have mentioned that they were called banān because the welfare of the states by which a person settles and stays depends on them. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: al-banān is every joint.

"لِكَ

It stands in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and the implied construction is: that is the matter, or the matter is that."اقُّوا اللَّهَ

That is, His allies. And shiqaq (opposition) means that each party goes to one side. It has already been discussed [see vol. 2, p. 143].

(ذلِكُمْ فَذُوقُوهُ وَأَنَّ لِلْكافِرِينَ عَذابَ النَّارِ) ﴿That, so taste it, and that for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "dhalikum" is in the nominative position, with an implied "the matter" or "the story": the matter is that, so taste it. It may also be in the accusative position, governed by "dhuqu" (taste), as in your saying: Zayd, so strike him. The meaning of the speech is a rebuke of the disbelievers. "Wa-anna" is in the nominative position, conjoined to "dhalikum." Al-Farra' said: It may also be in the accusative position, with the sense of "and [know] that for the disbelievers." He said: It may also be that "wa-i'lamu anna" (and know that) is implied. Al-Zajjaj said: If it were permissible to imply "wa-i'lamu," it would be permissible to say "Zayd munṭaliq wa-'Amran jalisan," rather it would be permissible at the beginning to say "Zaydan munṭaliqan," because the informant is informing; and no grammarian says this.
