There are seven issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words ﴿zahfan﴾ (in a advancing mass). Al-zahf is drawing near little by little. Its origin is pushing oneself forward on the buttocks, and then every one who walks in war toward another is called zahif (advancing). Al-tazahuf is drawing close and approaching one another; it is said: zahafa ila al-'aduww zahfan (he advanced upon the enemy in a mass), and izdahafa al-qawm, meaning some of them walked toward others. From this comes zihaf al-shi'r (zihaf in poetry), which is when a letter falls out between two letters and one of them creeps toward the other. The meaning is: when you approach one another and see each other, do not flee from them, and do not turn your backs to them. God forbade this to the believers when He prescribed jihad and fighting against the disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-adbar is the plural of dubr. The expression "dubr" in this verse has an eloquent force, because it is repugnant to the one who flees and condemns him.

The second: God, Mighty and Majestic, commanded in this verse that the believers not turn their backs before the disbelievers. This command is restricted by the condition stated concerning [a ratio of] two to one of the believers [[In b, j, h, k: "believing women."]], so if a band of believers meets a band that is double the believers [[In j, h: "before."]] of the polytheists, the obligation is that they not flee before them. Whoever flees from two is a fleer from the zahf. Whoever flees from three is not a fleer from the zahf, and the threat does not apply to him. Fleeing is a destructive major sin according to the apparent sense of the Qur'an and the consensus of the majority of the imams. A group among them, including Ibn al-Majishun in al-Wadiha, said: the weakness, strength and numbers are to be taken into account, so on their view it is permissible for a hundred horsemen to flee from a hundred horsemen if they know that what the polytheists possess of valor and courage is double what they have. As for the opinion of the majority, fleeing by a hundred is not lawful except from more than two hundred; so whenever there are more than two against one Muslim, fleeing is permitted, though steadfastness is better. The army of Mu'tah stood firm, being three thousand, against two hundred thousand, of whom one hundred thousand were Romans and one hundred thousand were Arabized tribes from Lakhm and Judham. I say: it is recorded in the history of the conquest of al-Andalus that Tariq, the client of Musa ibn Nusayr, marched with seventeen hundred men into al-Andalus, in Rajab of the year 93 AH. He met Ludhariq, the king of al-Andalus, who had seventy thousand squadrons. Tariq advanced upon him and stood firm, so God defeated the tyrant Ludhariq, and the conquest came about. Ibn Wahb said: I heard Malik being asked about people who meet the enemy, or who are in a guard post watching, when the enemy comes upon them while they are few: do they fight or withdraw and inform their companions? He said: if they are able to fight them, they fight them; otherwise they withdraw to their companions and inform them.

The third: People have differed as to whether fleeing on the day of the zahf is specific to the day of Badr or is general for all engagements until the Day of Resurrection. It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that this was specific to the day of Badr, and this was said by Nafi', al-Hasan, Qatadah, Yazid ibn Abi Habib and al-Dahhak, and Abu Hanifa also said it. The argument is that it was specific to the people of Badr: they were not permitted to withdraw, for if they had withdrawn they would have withdrawn to the polytheists, and there were no Muslims on earth that day other than them, and the Muslims had no fi'a except the Prophet ﷺ; but after that, some of them are a fi'a for others. Ilkiya said: this is open to question, for in Medina there was a large group of the Ansar whom the Prophet ﷺ had not ordered to go out, and they did not regard it as a battle; they thought it was only the caravan, so the Messenger of God ﷺ went out with those who were light (ready) with him. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and the rest of the scholars that the verse remains in force until the Day of Resurrection. The first group argued with what we have mentioned, and with God's words "that day" (yawma'idhin), saying: it is a reference to the day of Badr, and that the ruling of the verse was abrogated by the verse of the ratio. The ruling on fleeing from the zahf remains that it is not a major sin. The people fled on the day of Uhud and God pardoned them, and God said concerning them on the day of Hunayn: "Then you turned back, retreating" [[See vol. 8, p. 96.]], and no rebuke followed on that. The majority of scholars said: that is only a reference to the day of zahf that is contained in God's words: ﴿when you meet﴾. The ruling of the verse remains until the Day of Resurrection, subject to the condition of the ratio that God explained in another verse, and there is no abrogation in the verse. The evidence for this is that the verse was revealed after the fighting, after the battle had ended and the day had passed with what it contained. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and most scholars. In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins," and among them "turning away on the day of the zahf." This is a clear text on the matter. As for the day of Uhud, the people fled from more than double their number, and despite that they were rebuked. As for the day of Hunayn, likewise, whoever fled did so when the numbers had overwhelmed them, as will be explained.

The fourth: Ibn al-Qasim said: the testimony of one who fled from the zahf is not valid, and it is not permissible for them to flee even if their leader flees; and "whoever turns his back to them on that day" is the verse. He said: fleeing from more than double their number is permitted, as long as the number of Muslims has not reached twelve thousand. If it reaches twelve thousand, fleeing is not lawful for them even if the number of polytheists exceeds double, because of the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Twelve thousand will never be defeated for lack of numbers." Most scholars specified this number by this hadith from the general wording of the verse. I say: it was narrated by Abu Bishr and Abu Salamah al-'Amili, who is al-Hakam ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Khattaf, and he is abandoned (matruk). They both said: al-Zuhri narrated to us from Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "O Aktham ibn al-Jawn, campaign with people other than your own folk, your character will be good and you will be honored among your companions. O Aktham ibn al-Jawn, the best companions are four, the best vanguards are forty, the best detachments are four hundred, the best armies are four thousand, and twelve thousand will never be overcome for lack of numbers." It is also narrated from Malik something indicating this in his view: his saying to al-'Umari the worshipper [[Al-'Umari (with a dammah on the 'ayn and a fathah on the mim) is 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar al-'Aziz ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who was among the most ascetic people of his time. He died in 184 AH (from the Ansab of al-Sam'ani).]] when he asked him: "Do you have leeway in not striving against those who alter the rulings and change them?" He said: "If you have twelve thousand with you, then you have no leeway in that."

The fifth: If he flees, then let him seek God's forgiveness. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Bilal ibn Yasar ibn Zayd, who said: my father told me from my grandfather, who heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Whoever says, 'I seek forgiveness from God, besides whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and I turn to Him in repentance,' will be forgiven by God, even if he has fled from the zahf." He said: this is a gharib hadith, which we do not know except through this chain.

The sixth: God's words ﴿except one who swerves to fight or one who withdraws to a company﴾. Al-tahharuf is departing from the straight direction. So one who moves from side to side for the stratagems of war is not a fugitive, and likewise one who withdraws intending to join a company of Muslims in order to seek their help, then returns to the fighting, is also not a fugitive. Abu Dawud narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that he was in one of the detachments of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he said: "the people scattered in confusion (hasa haisa), and I was among those who scattered. When we emerged we said: how shall we act, since we have fled from the zahf and incurred God's anger? We said: let us enter Medina, settle there and go away, and no one will see us. He said: so we entered and said: let us present ourselves to the Messenger of God ﷺ; if there is repentance for us we will remain, and if not we will leave. He said: so we sat before the Messenger of God ﷺ before the dawn prayer, and when he came out we stood up before him and said: we are the fleers (farrarun). He turned to us and said: 'No, rather you are the 'akkarun (those who return).' He said: so we drew near and kissed his hand. He said: 'I am the fi'a of the Muslims.'" Tha'lab said: al-'akkarun are those who turn back. Others said: a man who turns away in battle and then charges back returning is called 'akkara and i'takara. Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim who said: a man fled from al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina and said: "O Commander of the Believers, I am ruined! I have fled from the zahf." 'Umar said: "I am your fi'a." Muhammad ibn Sirin said: when Abu 'Ubaydah was killed, the news reached 'Umar, and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a fi'a for him; for I am the fi'a of every Muslim." On these hadiths, fleeing is not a major sin, because the fi'a here means Medina, the imam, and the body of Muslims wherever they are. On the other view, it is a major sin, because the fi'a there means the group of people present for the battle. This is according to the view of the majority that fleeing from the zahf is a major sin. They said: that statement from the Prophet ﷺ and 'Umar was by way of caution for the believers, since in that era they would stand firm against their multiples many times over. And God knows best. His saying "and turning away on the day of the zahf" is sufficient.

The seventh: God's words ﴿then he has earned anger from God﴾: that is, he deserved the anger. The root of "ba'a" is to return, and it has been discussed before [[See vol. 1, p. 430.]].

(And his refuge is Hell) that is, his abode. This does not indicate eternity, as has been explained in more than one place. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever says, 'I seek forgiveness from God, besides whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Subsisting,' will be forgiven, even if he has fled from the zahf."

There are seven issues in this verse.

The first concerns God's words ﴿zahfan﴾ (in a advancing mass). Al-zahf is drawing near little by little. Its origin is pushing oneself forward on the buttocks, and then every one who walks in war toward another is called zahif (advancing). Al-tazahuf is drawing close and approaching one another; it is said: zahafa ila al-'aduww zahfan (he advanced upon the enemy in a mass), and izdahafa al-qawm, meaning some of them walked toward others. From this comes zihaf al-shi'r (zihaf in poetry), which is when a letter falls out between two letters and one of them creeps toward the other. The meaning is: when you approach one another and see each other, do not flee from them, and do not turn your backs to them. God forbade this to the believers when He prescribed jihad and fighting against the disbelievers. Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-adbar is the plural of dubr. The expression "dubr" in this verse has an eloquent force, because it is repugnant to the one who flees and condemns him.

The second: God, Mighty and Majestic, commanded in this verse that the believers not turn their backs before the disbelievers. This command is restricted by the condition stated concerning [a ratio of] two to one of the believers [[In b, j, h, k: "believing women."]], so if a band of believers meets a band that is double the believers [[In j, h: "before."]] of the polytheists, the obligation is that they not flee before them. Whoever flees from two is a fleer from the zahf. Whoever flees from three is not a fleer from the zahf, and the threat does not apply to him. Fleeing is a destructive major sin according to the apparent sense of the Qur'an and the consensus of the majority of the imams. A group among them, including Ibn al-Majishun in al-Wadiha, said: the weakness, strength and numbers are to be taken into account, so on their view it is permissible for a hundred horsemen to flee from a hundred horsemen if they know that what the polytheists possess of valor and courage is double what they have. As for the opinion of the majority, fleeing by a hundred is not lawful except from more than two hundred; so whenever there are more than two against one Muslim, fleeing is permitted, though steadfastness is better. The army of Mu'tah stood firm, being three thousand, against two hundred thousand, of whom one hundred thousand were Romans and one hundred thousand were Arabized tribes from Lakhm and Judham. I say: it is recorded in the history of the conquest of al-Andalus that Tariq, the client of Musa ibn Nusayr, marched with seventeen hundred men into al-Andalus, in Rajab of the year 93 AH. He met Ludhariq, the king of al-Andalus, who had seventy thousand squadrons. Tariq advanced upon him and stood firm, so God defeated the tyrant Ludhariq, and the conquest came about. Ibn Wahb said: I heard Malik being asked about people who meet the enemy, or who are in a guard post watching, when the enemy comes upon them while they are few: do they fight or withdraw and inform their companions? He said: if they are able to fight them, they fight them; otherwise they withdraw to their companions and inform them.

The third: People have differed as to whether fleeing on the day of the zahf is specific to the day of Badr or is general for all engagements until the Day of Resurrection. It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that this was specific to the day of Badr, and this was said by Nafi', al-Hasan, Qatadah, Yazid ibn Abi Habib and al-Dahhak, and Abu Hanifa also said it. The argument is that it was specific to the people of Badr: they were not permitted to withdraw, for if they had withdrawn they would have withdrawn to the polytheists, and there were no Muslims on earth that day other than them, and the Muslims had no fi'a except the Prophet ﷺ; but after that, some of them are a fi'a for others. Ilkiya said: this is open to question, for in Medina there was a large group of the Ansar whom the Prophet ﷺ had not ordered to go out, and they did not regard it as a battle; they thought it was only the caravan, so the Messenger of God ﷺ went out with those who were light (ready) with him. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and the rest of the scholars that the verse remains in force until the Day of Resurrection. The first group argued with what we have mentioned, and with God's words "that day" (yawma'idhin), saying: it is a reference to the day of Badr, and that the ruling of the verse was abrogated by the verse of the ratio. The ruling on fleeing from the zahf remains that it is not a major sin. The people fled on the day of Uhud and God pardoned them, and God said concerning them on the day of Hunayn: "Then you turned back, retreating" [[See vol. 8, p. 96.]], and no rebuke followed on that. The majority of scholars said: that is only a reference to the day of zahf that is contained in God's words: ﴿when you meet﴾. The ruling of the verse remains until the Day of Resurrection, subject to the condition of the ratio that God explained in another verse, and there is no abrogation in the verse. The evidence for this is that the verse was revealed after the fighting, after the battle had ended and the day had passed with what it contained. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i and most scholars. In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Avoid the seven destructive sins," and among them "turning away on the day of the zahf." This is a clear text on the matter. As for the day of Uhud, the people fled from more than double their number, and despite that they were rebuked. As for the day of Hunayn, likewise, whoever fled did so when the numbers had overwhelmed them, as will be explained.

The fourth: Ibn al-Qasim said: the testimony of one who fled from the zahf is not valid, and it is not permissible for them to flee even if their leader flees; and "whoever turns his back to them on that day" is the verse. He said: fleeing from more than double their number is permitted, as long as the number of Muslims has not reached twelve thousand. If it reaches twelve thousand, fleeing is not lawful for them even if the number of polytheists exceeds double, because of the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Twelve thousand will never be defeated for lack of numbers." Most scholars specified this number by this hadith from the general wording of the verse. I say: it was narrated by Abu Bishr and Abu Salamah al-'Amili, who is al-Hakam ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Khattaf, and he is abandoned (matruk). They both said: al-Zuhri narrated to us from Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: "O Aktham ibn al-Jawn, campaign with people other than your own folk, your character will be good and you will be honored among your companions. O Aktham ibn al-Jawn, the best companions are four, the best vanguards are forty, the best detachments are four hundred, the best armies are four thousand, and twelve thousand will never be overcome for lack of numbers." It is also narrated from Malik something indicating this in his view: his saying to al-'Umari the worshipper [[Al-'Umari (with a dammah on the 'ayn and a fathah on the mim) is 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar al-'Aziz ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who was among the most ascetic people of his time. He died in 184 AH (from the Ansab of al-Sam'ani).]] when he asked him: "Do you have leeway in not striving against those who alter the rulings and change them?" He said: "If you have twelve thousand with you, then you have no leeway in that."

The fifth: If he flees, then let him seek God's forgiveness. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Bilal ibn Yasar ibn Zayd, who said: my father told me from my grandfather, who heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Whoever says, 'I seek forgiveness from God, besides whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and I turn to Him in repentance,' will be forgiven by God, even if he has fled from the zahf." He said: this is a gharib hadith, which we do not know except through this chain.

The sixth: God's words ﴿except one who swerves to fight or one who withdraws to a company﴾. Al-tahharuf is departing from the straight direction. So one who moves from side to side for the stratagems of war is not a fugitive, and likewise one who withdraws intending to join a company of Muslims in order to seek their help, then returns to the fighting, is also not a fugitive. Abu Dawud narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar that he was in one of the detachments of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he said: "the people scattered in confusion (hasa haisa), and I was among those who scattered. When we emerged we said: how shall we act, since we have fled from the zahf and incurred God's anger? We said: let us enter Medina, settle there and go away, and no one will see us. He said: so we entered and said: let us present ourselves to the Messenger of God ﷺ; if there is repentance for us we will remain, and if not we will leave. He said: so we sat before the Messenger of God ﷺ before the dawn prayer, and when he came out we stood up before him and said: we are the fleers (farrarun). He turned to us and said: 'No, rather you are the 'akkarun (those who return).' He said: so we drew near and kissed his hand. He said: 'I am the fi'a of the Muslims.'" Tha'lab said: al-'akkarun are those who turn back. Others said: a man who turns away in battle and then charges back returning is called 'akkara and i'takara. Jarir narrated from Mansur from Ibrahim who said: a man fled from al-Qadisiyya and came to 'Umar in Medina and said: "O Commander of the Believers, I am ruined! I have fled from the zahf." 'Umar said: "I am your fi'a." Muhammad ibn Sirin said: when Abu 'Ubaydah was killed, the news reached 'Umar, and he said: "If he had withdrawn to me, I would have been a fi'a for him; for I am the fi'a of every Muslim." On these hadiths, fleeing is not a major sin, because the fi'a here means Medina, the imam, and the body of Muslims wherever they are. On the other view, it is a major sin, because the fi'a there means the group of people present for the battle. This is according to the view of the majority that fleeing from the zahf is a major sin. They said: that statement from the Prophet ﷺ and 'Umar was by way of caution for the believers, since in that era they would stand firm against their multiples many times over. And God knows best. His saying "and turning away on the day of the zahf" is sufficient.

The seventh: God's words ﴿then he has earned anger from God﴾: that is, he deserved the anger. The root of "ba'a" is to return, and it has been discussed before [[See vol. 1, p. 430.]].

(And his refuge is Hell) that is, his abode. This does not indicate eternity, as has been explained in more than one place. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever says, 'I seek forgiveness from God, besides whom there is no god, the Living, the Self-Subsisting,' will be forgiven, even if he has fled from the zahf."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 17–18:

Allah's words, ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾, i.e., on the day of Badr. It is narrated that when the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from Badr, each of them recounted what he had done: "I killed so-and-so, I did such-and-such," and so boasting and the like arose among them. Then the verse was revealed to inform them that Allah, exalted is He, is the one who causes death and decrees all things, and that the servant only takes part through his acquisition (kasb) and intention. This verse refutes those who say that the actions of servants are created for them. It was said: the meaning is, "So you did not kill them, but Allah killed them by driving them toward you until He enabled you over them." And it was said: "But Allah killed them" by means of the angels whom He sent to reinforce you.

﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ is similar to this: "but Allah threw." The scholars differed about this throwing, in four opinions:

The first: this throwing was at the pebbling (hasb) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Hunayn. This was related by Ibn Wahb from Malik. Malik said: "On that day no one remained who was not struck by that." Ibn al-Qasim also related this from him.

The second: this was on the day of Uhud, when he (ﷺ) struck Ubayy ibn Khalaf in the neck with a spear, and Ubayy turned back fleeing. The polytheists said to him, "By Allah, there is nothing wrong with you." He said, "By Allah, if he had spat on me it would have killed me. Did he not say, 'Rather, I will kill him'?" Ubayy had threatened the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with death in Makkah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to him, "Rather, I will kill you." The enemy of Allah died from the blow of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on his return to Makkah, at a place called Sarif. Musa ibn Uqbah related from Ibn Shihab: When the day of Uhud came, Ubayy approached, covered in iron armor on his horse, saying, "I will not be saved if Muhammad is saved," and he charged at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intending to kill him. Musa ibn Uqbah said, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: Some of the believers intercepted him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered them, so they cleared his path. Mus'ab ibn Umayr met him, protecting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Mus'ab ibn Umayr was killed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Ubayy ibn Khalaf's collarbone through a gap between the full helmet and the coat of mail, and he thrust at him with his spear, and Ubayy fell from his horse, and no blood came out from his wound. Sa'id said: He broke one of his ribs, and [Ubayy] said, "In that this was revealed: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾." But this is weak, because the verse was revealed after Badr.

The third: the intended throwing is the arrow that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) shot at the fortress of Khaybar, which flew through the air until it struck Ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. This is also invalid, and Khaybar and its conquest are much further from Uhud. The correct account of the killing of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq is other than this.

The fourth: it was on the day of Badr, said Ibn Ishaq. This is the most sound, because the surah is a Badr surah. That is because Jibril (peace be upon him) said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Take a handful of dust," so he took a handful of dust and threw it at their faces, and there was not one of the polytheists who did not have dust from that handful in his eyes, nostrils and mouth. Ibn Abbas also said this, and it will come later.

Tha'lab said: The meaning of "you did not throw" is the terror and fear in their hearts, "when you threw" with pebbles, and so they fled. "But Allah threw" means He helped you and granted you victory. The Arabs say, "Allah threw for you," meaning He helped you, granted you victory and arranged things for you. Abu Ubaydah related this in Kitab al-Majaz. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "You did not throw by your own strength when you threw, but you threw by the strength of Allah."

﴿And that He might test the believers with a good test from Him﴾. Al-bala' here means blessing. The lam is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "and that He might test the believers, He did that."

﴿That, and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾. This is the reading of the people of the two Sanctuaries and Abu Amr. The reading of the people of Kufa is ﴿mu'hinu kaydi al-kafirin﴾ (with the form of the verb "awhana"). In the doubled form there is a sense of intensity. It is narrated from al-Hasan "mu'hinu kaydi" with idafa and lightening, and this reading is that of Asim, the narration of Hafs. The meaning: Allah, mighty and majestic, casts terror into their hearts until they scatter and their gathering breaks up and they become weak. Al-kayd means plotting, and it has been discussed before.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 19:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿If you seek a decision, then the decision has certainly come to you﴾. Its condition and its answer. In it there are three opinions. It is addressed to the disbelievers, because they sought a decision and said: "O Allah, sever the ties of kinship for us and wrong the one of us who is more wrongful to his companion, so give victory to him over him." This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid and others. This statement of theirs was made at the time they went out to support the caravan. It was also said that Abu Jahl said it at the time of fighting. And al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment." He was among those killed at Badr. And al-istiftah (seeking a decision) means seeking victory. That is, "the decision has certainly come to you," but it was for the Muslims against you; that is, there has come to you what made the matter clear and revealed the truth to you. ﴿And if you desist﴾ (that is, [[from h, w, j, b.]]) from disbelief, ﴿it is better for you﴾.

﴿And if you return﴾, that is, to this statement and to fighting Muhammad.

﴿We will return﴾ to the support of the believers.

﴿And your company will avail you nothing﴾, that is (from [[from j.]]) your group, ﴿at all﴾.

﴿Even if it is numerous﴾, that is, in number.

The second opinion: it is addressed to the believers, meaning: if you seek help, then help has certainly come to you. And if you ﴿desist﴾, that is, from the like of what you did of taking spoils and captives before permission, ﴿it is better for you﴾. And ﴿if you return﴾, that is, to the like of that, ﴿We will return﴾ to rebuke you, as He said: ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded﴾ the verse [[See vol. 8, p. 50.]].

The third opinion: that ﴿If you seek a decision, then the decision has certainly come to you﴾ is addressed to the believers, and what follows it is addressed to the disbelievers, meaning: and if you return to fighting, We will return to the like of the event of Badr. Al-Qushayri said: The correct view is that it is addressed to the disbelievers, for when they set out to support the caravan, they clung to the curtains of the Ka'bah and said: "O Allah, give victory to the more rightly guided of the two parties and the better of the two religions." Al-Mahdawi said: It is narrated that the polytheists went out with them carrying the curtains of the Ka'bah, seeking a decision by them, that is, seeking victory. I say: There is no contradiction, since it is possible that they did both.

﴿And that Allah is with the believers﴾ with a kasra on the alif as a new sentence, and with a fatha as a conjunction with His words: ﴿and that Allah weakens the plot of the disbelievers﴾, or upon His words: ﴿that I am with you﴾. The meaning: "and because Allah," the implied sense being "because of its numerousness," and that Allah, that is, whoever has Allah in his support, will not be overcome by a company, even if it is numerous.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 20:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ [8:20]. The address is to the believers who affirm (the truth). He addressed them directly, without the hypocrites, out of honouring them. Allah renewed for them the command to obey Allah and the Messenger, and forbade them from turning away from it. This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). A group said: the address in this verse is in fact to the hypocrites, and the meaning is: O you who have believed with their tongues only. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This, although it is possible if far-fetched, is very weak, because Allah, may He be exalted, described those He addressed in this verse with faith, and faith is affirmation (tasdiq), while the hypocrites are not characterised by any affirmation whatsoever." Even further removed than this is the one who said: the address is to the Children of Israel, for it is unrelated to the verse.

(And do not turn away from him) [8:20]. Al-tawalli is al-i'rad (turning away). He said "from him" (ʿanhu) and did not say "from both of them" (ʿanhuma), because obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah; this is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [9:62]. (See vol. 8, p. 193 onwards.)

(And you hear) [8:20]. It is a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The meaning: while you hear what is recited to you of the proofs and evidences in the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear,"﴾ That is, like the Jews, or the hypocrites, or the polytheists. And this is from hearing with the ear.

(﴿while they do not hear﴾) That is, they do not contemplate what they heard, nor do they reflect upon it, so they are in the position of one who did not hear and turned away from the truth. He forbade the believers from being like them. The verse thus indicates that the statement of a believer, "I heard and I obeyed," has no benefit unless its effect appears upon him through carrying out the act. If he falls short in the commands, not doing them, and relies on the prohibitions, plunging into them, then what hearing does he have, and what obedience! He is then only in the position of the hypocrite who displays faith and conceals disbelief. This is what is meant by His saying: "And do not be like those who said, 'We hear,' while they do not hear." By this is meant the hypocrites, or the Jews, or the polytheists, as mentioned earlier. Then He, exalted is He, informed that the disbelievers are the worst of what crawls upon the earth. In al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, "Indeed the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and dumb who do not reason," he said: they are a group from the Banu Abd al-Dar. The original form is "asharr" (the superlative of "sharr," evil); the hamza was dropped due to frequent usage. Likewise "khayr" (good); its original form is "akhyar."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who said, "We hear,"﴾ That is, like the Jews, or the hypocrites, or the polytheists. And this is from hearing with the ear.

(﴿while they do not hear﴾) That is, they do not contemplate what they heard, nor do they reflect upon it, so they are in the position of one who did not hear and turned away from the truth. He forbade the believers from being like them. The verse thus indicates that the statement of a believer, "I heard and I obeyed," has no benefit unless its effect appears upon him through carrying out the act. If he falls short in the commands, not doing them, and relies on the prohibitions, plunging into them, then what hearing does he have, and what obedience! He is then only in the position of the hypocrite who displays faith and conceals disbelief. This is what is meant by His saying: "And do not be like those who said, 'We hear,' while they do not hear." By this is meant the hypocrites, or the Jews, or the polytheists, as mentioned earlier. Then He, exalted is He, informed that the disbelievers are the worst of what crawls upon the earth. In al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, "Indeed the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and dumb who do not reason," he said: they are a group from the Banu Abd al-Dar. The original form is "asharr" (the superlative of "sharr," evil); the hamza was dropped due to frequent usage. Likewise "khayr" (good); its original form is "akhyar."

**Qur'an 8:23:** ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾. It was said: [this refers to] the proofs and evidences, a hearing of comprehension (*ism'a tafahhum*). But His knowledge had already preceded their wretchedness. (And if He had made them hear) means: if He had made them understand, they would not have believed, given His eternal knowledge of their disbelief. It was also said: the meaning is that He would have made them hear the speech of the dead whom they asked to be revived, because they asked for the revival of Qusayy ibn Kilab and others so that they might bear witness to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH) said: He would have made them hear the answer to everything they asked about.

(And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were refusing) because it had preceded in His knowledge that they would not believe.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 24:

There are three issues (masa'il) in this.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger﴾. This address is to the believers who affirm (the truth), without any disagreement. Al-istijaba (responding) means al-ijaba (answering). As for "yuhyikum" (gives you life), its original form is "yuhyiykum," the damma was removed from the ya' because of its heaviness, and idgham (assimilation) is not permitted.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the meaning of "istajibu" is "ajibu" (answer), but the usage of speech is that istajaba is followed by the preposition lam, whereas ajaba is followed without lam. Allah, exalted is He, said: "O our people, answer the caller of Allah" [Qur'an 46:31]. Istajaba may also be followed without lam, and the evidence for this is the verse of the poet [it is Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi, lamenting his brother Abu al-Mughawwar]:

"And a caller who called, 'Who will answer to generosity?' — but no answerer answered him at that time."

One says: ajabahu and ajaba 'an su'alihi (he answered his question). The verbal noun is al-ijaba, and the noun is al-jaba, on the pattern of al-taqa and al-ta'a. One says: "asa'a sam'an fa-asa'a jaba" (he heard badly, so he answered badly). The origin of this proverb, as Zubayr ibn Bakkar mentioned, was that Sahl ibn 'Amr ibn Mad'un was asked by a man, "Where is your mother?" (with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the mim with damma), meaning "Where are you heading?", but he understood it as "Where is your mother?" (with damma on the hamza and the mim), so he said: "She has gone to buy flour." Then his father said: "He heard badly..." etc.

(From Lisan al-'Arab.)

This is how this letter is used in speech. Al-mujawaba and al-tajawub mean dialogue. And one says: "innahu la-hasanu al-jiba" (with kasra), meaning the answer.

"Li-ma yuhyikum" is connected to His saying "istajibu." The meaning: respond to what gives you life when He calls you. It was said: the lam means ila (to), i.e., to that which gives you life, that is, which gives life to your religion and teaches you. It was also said: that is, to that by which your hearts are given life so that you may affirm His oneness, and this is metaphorical life, since it is from the death of disbelief and ignorance. Mujahid and the majority said: the meaning is respond to obedience and to what the Qur'an contains of commands and prohibitions, for in it is eternal life and everlasting blessing. It was also said: the intended meaning of "li-ma yuhyikum" is jihad, for it is the outward cause of life, because if the enemy is not invaded, he invades, and in his invasion is death, and death in jihad is eternal life. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive" [Qur'an 3:169]. The sound view is generality, as the majority said.

The second: Al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, who said: "I was praying in the mosque when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called me, but I did not answer him. Then I came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I was praying.' He said: 'Did not Allah, mighty and majestic, say: "Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life"?'" and he mentioned the hadith. It has already been mentioned in al-Fatiha. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is evidence that an obligatory action or an obligatory utterance, if performed during prayer, does not invalidate the prayer, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the response even while one was in prayer.

I say: and in it is proof for the saying of al-Awza'i: if a man is praying and sees a boy about to fall into a well, and he shouts at him, turns toward him and rebukes him, there is no harm in that. And Allah knows best.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And know that Allah comes between a person and his heart﴾. It was said: this requires the explicit statement that Allah, exalted is He, creates disbelief and belief, so He comes between the disbelieving person and the faith which He commanded him to have, so he does not acquire it if He has not empowered him to it; rather He empowers him to its opposite, which is disbelief. Likewise, He comes between the believer and disbelief. Thus, by this text it is clear that He, exalted is He, is the creator of all the acquisitions [that is, their actions, since they are created by Him, glorified is He, while the acquisition belongs to the servant] of the servants, good and evil. This is the meaning of his, peace be upon him, saying: "No, and O Turner of hearts." And Allah's doing that is just regarding those whom He misguides and forsakes, since He does not withhold from them a right that was owed to them, so that the attribute of justice would cease; rather He withholds only what was His to bestow as a favour upon them, not what was due to them.

Al-Suddi said: He comes between a person and his heart, so he is not able to believe except by His permission, and he is not able to disbelieve except by His permission, that is, by His will. The heart is the seat of thought, and its explanation has already been given in al-Baqara. It is in the hand of Allah; whenever He wills, He comes between the servant and it with sickness or calamity, so that he does not understand, that is: hasten to respond before you become unable to do so through loss of reason.

Mujahid said: the meaning is that He comes between a person and his reason, until he does not know what he is doing. In the revelation: "Indeed in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart [qalb]" [Qur'an 50:37], that is, a mind (aql). It was also said: He comes between him and it through death, so he cannot make up for what has passed. It was also said: on the day of Badr the Muslims feared the great number of the enemy, so Allah informed them that He comes between a person and his heart, by changing their fear into security after fear, and changing the security of their enemy into fear. It was also said: the meaning is that He turns affairs from one state to another, and this is comprehensive. Al-Tabari's choice is that this is an information from Allah, mighty and majestic, that He is more sovereign over the hearts of the servants than they are, and that He comes between them and their hearts whenever He wills, so that a person grasps nothing except by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic.

﴿And that to Him you will be gathered﴾ is a conjunction (ataf). Al-Farra' said: if you begin a new sentence and put a kasra, "wa-innahu" would be correct.

There are two issues here.

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said that God commanded the believers not to tolerate wrongdoing among them, lest punishment overtake them all. Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam interpreted it in the same way. He said on the Day of the Camel (al-Jamal), in the year 36 AH: "I did not know that this verse was meant for us until today, and I thought it applied only to those addressed at that time." Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Suddi and others also interpreted it this way. Al-Suddi said: "The verse [from vol.] was revealed specifically concerning the people of Badr, and then the trial struck them on the Day of the Camel, so they fought one another." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "This verse was revealed concerning the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He also said: "Allah commanded the believers not to tolerate wrongdoing among themselves, lest Allah overtake them all with punishment."

From Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A trial will occur among some of my Companions. Allah will forgive it for them because of their companionship with me. But people after them will follow them in it, and Allah will cause them to enter the Fire because of it."

I say: These interpretations are those supported by the sound hadiths. In Sahih Muslim, it is narrated from Zaynab bint Jahsh that she asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, saying: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness becomes widespread." In Sahih al-Tirmidhi: "When people see the wrongdoer and do not restrain his hands, it is near that Allah will overtake them all with a punishment from Him." These hadiths have already been mentioned.

In Sahih al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi, it is narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The example of one who upholds the limits of Allah and one who violates them is like people who drew lots [[istahamu: they cast lots]] for a ship. Some of them got the upper part and some got the lower part. Those in the lower part, when they needed water, would pass by those above them and say: 'If only we made a hole in our portion and did not trouble those above us.' If they are left to do what they wish, they will all perish together, but if they take hold of their hands, they will be saved and all will be saved together."

In this hadith is the punishment of the general population for the sins of the elite, and the deserving of punishment for abandoning enjoining good and forbidding evil.

Our scholars said: When a trial takes effect, everyone perishes. This happens when sins become apparent, wickedness spreads, and no one changes it. If it is not changed, the believers who reject it in their hearts are obliged to abandon that town and flee from it. This was also the ruling for the nations before us, as in the story of the Sabbath, when they abandoned the disobedient and said: "We will not live with you." [[This was the view of the early pious predecessors, may Allah be pleased with them.]]

Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that he said: "The land in which wrongdoing is practised openly should be abandoned, and one should not settle in it." Malik cited the conduct of Abu al-Darda' when he left the land of Mu'awiya after the latter openly engaged in usury, and Abu al-Darda' permitted the sale of a gold water vessel for more than its weight. This was recorded by the authentic collections.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When Allah sends a punishment upon a people, the punishment strikes everyone among them, and then they will be raised according to their deeds." This indicates that a general destruction may be a purification for believers and a vengeance upon the wicked.

Muslim narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ moved [[abatha: his body moved, and it was said he moved his limbs as one who takes or pushes something]] in his sleep, so I said: "O Messenger of Allah, you did something in your sleep that you did not used to do?" He said: "It is strange that some people of my nation will head for this House [the Ka'bah] led by a man of Quraysh who has sought refuge in the House. When they reach al-Bayda', they will be swallowed up." We said: "O Messenger of Allah, the road may gather people together." He said: "Yes, among them will be the one who is clear about the matter and intends it deliberately, and the one who is compelled [[al-majbur: the one who is coerced]], and the traveller. They will all perish in one destruction, but they will depart in different ways, and Allah will raise them according to their intentions."

If it is said: Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿No bearer of burden shall bear the burden of another﴾, ﴿Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾, and ﴿It shall have what it has earned and it shall bear what it has earned﴾. This requires that no one be punished for the sin of another, and that punishment applies only to the one who committed the sin.

The answer is that when people openly display wrongdoing, it is an obligation upon everyone who sees it to change it. If they remain silent about it, then all of them are disobedient: this one by his action and that one by his approval. Allah, in His judgement and wisdom, has placed the one who approves on the same level as the one who acts, so the sin is combined with the punishment. [[Ibn al-'Arabi's expression: "so the sin is joined to the punishment".]] This was stated by Ibn al-'Arabi, and it is the substance of the hadiths we have mentioned. The intent of the verse is: "Beware of a trial that extends beyond the wrongdoer, striking both the righteous and the wicked."

Second issue: The grammarians differed concerning the attachment of the nun (nun al-tawkid, the emphatic nun) to ﴿لا تصيبن﴾. Al-Farra' said: It is equivalent to your saying: "Get down from the animal, lest it throw you down." It is the answer to the imperative in the form of a prohibition, meaning: if you get down from it, it will not throw you down. A similar example is the verse ﴿Enter your dwellings, lest they crush you﴾, meaning: if you enter, they will not crush you. The nun was attached because of the conditional sense it contains. It was also said that it came in the manner of an oath, and the nun is only attached to the imperative of prohibition or to the answer of an oath.

Al-Mubarrad said: It is a prohibition following a command, and the meaning is a prohibition for the wrongdoers, that is: do not approach wrongdoing.

Sibawayh related: "Lā arayannaka hāhunā" [I shall not see you here], meaning: do not be here, for whoever is here, I will see him.

Al-Jurjani said: The meaning is: "Beware of a trial that strikes specifically those who did wrong." Thus the phrase ﴿لا تصيبن﴾ is a prohibition in the position of describing a noun [[indefinite noun]], and its interpretation is a statement that it will strike those who did wrong.

'Ali, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿لتصيبن﴾ without an alif. Al-Mahdawi said: Whoever recites ﴿لتصيبن﴾ may read it as shortened from ﴿لا تصيبن﴾, with the alif dropped as it is dropped from "ma", whose sister is "la", as in "amma wallahi la-af'alanna" and similar expressions. It is also possible that it agrees with the recitation of the majority, and the meaning would then be that it strikes the wrongdoer specifically.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 8, verse 26:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And remember when you were few﴾. Al-Kalbi said: It was revealed concerning the Muhajirun (Emigrants), describing their condition before the hijrah (migration) and at the beginning of Islam.

(Musta'dafun) is a na't (adjective, descriptive modifier).

(Fi al-ardh) means, that is, the land of Makkah.

(Takhafun) is a na't (adjective).

(An yatakhattafakum) is in a position of nasb (accusative). Al-khatf means seizing quickly.

(Al-nas) is raf' (nominative) as the fa'il (subject). Qatadah and Ikrimah said: They are the polytheists of Quraysh. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: They are Persia and Rome.

(Fa-awakum) Ibn Abbas said: to the Ansar (Helpers). Al-Suddi said: to Madinah, and the meaning is the same. Awa ilayhi (with the madd, i.e., long vowel form) means he drew it to himself. Awa ilayhi (with the qasr, i.e., short form) means he joined himself to it.

(Wa-ayyadakum) means strengthened you.

(Bi-nasrihi) means with His help. It was also said: with the Ansar. And it was said: with the angels on the day of Badr.

(Wa-razaqakum min al-tayyibat) means, that is, the spoils of war.

(La'allakum tashkurun) its meaning has already been mentioned [see vol. 1, p. 397].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 27:

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba ibn Abd al-Mundhir when he signalled to the Banu Qurayza toward slaughter. Abu Lubaba said: "By Allah, my feet did not move until I knew that I had betrayed Allah and His Messenger," and then this verse was revealed. When it was revealed, he tied himself to one of the pillars of the mosque and said: "By Allah, I will not taste food or drink until I die, or until Allah accepts my repentance." The report is well known [[See vol. 8, p. 242.]]. And from Ikrima, who said: When the affair of Qurayza arose, the Prophet ﷺ sent Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, along with those people who were with him. When he reached them, they reviled the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Gabriel, peace be upon him, came on a piebald horse, and Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "It was as if I were looking at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wiping the dust from the face of Gabriel, peace be upon them both. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is this Dihya?' He said: 'This is Gabriel, peace be upon him.'" [Gabriel] said: "O Messenger of Allah, what prevents you from going to the Banu Qurayza to come to them?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "How can I [reach] their fortress?" Gabriel said: "I will enter my horse upon them." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mounted a horse, bareback [[i.e., naked, without saddle.]]. When Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, saw him, he said: "O Messenger of Allah, there is no harm in your not going to them, for they will revile you." He said: "No indeed, it will be a greeting." Then the Prophet ﷺ came to them and said: "O brothers of the apes and the swine!" They said: "O Abu al-Qasim, you were not one to use foul language!" They said: "We will not come down under the judgement of Muhammad, but we will come down under the judgement of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh," and so they came down. He judged concerning them that their fighting men be killed and their children taken captive. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By that the angel visited me at dawn." And concerning them was revealed: "O you who believe, do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know [better]." It was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba, who signalled to the Banu Qurayza when they said: "We will come down under the judgement of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh," [saying]: "Do not do it, for it is slaughter," and he gestured toward his throat. It is also said: the verse was revealed concerning those who hear something from the Prophet ﷺ and then convey it to the polytheists and spread it. It is also said: the meaning is betrayal through misappropriating the spoils of war. Its attribution to Allah is because He is the one who commanded their distribution, and to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ because he is the one who conveys from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the one responsible for them. Khiyana (betrayal) means treachery and concealing something, and from it [comes the verse]: "He knows the treachery of the eyes" [40:19] [[See vol. 15, p. 301 and following.]]. The peace be upon him used to say: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from hunger, for it is the worst of bedfellows, and from betrayal, for it is the worst of companions." Al-Nasa'i narrated it from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say, and then he mentioned it.

(And betray your trusts)

It is in the jussive position, coordinated with the first. It may also be in the response position, as one says: "Do not eat the fish and drink the milk." The amanat (trusts) are the duties that Allah entrusted to His servants. They are called amana because through them one is safe from withholding what is due, derived from al-amn (security). The discussion of the fulfilment of trusts and deposits has already been given in "al-Nisa'" [[See vol. 5, p. 255.]], and other matters.

(And you know) i.e., the ugliness and shame that is in betrayal. It is also said: you know that it is a trust.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾

Abu Lubaba had wealth and children among the Banu Qurayza, and it was this that led him to be lenient toward them. So this is an indication of that.

(Fitnah) 10

That is, a test; He tests them with them.

(And that Allah has with Him a great reward)

So prefer His right over your rights.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 29:

The meaning of "taqwa" (God-consciousness, piety) has already been explained. Allah knows whether they will be God-conscious or not. He is mentioned with the wording of a conditional, because He addresses the servants with what some of them address one another. So when the servant is God-conscious toward his Lord, which means following His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, abandoning doubtful matters out of fear of falling into what is forbidden, filling his heart with sincere intention and his limbs with righteous deeds, and guarding himself against the impurities of hidden and manifest shirk through seeking other than Allah in his actions, and through inclining toward this world by abstaining from wealth, He makes for him a criterion (furqan) between truth and falsehood, and grants him the ability to attain whatever good he desires.

Ibn Wahb said: I asked Malik about the saying of the Exalted and Glorified: "If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan)." He said: "A way out." Then he recited: "And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out" [[See vol. 18, p. 157 onward.]]. Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab related the same from Malik exactly, and Mujahid said it before him.

The poet said:

"What use to you is the furqan of long grief,
after the tribe departed and went far away?"

And another said:

"How can I hope for eternity when death is seeking me,
and I have no furqan from the cup of death?"

Ibn Ishaq: "furqanan" means a separation between truth and falsehood. Ibn Zayd said it. As-Suddi: salvation. Al-Farra': victory and triumph. It is also said: it refers to the Hereafter, where He will admit you to Paradise and admit the disbelievers to the Fire.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 30:

This is an report of what the polytheists agreed upon in terms of plotting against the Prophet ﷺ in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of the Quraysh). Their opinion converged on killing him, so they spent the night (outside his house) and kept watch at the door of the house all night, intending to kill him when he came out. The Prophet ﷺ ordered 'Ali ibn Abi Talib to sleep on his bed, and he prayed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to blind their sight to his trail, so Allah blinded their eyes, and he went out while sleep had overcome them. He placed dust on their heads and rose up. When they awoke, 'Ali came out to them and informed them that there was no one in the house, so they knew that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had escaped and got away. The report is well known in the biography (sirah) and elsewhere.

The meaning of ﴿to imprison you﴾ (liyuthbitukum) is to detain you; it is said: "athbattuhu" when I detained him. Qatadah said: "liyuthbitukum" means to bind in chains (wathaqan). And from him also, and Abdullah ibn Kathir: to imprison you (liyasjununka). Aban ibn Taghlib and Abu Hatim said: to wound you with injuries and severe beating. The poet said:

"I said: Woe to you both, what is in your document?
They said: The caliph has become afflicted and ill, detained."

﴿or kill you or expel you﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf).

﴿And they plot﴾ is a resumptive (mustanaf) clause. And al-makr (plotting) is planning a matter in secrecy.

﴿And Allah is the best of planners﴾ is an inceptive sentence with its predicate. And the plotting from Allah is their requital with punishment for their plotting, from where they do not perceive.

This was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. He had gone out to al-Hira for trade, and bought the stories of Kalila wa-Dimna, and of Kisra and Caesar. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related the accounts of the past peoples, al-Nadr said: "If I wished, I could say the like of this." This was impudence and lying. It was also said: they imagined that they could produce the like of it, just as the magicians of Musa imagined, then they attempted that and were unable to do it, and they said out of obstinacy: "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients." And this has been mentioned earlier [[See vol. 6, p. 404.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 32:

The reciters read "al-haqq" (the truth) in the accusative as the predicate of "kana" (was). The word "huwa" (it) has entered for separation (al-fasl, the pronoun of separation between subject and predicate). It is also permissible to read "huwa al-haqqu" with the nominative.

Regarding "min 'indika" (from You): al-Zajjaj said, "I do not know of anyone who recited it this way." There is no disagreement among the grammarians about its permissibility, but recitation is a sunnah (a prophetic practice transmitted by reliable chain), so nothing is recited except by a transmitted reading that is accepted.

There is disagreement about who made this statement. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr said: the one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. Anas ibn Malik said: the one who said it was Abu Jahl. (This is narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.) Then it is possible to say that they said it because of a doubt that was in their hearts, or out of obstinacy and to give the people the impression that they were upon insight. Then there befell them on the Day of Badr what they had asked for.

It is related that Ibn 'Abbas met a man from the Jews, and the Jew said: "Who are you from?" He said: "From Quraysh." He said: "You are from the people who said: 'O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You...' [the verse]." Would it not have been better for them to say: "If this is indeed the truth from You, then guide us to it!" Indeed these are a people who are ignorant. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And you, O Israelite, are from the people whose feet had not dried from the moisture of the sea in which Pharaoh and his people were drowned, and Musa and his people were saved, until they said: 'Make for us a god just as they have gods.' [See p. 273 of this part.] Musa said to them: 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant.'" Then the Jew lowered his head, silenced.

"Fa-amtir" (so rain down): amtara is used for punishment, and matara for mercy, according to Abu 'Ubayda. This has been mentioned before.

لَمَّا قَالَ أَبُو جَهْلٍ: "اللَّهُمَّ إِنْ كانَ هَذَا هُوَ الْحَقَّ مِنْ عِنْدِكَ" الْآيَةَ، نَزَلَتْ "وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ وَأَنْتَ فِيهِمْ" كَذَا فِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ.

When Abu Jahl said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You..." (the verse), the verse "But Allah would not punish them while you are among them" was revealed. Thus it is in Sahih Muslim.

وَقَالَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ: لَمْ يعذب أهل قرية حتى يخرج النبي ﷺ مِنْهَا وَالْمُؤْمِنُونَ، يَلْحَقُوا بِحَيْثُ أُمِرُوا.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The people of a town were not punished until the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers had left it and joined where they were commanded to go.

(وَما كانَ اللَّهُ مُعَذِّبَهُمْ وَهُمْ يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ) ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ: كَانُوا يَقُولُونَ فِي الطَّوَافِ: غُفْرَانَكَ. وَالِاسْتِغْفَارُ وَإِنْ وَقَعَ مِنَ الْفُجَّارِ يُدْفَعُ بِهِ ضَرْبٌ مِنَ الشُّرُورِ وَالْأَضْرَارِ.

("But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness.") Ibn 'Abbas said: They used to say during the circumambulation (tawaf): "Your forgiveness, (O Lord)." Even if seeking forgiveness comes from the wicked, a kind of evil and harm is thereby averted.

وَقِيلَ: إِنَّ الِاسْتِغْفَارَ رَاجِعٌ إِلَى الْمُسْلِمِينَ الَّذِينَ هُمْ بَيْنَ أَظْهُرِهِمْ أَيْ وَمَا كَانَ اللَّهُ مُعَذِّبَهُمْ وَفِيهِمْ مَنْ يَسْتَغْفِرُ مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ، فَلَمَّا خَرَجُوا عَذَّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ يَوْمَ بَدْرٍ وَغَيْرَهُ،. قَالَهُ الضَّحَّاكُ وَغَيْرُهُ.

It was also said: the seeking of forgiveness refers to the Muslims who were among them, meaning: "Allah would not punish them while among them are those of the Muslims who seek forgiveness." When they left, Allah punished them on the day of Badr and at other times. This was said by al-Dahhak and others.

وَقِيلَ: إِنَّ الِاسْتِغْفَارَ هُنَا يُرَادُ بِهِ الْإِسْلَامُ أَيْ "وَما كانَ اللَّهُ مُعَذِّبَهُمْ وَهُمْ يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ" أَيْ يُسْلِمُونَ، قَالَهُ مُجَاهِدٌ وَعِكْرِمَةُ.

It was also said: here seeking forgiveness is intended to mean Islam, i.e., "Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness," meaning they embrace Islam. This was said by Mujahid and 'Ikrimah.

وَقِيلَ: "وَهُمْ يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ" أَيْ فِي أَصْلَابِهِمْ مَنْ يَسْتَغْفِرُ اللَّهَ. رُوِيَ عَنْ مُجَاهِدٍ أَيْضًا.

It was also said: "while they seek forgiveness" means that among their loins there are those who will seek forgiveness from Allah. This is also narrated from Mujahid.

وَقِيلَ: مَعْنَى "يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ" لَوِ اسْتَغْفَرُوا أَيْ لَوِ اسْتَغْفَرُوا لَمْ يُعَذَّبُوا. اسْتَدْعَاهُمْ إِلَى الِاسْتِغْفَارِ، قَالَهُ قَتَادَةُ وَابْنُ زَيْدٍ.

It was also said: the meaning of "they seek forgiveness" is "if they sought forgiveness," i.e., if they had sought forgiveness they would not have been punished. It is an invitation to them to seek forgiveness. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

وَقَالَ الْمَدَائِنِيُّ عَنْ بَعْضِ الْعُلَمَاءِ قَالَ: كَانَ رَجُلٌ مِنَ الْعَرَبِ فِي زَمَنِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ مُسْرِفًا عَلَى نَفْسِهِ، لَمْ يَكُنْ يَتَحَرَّجُ، فَلَمَّا أَنْ تُوُفِّيَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ لَبِسَ الصُّوفَ وَرَجَعَ عَمَّا كَانَ عَلَيْهِ، وَأَظْهَرَ الدِّينَ وَالنُّسُكَ. فَقِيلَ لَهُ: لَوْ فَعَلْتَ هَذَا وَالنَّبِيُّ ﷺ حَيٌّ لَفَرِحَ بِكَ. قَالَ: كَانَ لِي أَمَانَانِ، فَمَضَى وَاحِدٌ وَبَقِيَ الْآخَرُ، قَالَ اللَّهُ تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى: "وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ وَأَنْتَ فِيهِمْ" فَهَذَا أَمَانٌ. وَالثَّانِي "وَما كانَ اللَّهُ مُعَذِّبَهُمْ وَهُمْ يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ".

al-Mada'ini related from some scholars that he said: There was a man among the Arabs in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) who was excessive toward himself and did not refrain from sin. When the Prophet (ﷺ) died, he wore wool, turned back from what he had been doing, and displayed religion and devotion. It was said to him: "If you had done this while the Prophet (ﷺ) was alive, he would have rejoiced in you." He said: "I had two protections. One has passed, and the other remains." Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, says: "But Allah would not punish them while you are among them" — this is one protection. The second is: "But Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness."

The Qur'an: "And what is [the matter] with them, that Allah should not punish them..."

The meaning: what prevents them from being punished? That is, they deserve punishment for the abominable deeds and causes [of punishment] they have committed. "But for every term there is a decree" — so Allah punished them by the sword after the Prophet ﷺ went out [from among them]. And concerning this it was revealed: "A questioner asked about a punishment that will befall" [70:1].

Al-Akhfash said: "in" (inna) here is extra (za'idah, redundant). Al-Nahhas said: "If it were as he said, it would have put 'yu'adhdhibahum' in the nominative case." "But most of them do not know" — that is, the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) are His allies (awliya').

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 35–37:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The Quraysh used to circumambulate the House (al-Bayt) naked, clapping and whistling, and they considered that to be an act of worship. Al-mukaʾ is whistling, and al-tasdiyah is clapping. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them. From it is the verse of ʿAntarah:

"And a husband of a beauty I left felled, his heart-muscle (farisah) twitching like the split lip of the one with a cleft lip (al-aʿlam)." [[al-Halil: the husband. It is also narrated as wa-khalil, with the letter kha' with a dot. al-Farisah: the place that trembles in an animal or a person when frightened. al-Aʿlam: the one whose upper lip is split.]]

That is, it makes a sound. From it comes makata, meaning the rear of the animal swelled with wind. al-Suddi said: al-mukaʾ is whistling, in the manner [[from j, h, k, z, and ʾ. In b: nahw (like).]] of a white bird in the Hijaz called al-makkaʾ. The poet said:

"When the makkaʾ sings in other than a meadow, then woe to the people of the sheep and the donkeys."

Qatadah said: al-mukaʾ is striking with the hands, and al-tasdiyah is shouting. On both interpretations, there is a refutation of the ignorant Sufis who dance and clap (and fall unconscious [[from b, j, h, z, k, and ʾ.]]). All of that is reprehensible, and sensible people are far removed from such things, and whoever does it resembles the polytheists in what they used to do at the House. Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujahid that he said: al-mukaʾ is their putting their fingers into their mouths. And al-tasdiyah is whistling, they wanting to distract Muhammad (ﷺ) from the prayer by it. al-Nahhas said: What is known in the language is what was narrated from Ibn ʿUmar. Abu ʿUbayd and others related that it is said: makā yamkū and mukāʾ when he whistled. And sadda yusaddī tasdiyah when he clapped, and from it is the verse of ʿAmr ibn al-Itnabah [[In al-Qamus and its commentary: "al-Itnabah was a woman from the tribe of Kinanah ibn al-Qays ibn Jasr ibn Qudaʿah, and ʿAmr her son was a famous poet, and his father's name was Zayd Manat."]]:

"And they all remained, for them a clamor of whistling by the House with clapping."

That is, with clapping. Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd: the meaning of tasaddiyah is their turning people away from the House, so the original on this is tasaddudah, and one of the two dals was changed into a yaʾ.

(That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good) i.e., the believer from the disbeliever. It has also been said: it is general in everything, including deeds, expenditures and other things.

(That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good) i.e., the believer from the disbeliever. It has also been said: it is general in everything, including deeds, expenditures and other things.

**Issue One:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve﴾. He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to say this meaning to the disbelievers, whether he said it in this wording or in another.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Had it been as al-Kisa'i (d. 189 AH) reported, that in the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it reads, 'Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, they will be forgiven what has passed,' the message would not have been conveyed except with those exact words. This is according to what the wording requires."

**Issue Two:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿if they cease﴾, meaning from disbelief. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is necessary, and what compels this interpretation is the response to the condition: 'they will be forgiven what has passed.' The forgiveness of what has passed is only for one who has ceased from disbelief."

The poet Abu Sa'id Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Zubayri said well:

*The young man deserves pardon when he confesses,*
*Then ceases from what he committed and perpetrated.*

*For the Exalted's saying regarding the one who confesses:*
*"If they cease, they will be forgiven what has passed."*

Muslim narrated from Abu Shammasa al-Mahri, who said: "We attended 'Amr ibn al-'As while he was in the throes of death, weeping for a long time." The hadith continues, and in it the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you not know that Islam demolishes what came before it, that emigration demolishes what came before it, and that Hajj demolishes what came before it?" [The hadith continues.]

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is a subtle favour from Allah, the Exalted, bestowed upon creation. The disbelievers plunge into disbelief and crimes, and commit sins and transgressions. Had that required that they be held accountable, they would never have obtained repentance, and forgiveness would never have reached them. So Allah, the Exalted, facilitated for them the acceptance of repentance upon returning, and the granting of forgiveness through Islam, and He erased everything that preceded it, so that this would be closer to their entry into the religion and more conducive to their acceptance of the word of the Muslims. Had they known that they would be held accountable, they would not have repented nor embraced Islam."

In Sahih Muslim: a man from among those before you had killed ninety-nine souls, then he asked whether he had any repentance. He came to a monk and asked whether he had any repentance. The monk said, "You have no repentance," so he killed him, completing a hundred. The hadith continues. Consider the monk's words, "You have no repentance." When he knew that the monk had despaired him, he killed him, the act of one who has despaired of mercy. Thus, deterring people is a corruption for the one addressed, and facilitating for them is a benefit to them.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that whenever a man who had not killed came to him and asked, "Is there repentance for a killer?" he would say, "There is no repentance," as a warning and a deterrent. But when a man who had killed came to him and asked, "Is there repentance for a killer?" he would say to him, "You have repentance," as facilitation and conciliation. This has already been mentioned.

**Issue Three:** Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb reported from Malik regarding one who divorced while in polytheism and then embraced Islam: "There is no divorce for him." Likewise, one who swore an oath and then embraced Islam incurs no breach upon him. Similarly, whoever was liable for these things is forgiven. As for one who slandered a Muslim and then embraced Islam, or stole and then embraced Islam, the prescribed punishment (hadd) for the slander and the theft is enforced upon him. If he committed adultery and then embraced Islam, or raped a Muslim woman, the prescribed punishment falls from him.

Ashhab reported from Malik that he said: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, only means what has passed before Islam, of property, blood, or anything else."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is the correct view, because of the generality of the Exalted's saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, they will be forgiven what has passed﴾, and His (ﷺ) saying: 'Islam demolishes what came before it,' and because of the meaning we have explained, namely facilitation and the avoidance of deterrence."

I say: As for the non-Muslim combatant (harbi), there is no disagreement on the removal of what he did while in a state of disbelief in the land of war. But if he enters our territory under safe-conduct (aman) and slanders a Muslim, he is subjected to the prescribed punishment; and if he steals, his hand is cut off. Likewise, the dhimmi (protected non-Muslim) who slanders is flogged eighty lashes, and if he steals his hand is cut off, and if he kills he is executed. Islam does not remove that from him, because he violated the covenant while in a state of disbelief, according to the narration of Ibn al-Qasim and others.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: "They differed regarding a Christian who committed adultery and then embraced Islam, when a Muslim evidence testified against him. It is related from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was in Iraq, that there is no hadd upon him and no exile, because of the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: 'Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, they will be forgiven what has passed.'" Ibn al-Mundhir said: "This is consistent with what was related from Malik."

Abu Thawr said: "If he confesses while a Muslim that he committed adultery while a disbeliever, the prescribed punishment is enforced upon him." It is related from the Kufan [school] that he said: "He is not subjected to the prescribed punishment."

**Issue Four:** As for the apostate (murtadd) who embraces Islam after having missed prayers, committed offences, and destroyed property: it is said that his ruling is the ruling of the original disbeliever who embraces Islam, so he is not held responsible for anything he did during his apostasy. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his two opinions, said: he is bound by every right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and of the human being, on the evidence that the rights of human beings bind him, so the rights of Allah, the Exalted, must also bind him. Abu Hanifa said: what is due to Allah falls away, and what is due to a human being does not fall away.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "This is the view of our scholars, because Allah, the Exalted, is free of need of His right, whereas the human being is in need of his right. Do you not see that the rights of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are not obligatory upon a child, but the rights of human beings bind him?"

They said: the Exalted's saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, they will be forgiven what has passed﴾ is general regarding the rights of Allah, the Exalted.

**Issue Five:** Allah the Exalted says: ﴿and if they return﴾, meaning to fighting, because the word "'ada" (return), when it comes unrestricted, implies a return to a state in which a person was, then moved away from. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "We do not find in this verse, for these disbelievers, a state resembling what we mentioned except fighting. It is not permissible to interpret it as a return to disbelief, because they had not separated from it. We only said that regarding 'ada when it is unrestricted, because it may come in Arabic speech governing a subject and predicate, so its meaning is that of 'sara' (became). For example, you say: 'Zayd returned (ʿāda) a king,' meaning he became a king." From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*Those are noble deeds, not two bowls of milk*
*Mixed with water, which afterwards became urine.*

This does not imply a return to a state in which the one returning had been before. Rather, it is restricted by its predicate, and it may not be limited without it, so its ruling is the ruling of "sara."

The Exalted's saying: ﴿then the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾ is an expression that combines the threat, the warning, and the example of those peoples of old who were destroyed by the punishment of Allah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾, i.e., disbelief. As for the rest of the verse, its meaning and the explanation of its words have already been given in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 353.]] and elsewhere, and praise be to God.
