Part Eight

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

[Continuation of the commentary on Surat al-Anfal]

The Qur'anic verse in your passage is quoted as follows. Al-Qurtubi's commentary opens with it:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils of war, one-fifth of it belongs to Allah, and to the Messenger, and to the near of kin, and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer, if you have believed in Allah.﴾ In it there are twenty-five issues [[Note: the issues are twenty-five.]].

**The first issue:** Allah's words "And know that whatever you obtain" (*ghanimtum*). In the language, *al-ghanimah* (spoils, booty) is what a man or a group obtains through effort. Among the evidence is the poet's saying:

*"I have roamed the horizons until I was content with the gain of return."*

Another said:

*"The one who feeds on spoils, on the day of spoils, is fed wherever he goes, while the deprived remains deprived."*

*Al-maghnam* and *al-ghanimah* have the same meaning. It is said: *ghanima al-qawm ghunman* (the people obtained spoils). Know that there is agreement that what is meant by Allah's words "whatever you obtain" is the property of the disbelievers when the Muslims gain it by victory and subjugation. Language does not necessitate this restriction, as we have explained [[In MS Z: "as we have mentioned earlier."]], but the usage of the Sharia restricted the term to this category. The Sharia named what reaches us from the disbelievers in property by two names: *ghanimah* (spoils) and *fay'* (revenue). What the Muslims obtain from their enemy through effort and *ijaf* [[Al-ijaf: speed of travel, meaning they did not run in obtaining it on horses or camels; it was acquired without fighting. Al-rikab: the camels on which one travels, which have no singular of their own form.]] of horses and riding camels is called *ghanimah*. This name became bound to this meaning until it became established usage. *Al-fay'* is derived from *fa'a yafi'u*, meaning "to return," and it is every property that comes to the Muslims without war or *ijaf*, such as the land tax (*kharaj al-aradin*), the poll tax (*jizyat al-jamajim*), and the one-fifth of the spoils (*khums al-ghana'im*). Sufyan al-Thawri and Ata ibn al-Sa'ib said something similar. It is also said that the two are one and the same, and that both contain the one-fifth, as Qatadah stated. It is also said that *fay'* is an expression for everything that has come to the Muslims as property without compulsion. The meanings are close.

**The second issue:** This verse abrogates (*nasikhah*) the beginning of the surah, according to the majority of scholars. Ibn Abd al-Barr claimed consensus that this verse was revealed after Allah's words: ﴿They ask you about the spoils (*al-anfal*)﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], and that four-fifths of the spoils are divided among those who fought, as will be explained. He also claimed that the words "They ask you about the spoils" were revealed when the people of Badr disputed over the spoils of Badr, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah.

I say: Among what supports the soundness of this is what Isma'il ibn Ishaq related, saying: Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib narrated to me from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: (When the day of Badr came, the Prophet (ﷺ) said:) "Whoever kills a slain enemy, for him is such-and-such; and whoever takes a captive, for him is such-and-such." They had killed seventy and captured seventy. Abu al-Yusr ibn Amr came with two captives and said: "O Messenger of Allah, you promised us that whoever kills a slain enemy gets such-and-such, and I have brought two captives." Then Sa'd stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, it was not the desire for extra reward nor cowardice before the enemy that prevented us, but we stood in that position out of fear that the polytheists would regroup. If you give these men, nothing will remain for your companions." He said: They began saying this and those began saying that, and then it was revealed: ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger; so fear Allah and set right the state of affairs among you﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. So they handed over the spoils to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then it was revealed: "And know that whatever you obtain, one-fifth of it belongs to Allah," and the verse continues.

It has also been said that this verse is decisive (*muhkamah*) and not abrogated, and that the spoils belong to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and are not divided among the fighters, and likewise for the imams after him. Al-Mazari related this from many of our companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and that the imam may dispense them from the fighters. They argued from the conquest of Makkah and the story of Hunayn. Abu Ubayd used to say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah by force (*anwatan*), then he granted its people amnesty and returned it to them. He neither divided it nor made it *fay'* for them. Some people held that this is permissible for the imams after him.

I say: On this view, the meaning of Allah's words "And know that whatever you obtain, one-fifth of it belongs to Allah," and the four-fifths are for the imam, who may withhold them if he wishes or divide them among the fighters if he wishes. This is worthless, for the reason we have mentioned, and because Allah, glory be to Him, attributed the spoils to those who fought, saying: "And know that whatever you obtain," then specified the one-fifth for those He named in His Book, and remained silent about the four-fifths, just as He remained silent about the two-thirds in His words: ﴿And his parents inherit from him, so his mother has the third﴾ [al-Nisa': 11] [[See vol. 5, p. 71.]], so the father had two-thirds by consensus. Likewise, the four-fifths belong to the fighters by consensus, as stated by Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abd al-Barr, al-Dawudi, al-Mazari also, al-Qadi Iyad, and Ibn al-Arabi. The reports with this meaning are widespread, and some of them will come. The meaning of His words "They ask you about the spoils" and the rest of the verse is what the imam grants as a special share (*nafl*) to whomever he wishes, according to what he sees as beneficial, before the division. Ata and al-Hasan said: It is specific to what escaped from the polytheists to the Muslims, such as a male slave, a female slave, or a beast, about which the imam decides as he wishes. It is also said that what is meant by it is the *anfal* of the raiding detachments (*sara-ya*), i.e., their spoils: if the imam wishes, he takes one-fifth of them, and if he wishes, he grants them all as special shares. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said, concerning an imam who sends a raiding detachment and they obtain spoils: If the imam wishes, he grants all of it as a special share, and if he wishes, he takes one-fifth of it. Abu Umar related this from Makhul and Ata. Ali ibn Thabit said: I asked Makhul and Ata about an imam who grants the people special shares of what they obtained. He said: That is theirs. Abu Umar said: Whoever holds this view interprets Allah's words, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1] as meaning that this belongs to the Prophet (ﷺ), who places it wherever he wishes. He did not regard this verse as abrogated by Allah's words: "And know that whatever you obtain, one-fifth of it belongs to Allah." It has also been said that other than this, which we have addressed in the book *al-Qabas fi Sharh Muwatta' Malik ibn Anas*. None of the scholars, to my knowledge, has said that Allah's words "They ask you about the spoils," and the rest of the verse, abrogate His words "And know that whatever you obtain, one-fifth of it belongs to Allah." Rather, the majority, as we have mentioned, held that His words "whatever you obtain" are the abrogating text, and they are the ones about whom it is not permissible to suppose distortion or alteration of the Book of Allah, the Exalted.

3. The story of the conquest of Makkah provides no proof, because the scholars differ over whether it was conquered by force. Abu 'Ubayd said: "We do not know of any city that resembles Makkah in two respects. The first is that Allah had singled out the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with spoils (al-anfal, what is taken without a regular battle) and booty (al-ghana'im, what is taken in war) that He had not granted to anyone else. This is based on His saying: ﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ [al-Anfal: 1], and so on. We hold that this was specific to him. The second is that he established for Makkah rulings that do not apply to any other land."

As for the story of Hunayn, he compensated the Ansar when they said: "He gives the spoils to Quraysh and leaves us, while our swords are still dripping with their blood!" He said to them: "Are you not content that the people should return with worldly goods while you return with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to your homes?" Muslim and others transmitted it. No one else may say this statement, although some of our scholars say that it was specific to him. And Allah knows best.

The third matter: The scholars have not differed that His saying, ﴿And know that whatever you gain of any spoil﴾, is not to be taken in its full generality, and that it admits of specification. Among what they have specified by consensus is that the spoils of a slain enemy (salab) belong to his slayer if the imam announces it. Likewise, the captives (ar-riqab, meaning the prisoners of war), the choice regarding them rests with the imam without disagreement, as will be explained. Among what has also been specified is the land. The meaning is: what you gain of gold, silver, all other goods, and captives. As for the land, it does not fall under the generality of this verse, because Abu Dawud transmitted from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "Had it not been for the last of the people, no town would have been conquered without my dividing it, just as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided Khaybar."

What supports this position is the authentic report from Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Iraq has withheld its qafiz and its dirham, and Syria has withheld its mudd and its dinar," and the hadith continues. al-Tahawi said: "'Withheld' here means 'will withhold' (in the future). This shows that these are not for the warriors (al-ghanimun), because what the warriors own would not include a qafiz or a dirham. And if the land were to be divided, nothing would remain for those who came after the warriors." Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And those who came after them﴾ [al-Hashr: 10], coordinated with His saying: ﴿for the poor emigrants﴾ [al-Hashr: 8].[[See vol. 18, p. 31.]] He said: "Only what is moved from one place to another is divided."

Al-Shafi'i said: "Whatever is obtained as spoils from the people of the abode of war, of any amount, whether a house, land, goods or anything else, is divided, except the adult men, for the imam has the choice regarding them: he may release them, kill them, or enslave them. The rule for what is taken from them and enslaved is the rule of spoils." He argued from the generality of the verse, saying: "Land is certainly spoils, so it must be divided like the rest of the spoils. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided what he conquered by force (anwatan) at Khaybar." They said: "If it were permissible to claim specification for land, it would be permissible to claim it for other things, and the ruling of the verse would be nullified."

As for the verse of al-Hashr, there is no proof in it, because that concerns fay' (property gained without fighting) and not ghanimah (spoils of war). His saying: ﴿And those who came after them﴾ [al-Hashr: 10] is the beginning of a new statement, a supplication for those who preceded them in faith, and nothing else.

They said: "The action of 'Umar in holding back the land must be one of two things. Either it was spoils whose owners' hearts were pleased, and they consented, so he held it in trust (waqf). Jarir narrated similarly that 'Umar sought the consent of its people. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did likewise regarding the captives of Hawazin: when they came to him, he sought the hearts of his companions regarding what was in their hands. Or what 'Umar held in trust was fay', so he had no need to seek anyone's approval."

The Kufans held that the imam has the choice between dividing the land, leaving it in its owners' hands and imposing kharaj (land tax) on it, in which case it becomes their property, like the land conquered by treaty. Our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It seems that this is a reconciliation between the two proofs and a middle way between the two positions, and it is what 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, definitively understood. For this reason he said: 'Had it not been for the last of the people.' He did not report that the Prophet's (ﷺ) action had been abrogated, nor that it was specific to those people. However, the Kufans went beyond what 'Umar did, for 'Umar held it in trust only for the public interests of the Muslims and did not make it the property of the people of the treaty, whereas they said the imam may make it their property."

4. Malik, Abu Hanifah and al-Thawri held that the salab does not belong to the slayer, and that its ruling is the ruling of spoils, unless the commander says: "Whoever kills an enemy, his salab is for him," in which case it becomes his. al-Layth, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, al-Tabari and Ibn al-Mundhir held that the salab belongs to the slayer in all cases, whether or not the imam says so. However, al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The salab belongs to the slayer only if he killed the enemy while the enemy was facing him. But if he killed him while the enemy was turning away, it does not."

Abu al-'Abbas ibn Surayj, one of al-Shafi'i's companions, said: "The hadith 'Whoever kills an enemy, his salab is for him' is not to be taken in its general sense, because the scholars agree that whoever kills a captive, a woman, or an elderly man does not gain the salab of any of them. The same applies to one who finishes off a wounded man (tadhfif al-jarih)[[Tadhfif al-jarih: finishing off the wounded.]], and one who kills a man whose hands and feet have been cut off." He said: "Likewise, a man who is routed and cannot defend himself while fleeing is like a bound man." He said: "It is thereby known that the hadith assigns the salab only to the one whose killing has an additional significance, or to the one in whose killing there is merit, namely the slayer who fought facing the enemy, because of the hardship involved. But as for one who has been incapacitated by wounds, no."

al-Tabari said: "The salab belongs to the slayer, whether he killed the enemy while facing him or while he was turning away, fleeing, or fighting him one-on-one, provided it was on the battlefield."

This is refuted by what 'Abd al-Razzaq and Muhammad ibn Bakr narrated from Ibn Juraij, who said: "I heard Nafi', the mawla (freed slave) of Ibn 'Umar, say: 'We have always heard that when the Muslims and the disbelievers meet, and a Muslim man kills a disbeliever, his salab is his, unless it happens in the midst of the fighting, for then no one knows who killed whom.'" The apparent sense of this refutes al-Tabari's position, since he makes killing on the battlefield a specific condition for the salab.

Abu Thawr and Ibn al-Mundhir said: "The salab belongs to the slayer whether the killing takes place on a battlefield or not, whether the enemy is facing him, turning away, fleeing or retreating, in all circumstances, because of the generality of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: 'Whoever kills an enemy, his salab is for him.'"

I say: Muslim narrated from Salamah ibn al-Akwa' who said: "We fought with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) against Hawazin. While we were having a midday meal[[Ayy natagha. (i.e., eating a meal).]] with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a man came on a red camel, made it kneel, then pulled a strap from its saddle-bag"[[Al-talaq (with a vowel): a leather strap. And al-haqab: the rope tied around the camel's loins, or from its saddle, that is, the extra piece placed at the back of the saddle, and the bag in which a man puts his provisions.]]

(Narrated by Ibn al-Athir.) He tethered the camel, then went forward to eat his lunch with the people, while he kept watching. Among us were weak and emaciated animals [[i.e., the camels were in a state of weakness and emaciation]], and some of us were on foot. Then he came running [[i.e., he came out running quickly]], went to his camel, released its tether, made it kneel, sat on it, and urged it on, and the camel ran swiftly with him. A man followed him on a grey camel [[al-awraq: a camel whose colour is a mixture of white and black]]. Salamah said: I went out running and was at the thigh of the she-camel. Then I advanced until I was at the thigh of the camel. Then I advanced until I took hold of the camel's halter and made it kneel. When it placed its knee on the ground, I drew my sword and struck the man's head, and he fell [[nadara: fell]]. Then I brought the camel leading it, with its saddle and weapons on it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met me with the people, and he said: "Who killed the man?" They said: "Ibn al-Akwa'." He said: "He shall have all his spoils (salab)." So this is Salamah, who killed him while he was fleeing, not facing him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) gave him his spoils.

In this is evidence for Malik's view that the slayer does not deserve the spoils (salab) except with the permission of the Imam, for if it were due to him by the act of killing itself, there would have been no need to repeat this statement.

Among his evidence also is what Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Bishr ibn 'Alqamah, who said: I fought a man in single combat on the day of al-Qadisiyyah, killed him, and took his spoils. I came to Sa'd, and Sa'd addressed his companions, then said: "This is the spoils of Bishr ibn 'Alqamah, and it is worth more than twelve thousand dirhams, and we have given it to him as a reward (nafl)." So if the spoils had been for the slayer by a judgment of the Prophet (ﷺ), the matter would not have needed them to attribute that to their own ijtihad, and the slayer would have taken it without their order. And Allah knows best.

In the Sahih it is reported that Mu'adh ibn 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh and Mu'adh ibn 'Afra' struck Abu Jahl with their two swords until they killed him. They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Which of you killed him?" Each of them said: "I killed him." He looked at the two swords and said: "Both of you have killed him," and he awarded his spoils to Mu'adh ibn 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh. This is a clear text that the spoils are not for the slayer, for if they were his, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have divided them between them.

Also in the Sahih, from 'Awf ibn Malik, who said: I went out with those who went out with Zayd ibn Harithah in the battle of Mu'tah, and a reinforcement (madadi) [[i.e., a man from the reinforcements who came to support the army of Mu'tah and assist them]] from Yemen accompanied me. He narrated the hadith, and in it: 'Awf said: "O Khalid, did you not know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided that the spoils belong to the slayer?" He said: "Yes, but I considered it too much." Abu Bakr al-Barqani also transmitted it with his chain that Muslim had used, and he added clarification that 'Awf ibn Malik said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not take a fifth (khums) from the spoils. The reinforcement was a companion of theirs in the battle of Mu'tah on the edge of Syria. He said: A Roman among them began charging at the Muslims, on a chestnut horse, with a gilded saddle, a tarnished belt, and a sword decorated with gold. He said: He was inciting them against the Muslims. He said: The reinforcement subtly approached him until he passed by him, struck the hamstring of his horse so that it fell, then overpowered him with the sword, killed him, and took his weapons. He said: Khalid ibn al-Walid gave him (the spoils) and withheld part of them. 'Awf said: I said to him: "Give him all of it, have you not heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The spoils belong to the slayer'?" He said: "Yes, but I considered it too much." 'Awf said: There was a dispute between me and him, so I said to him: "I will inform the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." 'Awf said: When we gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'Awf mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to Khalid: "Why did you not give it to him?" He said: "I considered it too much." He said: "Then give it to him." I said to him: "Did I not fulfil for you what I promised you?" He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry and said: "O Khalid, do not give it to him. Will you leave my commanders for me?" [[In (b) and (z): "Umara'i" (my commanders) appears as "Asra" (my captives)]]. This clearly indicates that the slayer does not deserve the spoils by the act of killing itself, but by the opinion and judgment of the Imam.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: The spoils belong to the slayer only in single combat (mubarazah) specifically.

The fifth matter: The scholars differed concerning the taking of a fifth from the spoils (takhmis al-salab). Al-Shafi'i said: It is not subject to a fifth. Ishaq said: If the spoils are small, they belong to the slayer; if they are large, a fifth is taken from them. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab did this with al-Bara' ibn Malik when he fought the marzuban in single combat and killed him. The value of his belt and his two bracelets was thirty thousand, and he took a fifth of that. Anas narrated from al-Bara' ibn Malik that he killed a hundred men of the polytheists in single combat except one man, and that when they invaded al-Zara [[al-Zara: a village in Bahrain]], the dihqan (landowner) of al-Zara came out and said: "A man and a man." Al-Bara' came forward, and they struggled with their swords, then embraced. Al-Bara' threw him down and sat on his liver, then took the sword and slaughtered him, and took his weapons and his belt. He brought them to 'Umar, who gave him the weapons as a reward, and valued the belt at thirty thousand and took a fifth of it, and said: "It is wealth."

Al-Awza'i and Makhul said: The spoils are booty (maghnam), and in it there is a fifth. Something similar is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.

The evidence for al-Shafi'i is what Abu Dawud narrated from 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i and Khalid ibn al-Walid: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) decided concerning the spoils that they belong to the slayer, and did not take a fifth from the spoils.

The sixth matter: The majority of scholars held that the spoils are not given to the slayer unless he establishes evidence (bayyinah) of his killing. Most of them said: A single witness suffices, based on the hadith of Abu Qatadah. It was also said: Two witnesses, or one witness and an oath. Al-Awza'i said: It is given to him by the mere claim, and evidence is not a condition for entitlement; rather, if it happens, it is preferable to prevent dispute. Do you not see that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave Abu Qatadah the spoils of the one he killed without testimony or oath? A single witness is not sufficient, and no ruling is attached to it by itself. This is also the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd.

I say: I heard our shaykh, the hafiz al-Mundhiri al-Shafi'i, Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-'Azim, say: The Prophet (ﷺ) only gave him the spoils on the testimony of al-Aswad ibn Khuza'i and 'Abd Allah ibn Unays. On this basis the dispute is removed, the difficulty disappears, and the ruling is consistent. As for the Malikis, it follows from their view that the Imam does not need evidence in this matter, because it is, from the Imam at the outset, a gift (atiyyah). If he stipulates testimony, it is his right; and if he does not stipulate it, it is permissible for him to give it without testimony.

The seventh matter: They differed about what the spoils (salab) consist of. As for weapons and everything needed for fighting, there is no disagreement that it is part of the spoils, and so is his horse if he fought on it and was thrown from it. Ahmad said concerning the horse: It is not part of the spoils. Likewise, if in his money-belt (himyan) [[al-himyan: that in which provision is placed, or the drawstring of trousers]] and in his belt there are dinars, jewels, or the like, there is no disagreement that these are not part of the spoils. They differed concerning what is adorned for war. Al-Awza'i said: All of that is part of the spoils. A group said: It is not part of the spoils. This is narrated from Sahnun, may Allah have mercy on him, except that the belt is part of the spoils in his view. Ibn Habib said in al-Wadihah: The two bracelets are part of the spoils.

The eighth matter: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then to Allah belongs one-fifth of it﴾. Abu 'Ubayd said: This abrogates (nasikh) His saying, mighty and majestic, at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not take a fifth of the spoils of Badr, so his ruling regarding not taking a fifth was abrogated by this verse. However, it appears from the statement of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, in Sahih Muslim: "I had a she-camel (shari) from my share of the spoils on the day of Badr, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had given me a she-camel from the fifth on that day," the hadith, that he (the Prophet) did take a fifth. If this is so, then Abu 'Ubayd's view is rejected. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that the fifth which 'Ali mentioned was from one of the expeditions that took place between Badr and Uhud. There were the expedition of Banu Sulaym, the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, the expedition of Dhu Amarr, and the expedition of Buhran, and no fighting is recorded in them, but it is possible that booty was taken. And Allah knows best.

I say: This interpretation is refuted by the statement of 'Ali on that day, which refers to the day of the division of the spoils of Badr. However, it is possible that it was from the fifth of the expedition (sariyyah) of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, if no fifth had been taken at Badr, for it was the first booty taken in Islam and the first fifth in Islam. Then the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoils, then to Allah belongs one-fifth of it﴾. This is better than the first interpretation. And Allah knows best.

The ninth matter: The "ma" in His saying ﴿what you obtain﴾ is in the sense of "alladhi" (that which), and the pronoun is omitted, meaning "that which you obtained." The fa' ("then") entered because the sentence carries the sense of a conditional. The second "inna" is an emphasis of the first, and it may be pronounced with a kasra [i.e., "innama"], which is also narrated from Abu 'Amr. Al-Hasan [i.e., al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali, known as Ibn al-Hanafiyyah] said: This is the key to speech: "the world and the Hereafter belong to Allah," narrated by al-Nasa'i. Exalted and mighty is He, began the discourse on fay' (war-booty without fighting) and the fifth by mentioning Himself, because they are the most noble of earnings, and He did not attribute charity (sadaqah) to Himself because it is the dirt of people [[i.e., the impurities removed from people's wealth]].

The tenth matter: The scholars differed concerning how the fifth is to be divided, in six opinions.

The first: A group said: The fifth is divided into six parts. One sixth is given to the Ka'bah, and this is what belongs to Allah. The second is for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The third is for the near kin. The fourth is for orphans. The fifth is for the needy. The sixth is for the wayfarer. Some of the proponents of this view said: The share that belongs to Allah is returned to those in need.

The second: Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi' said: The booty is divided into five parts. One part is set aside, and the four parts are divided among the people. Then he strikes with his hand on the share he had set aside, and whatever he grasps from it he makes for the Ka'bah. Then he divides the rest of the share he had set aside into five: one part for the Prophet (ﷺ), one part for the near kin, one part for the orphans, one part for the needy, and one part for the wayfarer.

The third: al-Minhal ibn 'Amr said: I asked 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn about the fifth, and he said: "It belongs to us." I said to 'Ali: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿and the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾." He said: "Our orphans and our needy."

The fourth: al-Shafi'i said: It is divided into five. He held that the share of Allah and His Messenger is one, and that it is spent on the interests of the believers, and the four-fifths go to the four categories mentioned in the verse.

Fifth: Abu Hanifa said: it is divided into three: orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil). For him, the ruling concerning the kinship of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lapsed with his death, just as the ruling concerning his share lapsed. They said: from the khums one begins with the repair of bridges, the building of mosques, and the stipends of judges and soldiers. A similar view is also reported from al-Shafi'i.

Sixth: Malik said: it is left to the judgment and effort (ijtihad) of the imam (ruler). He takes from it without fixed measure, gives the relatives from it according to his judgment, and spends the remainder on the public interests of the Muslims. The Four Caliphs also said this and acted upon it. And the Prophet's ﷺ saying indicates it: "I have no share of what Allah has bestowed upon you except the khums, and the khums is returned to you." He did not divide it into fifths or thirds. Rather, the verse mentions those it mentions as a reminder about them, because they are among the most important recipients of it. Al-Zajjaj, arguing for Malik's view, said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents and near relatives, orphans, the needy and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215]. And it is permissible by consensus for a man to spend on other categories than these if he sees fit. Al-Nasa'i reported from Ata' who said: "The khums of Allah and the khums of His Messenger are one; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would take from it, give from it, place it wherever he wished, and do with it whatever he willed."

Eleventh: His saying, Exalted is He: "and to the near kin" (dhi al-qurba). The lam is not for indicating entitlement and ownership; rather it indicates the destination and the recipient. The evidence for this is what Muslim narrated: that al-Fadl ibn Abbas and Rabi'a ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib came to the Prophet ﷺ, and one of them spoke, saying: "O Messenger of Allah, you are the most righteous of people and the most connected of people, and we have reached the age of marriage. We have come so that you may appoint us over some of these charities, so that we may pay what people pay and receive what people receive." He remained silent for a long time until we wanted to speak to him. He said: "Zaynab began signaling to us from behind the screen not to speak to him." Then he said: "Indeed, charity is not lawful for the family of Muhammad; it is only the filth of people. Call for me Mahmiyya [he was Mahmiyya ibn Jaz', a man of Banu Asad] – and he was over the khums – and Nawfal ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib." So they came to him. He said to Mahmiyya: "Marry this youth your daughter" – meaning al-Fadl ibn Abbas – and he married him. And he said to Nawfal ibn al-Harith: "Marry this youth your daughter," meaning Rabi'a ibn Abd al-Muttalib. And he said to Mahmiyya: "Give as dowry from the khums such and such." And the Prophet ﷺ said: "I have no share of what Allah has bestowed upon you except the khums, and the khums is returned to you." He gave all of it and part of it, and he gave from it to those whose hearts were to be reconciled, and they are not among those Allah mentioned in the division. This indicates what we have mentioned. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Twelfth: Scholars differed about the near kin (dhawu al-qurba) in three opinions: that it is all of Quraysh – said by some of the early scholars, because when the Prophet ﷺ ascended al-Safa he began calling out: "O Banu so-and-so, O Banu Abd Manaf, O Banu Abd al-Muttalib, O Banu Ka'b, O Banu Murra, O Banu Abd Shams, save yourselves from the Fire" – the hadith, which will come in "al-Shu'ara'." Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Thawr, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj and Muslim ibn Khalid said: Banu Hashim and Banu Abd al-Muttalib, because when the Prophet ﷺ divided the share of the near kin between Banu Hashim and Banu Abd al-Muttalib, he said: "They never separated from me in the Jahiliyya or in Islam; indeed Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib are one thing," and he interlaced his fingers. Al-Nasa'i and al-Bukhari reported it. Al-Bukhari said: Al-Layth said: Yunus narrated to me, and added: "The Prophet ﷺ gave nothing to Banu Abd Shams or Banu Nawfal." Ibn Ishaq said: Abd Shams, Hashim and al-Muttalib were full brothers, their mother being Atika bint Murra, and Nawfal was their paternal half-brother. Al-Nasa'i said: The Prophet ﷺ assigned a share to the near kin, who are Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib, among whom the wealthy and the poor are alike. It has been said that it is for the poor among them only, not the wealthy, like orphans and the wayfarer – and this is, in my opinion, the more correct of the two views, and Allah knows best – and the young and the old, the male and the female, are equal, because Allah Most High assigned it to them, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided it among them. And there is nothing in the hadith that he preferred some of them over others. Third: Banu Hashim exclusively, said by Mujahid and Ali ibn al-Husayn. It is also the view of Malik, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i and others.

Thirteenth: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained the ruling of the khums and remained silent about the four-fifths, this indicates that they are the property of the warriors. The Prophet ﷺ made this explicit by his saying: "Any town that disobeys Allah and His Messenger, its khums is for Allah and His Messenger, and then the rest is yours." There is no disagreement about this among the community or among the imams, as Ibn al-Arabi related in his *Ahkam* and others. However, if the imam sees fit to show favor to the captives by releasing them, he may do so, and the rights of the warriors concerning them lapse, as the Prophet ﷺ did with Thumama ibn Uthal and others, and said: "If al-Mut'im ibn Adi were alive and then spoke to me about these stinking ones" – meaning the captives of Badr – "I would have left them to him." Al-Bukhari reported it, as a reward to him for his standing up regarding the annulment of the document [the document Quraysh had written not to trade with the Hashimites or the Muttalibites nor to marry them]. And it is permissible for him to kill all of them, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had killed Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it from among the captives by ṣabr (tying and shooting until death); likewise al-Nadr ibn al-Harith he killed at al-Safra' by ṣabr, and this is not disputed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had a share like the share of the warriors, whether he was present or absent. And there was the share of the ṣafiyy (the chosen portion), which he selected: a sword, an arrow, a servant, or a mount. Safiyya bint Huyayy was from the ṣafiyy from the spoils of Khaybar. Likewise Dhu al-Fiqar (the sword of the Prophet, peace be upon him, named so because it had small hollows, called fiqra) was from the ṣafiyy. It ended with his death, except according to Abu Thawr, who held that it remains for the imam, who would treat it as the share of the Prophet ﷺ. The wisdom behind this was that the people of the Jahiliyya used to consider that the leader takes a quarter of the booty. A poet of theirs said:

"For you is the quarter of it, and the chosen portions, and your judgment, and the nashita and the fudul."

The explanation: al-mirba' is a quarter; the ṣafaya is what is chosen; the nashita is what the chief obtains on the road before reaching the gathering of the tribe; the fudul is the surplus of the division that cannot properly be divided by the number of raiders, such as a camel or a horse and the like (from Lisan al-Arab).

Another said:

"From us is he who took the quarter of the armies for himself, twenty of his own offspring, and he is counted among the living."

It is said: "He quartered the army" (rabba'a al-jaysh, yarba'uhu, raba'a) when he took a quarter of the booty. Al-Asma'i said: A quarter in the Jahiliyya and a fifth in Islam. He used to take, without law or religion, the quarter of the booty, and select from it, and then after the ṣafiyy he would dispose of whatever he wished. Whatever was left over and surplus was of the household goods (khurthiyy) and his effects. So Allah, Glorified is He, perfected the religion by His saying: "And know that whatever you gain of spoil, a fifth of it belongs to Allah." He kept the share of the ṣafiyy for His Prophet ﷺ and abolished the ruling of the Jahiliyya. Amir al-Sha'bi said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had a share called the ṣafiyy: if he wished, a slave, a maid, or a horse which he chose before the khums; reported by Abu Dawud. In the hadith of Abu Hurayra, he said: "He meets the slave and says: 'O so-and-so, did I not honour you, make you a leader, marry you, subject for you horses and camels, and leave you to preside and take the quarter?'" – the hadith. Reported by Muslim. "Tarba'" with a ba' below: takes the mirba', that is, the quarter of what comes to your people of booty and earnings.

Some of al-Shafi'i's companions (may Allah be pleased with him) went so far as to say that the Prophet ﷺ used to spend a fifth of the khums on the sufficiency of his children and wives, and would store from it the provision for a year, and spend the rest on horses (al-kura') and weapons. This is refuted by what Umar narrated: the properties of Banu al-Nadir were among what Allah bestowed on His Messenger, which the Muslims had not pursued with horses or riding camels, so they were exclusively for the Prophet ﷺ, and he would spend on himself from them the provision of a year, and what remained he placed in horses and weapons as preparation in the way of Allah. Reported by Muslim. He also said: "And the khums is returned to you."

Fourteenth: There is no indication in the Book of Allah that the horseman is preferred over the foot soldier; rather it indicates that they are equal, because Allah Most High made the four-fifths theirs and did not single out a foot soldier from a horseman. Were it not for the reports from the Prophet ﷺ, the horseman would be like the foot soldier, the slave like the free man, and the child like the adult. The scholars have differed about the division of the four-fifths, and what the majority of the people of

The Fifteenth issue: a horseman is not given more than one horse's share over the foot soldier, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i.

Ibn al-Mundhir said that, among the scholars, a horseman receives two shares and a foot soldier one. Among those who held this view were Malik ibn Anas and those who followed him from the people of Madina; likewise al-Awza'i and those who agreed with him from the people of al-Sham; likewise al-Thawri and those who agreed with him from the people of Iraq; it is also the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd and those who followed him from the people of Egypt; likewise al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) and his companions; Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, Ya'qub and Muhammad also held it.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: We know of no one who opposed this except al-Nu'man (Abu Hanifa), for he opposed the Sunan and what most of the people of knowledge, both earlier and later, have held. He said: A horseman receives only one share.

I say: Perhaps he was confused by the hadith of Ibn Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the horseman two shares and the foot soldier one share. Al-Daraqutni narrated it and said: al-Ramadi said, "This is what Ibn Numayr says." Al-Nisaburi told us: "In my opinion this is a mistake either from Ibn Abi Shayba or from al-Ramadi, because Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abd al-Rahman ibn Bishr and others narrated it from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) with something different: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave a man and his horse three shares, one share for him and two shares for his horse. Abd al-Rahman ibn Bishr narrated it thus from Abd Allah ibn Numayr, from Ubayd Allah ibn Umar, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, and he mentioned the hadith." In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn Umar, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave the horse two shares and its rider one share. This is an explicit text.

Al-Daraqutni also narrated from al-Zubayr who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave me four shares on the day of Badr: two shares for my horse, one share for me, and one share for my mother from the kinsfolk. In another narration: "and one share for his mother, the share of the kinsfolk." And he narrated from Bashir ibn Amr ibn Muhsan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave my horse four shares and me one share, so I took five shares.

It was said that this matter is subject to the ruling of the Imam's ijtihad, so he implements what he sees. And Allah knows best.

The Fifteenth issue: No more than one horse is counted in the division between horseman and foot soldier, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: a share is given for more than one horse, because it brings more benefit and greater utility, and Ibn al-Jahm of our companions held this too, and Sahnun narrated it from Ibn Wahb. Our proof is that no report has come from the Prophet (ﷺ) that shares should be given for more than one horse, and likewise the Imams after him. Also, the enemy cannot be fought except on one horse, and anything beyond that is for comfort and an increase in equipment, and this does not affect the increase of shares, like one who carries extra swords or spears; and by analogy with the third and fourth (horses). It is narrated from Sulayman ibn Musa that a share is given to one who has horses, one share for each horse.

The Sixteenth issue: A share is only given for purebred horses (al-'itaq min al-khayl), because of their charging and retreating; and what is among the baradhin and the hujun is similar to them in this. What is not like this is not given a share. It was said: if the Imam permits them, he gives a share for them, because the benefit of them varies according to the place; the hujun and the baradhin are suitable for rough terrain like ravines and mountains, and the purebred horses are suitable for places where charging and retreating are possible, so this depends on the opinion of the Imam. Al-'itaq are the horses of the Arabs, and the hujun and baradhin are the horses of the Romans.

The Seventeenth issue: Our scholars differed about a weak horse. Ashhab and Ibn Nafi' said: no share is given for it, because fighting on it is impossible, so it resembles a broken (horse). It was said: a share is given for it, because its recovery is hoped for. No share is given for an emaciated horse when it is in the category of what gives no benefit, just as no share is given for a broken horse. As for a horse with a mild illness, such as one with a bruise (ruhaṣ, a sore on the sole of the hoof that weakens it), and what is similar to it, which does not prevent the sickness from achieving the benefit intended from it, a share is given for it. The borrowed horse and the hired horse are given (a share), and likewise the usurped horse, and its share goes to its owner. A share is due for horses even if they are on ships and the spoils are taken at sea, because they are prepared to land on the shore.

The Eighteenth issue: There is no right to spoils for the hashwa (the dregs of people), such as hired workers and craftsmen who accompany the army for livelihood, because they did not intend fighting nor did they go out as fighters. It was said: a share is given to them, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The spoils belong to whoever witnessed the battle." Al-Bukhari narrated it. But there is no proof in this, because it came as an explanation for those who engaged in war and went out to it; and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sufficed as explanation of the fighters and the livelihood-seekers among the Muslims, when He made them two distinct groups, each with its own ruling. He said: ﴿He knows that there will be among you some who are sick, and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others who fight in the cause of Allah﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. However, when these people fight, their being engaged in livelihood does not harm them, because the cause of entitlement has been met in them. Ashhab said: none of them is entitled, even if he fights; and Ibn al-Qassar, regarding the hired worker, said: no share is given to him even if he fights. This is refuted by the hadith of Salama ibn al-Akwa', who said: I was a servant of Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, giving his horse water, cleaning it and serving it, and eating from its food, the hadith... and in it: Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave me two shares, the share of the horseman and the share of the foot soldier, and he combined them for me. Muslim narrated it.

Ibn al-Qassar and those who agreed with him used the hadith of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, which Abd al-Razzaq mentioned, and in it: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Abd al-Rahman: "These three dinars are his portion and his share from his raid, in matters of his worldly life and his afterlife."

The Nineteenth issue: As for slaves and women, the position of al-Kitab is that no share is given to them, and they are not given a rada' (a gift that is not large). It was said: a rada' is given to them, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. Al-Awza'i said: if a woman fights, a share is given to her. He claimed that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave shares to women on the day of Khaybar. He said: The Muslims in our land act according to this. Ibn Habib of our companions also inclined to this view. Muslim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he wrote in his letter to Najda (Najda ibn Amir al-Hanafi, one of the leaders of the Kharijites): "You ask me whether the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to fight with women? He used to fight with them, and they would treat the wounded and give them a hudhwa (a gift) from the spoils, but they were not given a share." As for boys, if he is capable of fighting, there are three opinions among us: that a share is given and that it is withheld until he reaches puberty, based on the hadith of Ibn Umar, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i; and a distinction between one who fights, so a share is given to him, and one who fights but is not given a share. The correct one is the first, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) command regarding the Banu Qurayza that those among them who had grown hair (the pubic hair sign of puberty) be killed, and those who had not grown hair be spared. This is a consideration of capacity for fighting, not of puberty. Abu Umar narrated in al-Istiab from Samura ibn Jundub who said: The young men of the Ansar were presented to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he would admit those among them who had reached (fighting age). I was presented to him one year, and he admitted a young man and sent me back. I said: O Messenger of Allah, you admitted him and sent me back, and if he wrestled with me I would have thrown him. He said: So he wrestled with me, and I threw him, and he admitted me. As for slaves, no share is given to them either, but a rada' is given to them.

The Twentieth issue: If a disbeliever attends with the permission of the Imam and fights, there are three opinions among us regarding giving him a share: a share is given, and it is withheld; this is the view of Malik and Ibn al-Qasim. Ibn Habib added: and they have no portion at all. The third opinion, which is Sahnun's, distinguishes between the Muslims being able to manage on their own, so no share is given to him, or not being able to manage and needing his help, so a share is given to him. If he does not fight, he is not entitled to anything. The same applies to slaves alongside free men. Al-Thawri and al-Awza'i said: when the people of dhimma are called upon for help, a share is given to them. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: no share is given to them, but a rada' is given to them. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the Imam should hire them from money that has no specific owner; if he does not do so, he gives them the share of the Prophet (ﷺ). In another place he said: a rada' is given to polytheists if they fight alongside the Muslims. Abu Umar said: All agree that a slave, who is among those whose safe-conduct is valid [in b: "and he is a believer, it is permissible..."], if he fights, is not given a share but is given a rada'; so a disbeliever is even more deserving of not being given a share.

The Twenty-first issue: If slaves and people of the dhimma go out as highwaymen and seize the property of the people of war, it belongs to them and is not subject to the one-fifth, because they are not included in the general scope of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, saying: "And know that whatever you gain of spoil, one-fifth of it is for Allah." None of them is included, nor women. As for disbelievers, they have no entitlement, without dispute. Sahnun said: what falls to the slave is not subject to the one-fifth. Ibn al-Qasim said: it is subject to the one-fifth, because it is possible that his master permits him to fight and he fights for the religion, unlike the disbeliever. Ashhab said in the Kitab of Muhammad: If a slave and a dhimmi go out from the army and seize booty, the spoils belong to the army and not to them.

**The twenty-second issue:** The reason for entitlement to a share (*sahm*) is attending the battle to support the Muslims, as already explained. If someone joins at the end of the battle, he is entitled. If he arrives after the fighting has ended, he is not. If he was absent because he fled in defeat, the ruling is the same. If, however, he withdrew with the intention of rejoining a company (*fi'ah*) of fighters, his entitlement is not forfeited.

Al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent Aban ibn Sa'id on an expedition (*sariyyah*) from Madinah towards Najd. Aban ibn Sa'id and his companions came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at Khaybar after he had conquered it, and the saddle-bags of their horses were made of palm fibre. Aban said, "Give us a share, O Messenger of God." Abu Hurayrah said: [I said [[From manuscripts J, Z, K.]] "Do not give them a share, O Messenger of God." Aban said, "You, O Wabr, have come down upon us from the top of a *dall* tree."[[*Al-wabr*: a small creature about the size of a cat, greyish or white, with beautiful eyes and very shy. *Al-dall*: the sidr tree, one of the thorny trees. In manuscript B: "came down upon us from the top of a dall."]] The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, "Sit down, O Aban," and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not give them a share.

**The twenty-third issue:** The scholars differed regarding a person who set out to attend the battle but was prevented by an excuse, such as illness. Concerning whether a share is granted to him or denied, there are three opinions. The third opinion distinguishes, and it is the well-known one: he is granted a share if he went astray (*dalal*) before the fighting and after the troops had entered enemy territory (*idrab*),[[*Adraba al-qawm*: when the people entered the land of the enemy.]] and this is the most sound view, as stated by Ibn al-Arabi. He is denied a share if he went astray before that point.

If the commander sent him from the army on a matter of the army's interest, and this occupied him so that he missed attending the battle, then he is granted a share. This was said by Ibn al-Mawwaz, and Ibn Wahb and Ibn Nafi' narrated it from Malik. It was also narrated that he is not given a full share but a *rudkh*, a small gift, because the reason which entitles one to a full share is absent. And God knows best.

Ashhab said: a prisoner is given a share even if he is in chains. The sound view, however, is that he is not given a share, because the share is an ownership (*milk*) that is earned by fighting, so whoever is absent, or present but ill, is treated like one who did not attend.

**The twenty-fourth issue:** A person who is absent without any particular reason is not granted a share. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) never gave a share to an absent person except on the day of Khaybar, when he gave a share to the people of Hudaybiyyah who were present and to those who were absent, in accordance with God's words, ﴿God has promised you many spoils that you will take﴾ [al-Fath: 20].[[See vol. 16, p. 278.]] This was said by Musa ibn Uqbah, and it was narrated from a group of the early scholars (*salaf*).

On the day of Badr, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave a share to Uthman, Sa'id ibn Zayd and Talhah, who were absent. They are therefore counted like those who attended, if God the Exalted wills. As for Uthman, he stayed behind to care for Ruqayyah, the daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by his command, because she was ill. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) assigned him his share and his reward, and he was counted as one who attended. As for Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah, he was in Syria on trade, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) assigned him his share and his reward, and so he is counted among the people of Badr. As for Sa'id ibn Zayd, he was also absent in Syria, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) assigned him his share and his reward, so he is counted among those of Badr.

Ibn al-Arabi said: As for the people of Hudaybiyyah, it was a promise from God specific to those men, so no one else shares in it. As for Uthman, Sa'id and Talhah, it is possible that a share was given to them from the *khums* (one-fifth of the spoils),[[*Khums*: the one-fifth of the spoils set aside for the public treasury and specified recipients.]] because the community is agreed that whoever remains behind for an excuse is not given a share.

I say: The apparent meaning is that this is specific to Uthman, Talhah and Sa'id, so others cannot be compared to them, and that their share came from the main body of the spoils (*sulb al-ghanimah*), like everyone else who attended, not from the *khums*. This is the apparent meaning of the traditions, and God knows best.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: When Uthman was absent from Badr, he was married to the daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who was ill. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "You have the reward of a man who attended Badr, and his share."

**The twenty-fifth issue:** God the Exalted says, ﴿if you have believed in God﴾. Al-Zajjaj reported from a group of scholars that the meaning is: "Know that God is your protector, if you are [believers]." Thus the *in* (if) is connected to this promise. Another group said that the *in* is connected to His words, ﴿and know that whatever you gain as spoils﴾. Ibn Atiyyah said: This is the sound view, because His words "and know" include the command to submit and to comply with God's ruling concerning the spoils. So the *in* is connected to "and know" on this meaning, that is: if you are believers in God, then submit and comply with God's ruling concerning what He has made you know about the division of the spoils.

**The twenty-sixth issue:** God the Exalted says, ﴿And what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of the Criterion﴾.[[It is evident that the twenty-sixth issue is this verse, because it is part of the same discussion.]] The word *ma* (what) is in the genitive position, coordinated with the word "God" (*ism Allah*) in "the Day of the Criterion", meaning the day on which I separated truth from falsehood, and that is the day of Badr. ﴿The day the two hosts met﴾: the party of God and the party of Satan. ﴿And God is over all things competent﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you were on the near side of the valley, and they were on the far side﴾. That is, We sent down [the event] at the time when you were in this condition. Or the meaning may be: "Remember when you were..."

Al-'Adwah (the side or bank of a valley). It is also read with a damma and with a kasra on the ain. With a damma, the plural is 'Uda; with a kasra, it is 'Idan, like liḥyah (beard) and liḥan, and firyah (falsehood) and firan.

Al-Dunya is the feminine of al-adna (the nearer), and al-Quswa is the feminine of al-aqsa (the farther). They derive from dana yadnu and qasa yaqsu. It is also said al-Qusya, though the original root is waw, and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz: quswa. So al-Dunya was the side nearer to Madinah, and al-Quswa the side nearer to Makkah. That is, when you were camped on the edge of the valley on the nearer side to Madinah, your enemy was on the farther side.

﴿And the caravan was below you﴾. He means the caravan of Abu Sufyan and others. They were in a place lower than them, down to the seashore, where the goods were. It is also said that it refers to the camels carrying their goods, which were in a place where they were safe, as a success from Allah, mighty and majestic, granted to them; so He reminded them of His favour upon them. "Al-Rakb" is the subject (mubtada'), and "asfala minkum" is an adverbial complement (zarf) in the position of the predicate, meaning: in a place lower than you. Al-Akhfash, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' permitted "wal-rakbu asfala minkum," meaning: more lowly than you. Al-Rakb is the plural of rakib (rider). The Arabs do not say rakb except for a group of riders on camels. Ibn al-Sikkit and most lexicographers related that rakib and rakb are used only for one who is on camels, and one on a horse or other mount is not called rakib. Al-Rakb, al-Arkub, al-Rukban and al-Rakibun refer only to those on camels, according to Ibn Faris.

﴿Even if you had made an appointment together, you would have differed about the appointment﴾. That is, agreement would not have occurred because of their number and your small number, for if you had known their great number, you would have held back; so Allah, mighty and majestic, brought you together [despite it] (in another reading: "you would have fallen behind").

﴿That Allah might accomplish a matter that was to be done﴾. This is the victory of the believers and the manifestation of the religion. The lam in "li-yaqdiya" is connected to an omitted verb, and the meaning is: He gathered them so that Allah might accomplish [it]. Then He repeated it, saying: "li-yahlika," meaning: He gathered them there so that He might decree a matter.

﴿So that whoever perished might perish by clear proof﴾. "Man" is in the nominative position.

﴿And whoever lived might live by clear proof﴾. "Yahya" is in the accusative position, coordinated with "li-yahlika." Al-bayyinah is the establishment of proof and evidence, meaning: whoever dies, dies after a clear sign he has seen and a lesson he has witnessed, so that proof is established against him; and likewise the life of whoever lives. Ibn Ishaq said: "li-yakfura man kafara ba'da hujjatin qamat 'alayhi" means that whoever disbelieves after a proof has been established against him and his excuse cut off, and whoever believes believes on that basis.

It was also read as "man hayy" with two yas in accordance with the original form, and with a single shaddah yā'. The first (reading) is that of the people of Madinah, al-Bazzi and Abu Bakr. The second is the reading of the rest, and it is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, because it is written thus in the Mushaf.

Mujahid said: The Prophet (ﷺ) saw them (the disbelievers) as few in his dream, so he related that to his Companions, and Allah strengthened them thereby. It was also said: by "the dream" is meant the place of sleep, which is the eye, i.e., "in the place of your sleep," with an ellipsis; this is from al-Hasan. Al-Zajjaj said: This is a good opinion, but the first is more fitting in Arabic, because it has come (in the Qur'an): ﴿And when He showed them to you as few when you met, and He made you few in their eyes﴾. This indicates that the former is the seeing at the encounter, and that the latter is the seeing in sleep. The meaning of (lafashiltum) is: you would have become cowardly in the war.

(Wa-latana'aztum fi al-amr) means: you would have disagreed.

(Wa-lakinna Allaha sallama) means: He protected you from opposition. Ibn 'Abbas said: from failure (fashal). It may include both of them. It was also said: sallama means He completed the affair of the Muslims with victory.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when He showed them to you as few in your eyes when you met [in battle]﴾. This refers to wakefulness. It is also permissible to read the first [sighting] as referring to wakefulness, if you say that al-manam (the place of sleep) is the eye. In that case the first [sighting] is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, and this one applies to everyone.

Ibn Mas'ud said: I said to a man beside me on the day of Badr, "Do you see them as seventy?" He said, "They are about a hundred." Then we took a man prisoner and asked him, "How many were you?" He said, "We were a thousand."

(And He makes you appear few in their eyes.) This occurred at the beginning of the fighting, until Abu Jahl said on that day, "They are only camel-eaters [i.e., they are few; the meat of one camel is enough to satisfy them], seize them alive and bind them with ropes." When they engaged in the fighting, the Muslims became great in their eyes, and so they appeared many, as He said: ﴿They see them as twice their number with their own eyes﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13], as its explanation has been given earlier in (Al 'Imran) [see vol. 4, p. 25].

(That Allah may accomplish a matter that was decreed to be done.) This is repeated, because the meaning of the first [mention] concerns the encounter, and the meaning of the second concerns the killing of the polytheists and the exaltation of the religion, which is the completion of His favour upon the Muslims.

(And to Allah are all matters returned.) That is, their final outcome and their return are to Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 45:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when you encounter a company [fi'ah]﴾, meaning a group, (fa-uthbutu) "then stand firm" is a command to steadfastness when fighting the disbelievers. As in the verse before it there is a prohibition against fleeing from them, so the command and the prohibition meet on equal footing. This is an emphasis on standing firm before the enemy and bearing up against him.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and remember Allah much, so that you may prosper﴾. The scholars have three opinions regarding this remembrance. The first: remember Allah at the moment your hearts tremble, for His remembrance helps one to stand firm in hardship. The second: stand firm with your hearts and remember Him with your tongues, for the heart does not stay calm at the meeting and the tongue becomes agitated; so He commanded remembrance so that the heart may stand firm upon certainty and the tongue may stand firm upon remembrance, and so that one says what the companions of Talut said: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 256.]] [al-Baqarah: 250]. This state is only attained through strength of knowledge and kindling of insight, and it is the praiseworthy courage among people. The third: remember what you have of Allah's promise to you in His purchase of your selves and His exchange with you.

I say: the most apparent meaning is the remembrance of the tongue in agreement with the heart. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: If anyone were given leave to abandon remembrance, Zakariyya would have been given leave, since Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿that you shall not speak to the people for three days except by gesture; and remember your Lord much﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 80.]] [Al 'Imran: 41]. And a man in battle would be given leave, since Allah, mighty and majestic, says: "When you encounter a company, stand firm and remember Allah much." Qatadah said: Allah, mighty and majestic, made His remembrance obligatory upon His servants, and they are most occupied with it at the clash of swords [[In manuscripts b, j, k, z and al-Bahr: "al-dirab" (the clashing) and "al-suyuf" (the swords).]]. The ruling on this remembrance is that it should be silent, because raising the voice in places of fighting is reprehensible and disliked when the one remembering is alone. But if it comes from all together at the charge, it is good, because it weakens the enemy's arms. Abu Dawud related from Qays ibn 'Abbad who said: The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked raising the voice during fighting. Abu Burdah related from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. Ibn 'Abbas said: Covering the face (talaththum) is disliked during fighting. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: By this, and Allah knows best, the garrison soldiers adopted the practice of removing it during fighting, to protect themselves through it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute with one another﴾. This is a continuation of the admonition to them, and of restraining them (from wrongdoing), regarding their disagreement and dispute over the matter of Badr.

(﴿And lose heart﴾) is in the accusative by the fa' (فَ), as a response to the prohibition. Sibawayh does not permit omitting the fa' and the jussive (jazm), but al-Kisa'i permitted it. It has been read as "تَفْشِلُوا" with a kasra on the shin, but this reading is not well known.

(﴿And your strength will depart﴾): that is, your power and your victory, just as one says: "the wind (rih) is for so-and-so" when he prevails in the matter. The poet said:

إِذَا هَبَّتْ رِيَاحُكَ فَاغْتَنِمْهَا ... فَإِنَّ لِكُلِّ خَافِقَةٍ سكون
When your winds blow, seize them, for every fluttering (wind) has a calm.

[The rhyme is in the nominative, and the noun of (inna) here is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). And his saying "(li-kulli khafiqatin sukūn)" is its predicate. In manuscripts ج and هـ it reads "ʿāṣifa" (stormy), which is a variant reading. From this qasida also:

وَلَا تَغْفُلْ عَنِ الْإِحْسَانِ فِيهَا ... فَمَا تَدْرِي السكون متى يكون
Do not neglect kindness in it, for you do not know when the calm will come.]

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: there has never been a victory except by a wind that blows and strikes in the faces of the disbelievers. From this is his saying, peace be upon him (ﷺ): "I was given victory by the east wind (al-Saba), and 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (al-Dabur)." [Al-Saba (with a fatha): the east wind. Al-Dabur: the west wind.] Al-Hakam said: "And your strength will depart" means al-Saba, for by it Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community were given victory. Mujahid said: the wind of the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) departed when they disputed with him on the day of Uhud.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And be patient; indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾. This is a command to patience, which is praiseworthy in all situations, and especially in the place of battle, as He said: "When you meet a company, then stand firm."

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 47:

He means Abu Jahl and his companions who set out on the day of Badr to protect the caravan. They went out with the *qiyan* [[al-qiyan: plural of qayna, meaning a female slave, whether she sings or not. al-Ma'azif: the musical instruments.]] and the singing girls and the instruments of entertainment. When they reached al-Juhfa, Khufaf al-Kinani, who was a friend of Abu Jahl, sent gifts to him with his son, and said: "If you wish, I will send you men, and if you wish, I will send you myself with whoever of my people is able to go." Abu Jahl said: "If we are fighting God, as Muhammad claims, then by God we have no power against God. But if we are fighting people, then by God we have strength over people. By God, we will not turn back from fighting Muhammad until we reach Badr, where we will drink wine and the singing girls will play for us, for Badr is one of the seasons of the Arabs and one of their markets, so that the Arabs will hear of our going forth and will fear us forever."

So they arrived at Badr [[من ج وك وى.]] [but [[from ج, ك and ى.]]] what happened to them of destruction happened.

*Al-batar* in the language is the exultation in the blessings of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and in the well-being He has clothed them with, while committing sins. It is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial state (hal). That is, they went out *bataran* (insolent) and *mura'in* (showing off) and *sadin* (barring others). And their barring was the misguiding of people.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 48:

It is narrated that Satan appeared to them that day in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, who was from Banu Bakr ibn Kinanah. The Quraysh feared Banu Bakr, lest they attack them from behind, because they had killed a man from among them. So when he appeared to them, he said what Allah has reported of him. Al-Dahhak said: Iblis came to them on the day of Badr with his banner and his troops, and cast into their hearts that they would not be defeated while they were fighting for the religion of their forefathers. From Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah reinforced His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the believers with a thousand angels. Jibril (peace be upon him) was with five hundred angels in a flank (mujannibah) [[Mujannibat al-jaysh (the flank of an army): it is that which is on the right wing and the left wing, and they are two flanks, with the nun pronounced with a kasra. It was also said: it is the detachment that occupies one of the two sides of the road.]], and Mika'il was with five hundred angels in a flank. Iblis came with a troop of devils, and with him a banner, in the form of men from Banu Mudlij, while Satan was in the form of Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum. Satan said to the polytheists: "No one among the people will overcome you today, and I am a protector for you." When the two sides lined up, Abu Jahl said: "O Allah, grant victory to whichever of us is upon the truth." And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ raised his hands and said: "O Lord, if You destroy this band, You will not be worshipped on the earth ever." Then Jibril said: "Take a handful of dust," so he took a handful of dust and threw it at their faces, and there was not one of the polytheists who was not struck in his eyes, his nostrils and his mouth. Then they turned their backs in flight. Jibril (peace be upon him) approached Iblis, and when Iblis saw him, his hand was in the hand of a man from the polytheists. Iblis withdrew his hand and turned his back in flight, along with his followers. The man said to him: "O Suraqah, did you not claim that you were a protector for us?" He said: "I am innocent of you; I see what you do not see." Related by al-Bayhaqi and others. In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Ablah, from Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Kurayz, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Satan has never been seen to be smaller, more humiliated, more repelled, or more enraged on any day than on the Day of Arafah. That is only because of what he sees of the descent of mercy and Allah's forgiveness of great sins. Except what he saw on the Day of Badr." It was said: "And what did he see on the Day of Badr, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Indeed, he saw Jibril arranging the angels (yaza'u al-mala'ikah)." [[Yaza' al-mala'ikah: i.e., arranging them, setting them in order, and lining them up for battle.]]

The meaning of nakasa is "to return," in the dialect of Sulaym, according to Mu'arrij [[This is Mu'arrij ibn 'Amr al-Sadusi, kunyah Abu Fayd, who died in 195 AH.]] and others. The poet said:

"Retreating on one's heels is no nobility; indeed, nobility is advancing upon the spears."

[[Al-asal: spears and arrows.]]

And another said:

"Their retreat does not benefit those who hang back, nor does advancing harm the people of the forward charge."

Here, however, nakas does not mean backward stepping (qahqara) but flight, as he said: "When he hears the call to prayer, he turns his back and has a fart."

("Indeed I fear Allah.") It was said: Iblis feared that the Day of Badr was the day he had been reprieved until. It was also said: Iblis lied in his saying, "Indeed I fear Allah," but he knew that he had no power.

The word jar (neighbor/protector) is pluralized as ajwar and jiran, and in the rare usage, jirah.

"It has been said: 'The hypocrites' are those who openly showed faith while concealing disbelief. 'Those in whose hearts is a disease' are the doubters, who are below the hypocrites, because they were recent converts to Islam and there is in them some weakness of intention. They said, when going out to fight and when the two armies met: ﴿Their religion has deluded these people﴾. It has also been said that they are one and the same, and this is the more likely view. Do you not see the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:3], then He said: ﴿and who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾[[See vol. 1, p. 162.]] [al-Baqarah 2:4], and they are one and the same."

Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, commentary on Surah 8, verses 50–51:

It has been said: he meant those who remained and were not killed on the day of Badr. And it has been said: it refers to those who were killed at Badr. The response to "law" (if/had) is omitted, its implied sense being: "you would have seen a tremendous matter."

(yadribuna) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

(wujuhahum wa adbarahum): i.e., their buttocks (astahahum); he used "backs" (adbar) as a euphemism for them. This was said by Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Hasan said: their backs. He said: A man said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah, I saw on the back of Abu Jahl something like a shirak?" [[Al-shirak: the strap of a sandal.]] He said: "That is the striking of the angels." It has also been said: this striking takes place at the time of death. It may also occur on the Day of Resurrection, when they are driven to the Fire.

(wa dhuqu 'adhab al-hariq): Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "and they say, 'Taste...'", so it was omitted. Al-Hasan said: this is on the Day of Resurrection; the keepers of Hell say to them: "Taste the punishment of the burning." It is also reported in some tafsirs that with the angels there were iron maces, and whenever they struck, the fire flared up in the wounds; this is the meaning of His words: "and taste the punishment of the burning." Tasting (dhawq) can be sensory and can be figurative. It may also be used in place of testing and trial. You say: "Ride this horse and taste it," and "Look at so-and-so and taste what he has." Al-Shammakh, describing a horse, said:

"So it tasted, and it gave him a side of its softness... sufficient for its ardor that the arrow-shaft's barrier keeps it from sinking."

[[In al-Lisan: that is, there is a barrier that prevents sinking; i.e., there is in it both softness and firmness.]]

Its origin is from tasting with the mouth.

(dhalika) is in the nominative position: i.e., the matter is that; or "dhalika" is your recompense.

(bima qaddamat aydikum): i.e., what you earned of sins.

(wa anna Allaha laysa bizallamin lil-'abid): since He has made the path clear and sent the messengers, so why did you oppose? "Wa anna" is in the genitive position, conjoined with "ma"; if you wish, you may put it in the accusative, meaning "and by that" (wa bi-anna), with the preposition elided; or in the sense "and that is because Allah..." It is also permissible for it to be in the nominative position, conjoined to "dhalika."
