Al-Da'b means the habit or custom (al-'adah). It was discussed earlier in "Al 'Imran" [see vol. 4, p. 22]. That is, the custom regarding their punishment at the taking of souls and in the graves is like the custom of the family of Pharaoh.

It has also been said: the meaning is that these people were requited with killing and captivity, just as the family of Pharaoh were requited with drowning. That is, their case (da'b) is like the case of the family of Pharaoh.

This punishment is because they changed and altered [the favour], and God's favour upon Quraysh was abundance and plenty, and security and well-being. ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67] and the rest of the verse. [See vol. 13, p. 363.] Al-Suddi said: God's favour upon them was Muhammad (ﷺ), but they disbelieved in him, so he was moved to Medina, and the punishment descended upon the polytheists.

This is not a repetition, because the first (occurrence) refers to the customary practice regarding denial, and the second refers to the customary practice regarding change. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 55–56:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living beings in the sight of Allah﴾, i.e., whoever crawls upon the face of the earth in the knowledge and judgment of Allah.

(Those who disbelieve, for they will not believe.) Its parallel is ﴿the deaf and the dumb who do not reason﴾ [al-Anfal: 22].[[See vol. 7, p. 388.]] Then He described them, saying: (Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they do not fear [Allah].) I.e., they do not fear retribution. The "min" (from) in His saying "minhum" (from among them) is partitive (lit-tab'id), because the covenant was only made with their nobles, and then they would break it. Those meant are Qurayzah and al-Nadir, according to Mujahid and others. They broke the covenant and aided the polytheists of Makkah with weapons. Then they made excuses, saying: "We forgot." So he (ﷺ) made a covenant with them a second time, and they broke it on the day of the Trench (Yawm al-Khandaq).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 55–56:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living beings in the sight of Allah﴾, i.e., whoever crawls upon the face of the earth in the knowledge and judgment of Allah.

(Those who disbelieve, for they will not believe.) Its parallel is ﴿the deaf and the dumb who do not reason﴾ [al-Anfal: 22].[[See vol. 7, p. 388.]] Then He described them, saying: (Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time, and they do not fear [Allah].) I.e., they do not fear retribution. The "min" (from) in His saying "minhum" (from among them) is partitive (lit-tab'id), because the covenant was only made with their nobles, and then they would break it. Those meant are Qurayzah and al-Nadir, according to Mujahid and others. They broke the covenant and aided the polytheists of Makkah with weapons. Then they made excuses, saying: "We forgot." So he (ﷺ) made a covenant with them a second time, and they broke it on the day of the Trench (Yawm al-Khandaq).

The condition and its response. The nun was added for emphasis when *mā* was added. This is the view of the Basrans. The Kufans said: the heavy and light nun both occur with *immā* in conditional constructions, to distinguish the conditional from the optional (*al-takhyīr*). The meaning of *tathqafannahum* is: you capture them and put them in a *thiqāf* (a state of being bound), or you meet them in a state of weakness in which you have power over them and overcome them. This is required by the wording, because of His words, "in the war." Some people said: you encounter them and come upon them. It is said: *thaqiftuhu athqafuhu thaqafan*, meaning I found him. A man is *thaqif laqif*, meaning quick to find what he seeks and tries to reach. Also *thaqf laqf*. A woman is *thaqaf*. The first view is better, because it is connected to the verse, as we have explained. Whoever is encountered may be overcome, so one may be made an example of him, or he may not be overcome. *Al-thiqāf* in the language is that with which a spear-shaft or the like is bound. From it is the verse of al-Nabigha:

*You call Qu'ayn while the iron has bitten them,*
*bitten as the thiqāf bites over the hollow joints of the spear.*

[[Qu'ayn (with a vowel on the first letter): a short nose, extremely flat. Qu'ayn is a tribe derived from it; there are two Qu'ayns: one among Banu Asad and one among Qays 'Aylan. *Al-anābīb* is the plural of *unbūba*, which is the joint of the reed and of the spear.]]

﴿So make an example of those behind them﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is, warn by means of them those behind them. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is the dialect of Quraysh: *sharrid bihim* means *sammi' bihim* (make them a warning). al-Dahhak said: *nakkil bihim* (make an example of them). al-Zajjaj: do to them an act of killing by which you scatter those behind them. *Al-tashrīd* in the language means dispersal and scattering. It is said: *sharraddtu banī fulān* meaning I uprooted them from their places and drove them away from them until they left them. The same applies to the individual: you say, "I left him a fugitive (*sharīd*) from his homeland and his family." The poet of Hudhayl said:

*I roam the valleys every day,*
*for fear that Hakim will drive me out as a fugitive.*

From it: *sharada al-ba'īr* and *al-dābba* when they break away from their owner. "Man" means "those who" (*alladhī*), said al-Kisa'i. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud: *fa-sharridh* with the dotted *dhāl*, and both are two dialects. Qutrub said: *al-tashrīdh* (with the dotted *dhāl*) is making an example, and with the undotted *dāl* it is scattering, as related by al-Tha'labi. al-Mahdawi said: the *dhāl* has no basis, unless it is a substitute for the undotted *dāl* because of their closeness; and *fasharidh* is not known in the language. It is also read *min khalfihim* with a kasra on the *mīm* and the *fā'*.

﴿So that they may remember﴾: that is, they may remember through your promise to them. It was also said: this refers to those behind them, because whoever is killed does not remember. That is, make an example of them to those behind them who act as they acted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 58:

There are three issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾, meaning deceit and the breaking of the covenant.

(﴿Then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾). This verse was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir, and al-Tabari related it from Mujahid. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What appears from the wording of the Qur'an is that the address concerning the Banu Qurayzah ended at His saying, "so scatter those behind them," and then, blessed and exalted is He, began in this verse with a command concerning what he should do in the future with those whom he fears treachery from, so this verse is placed in relation to them. [The Banu Qurayzah were not among those whose treachery is feared, rather their treachery was manifest and well known.] [[Supplement from the tafsir of Ibn 'Atiyyah.]]

The second: Ibn al-'Arabi said: If it is asked, how is it permissible to break a covenant out of fear of treachery, given that fear is a supposition and not certainty, so how can the certainty of the covenant be dropped on the basis of suspicion of treachery? The answer is in two respects. The first: fear may come with the meaning of certainty, just as hope may come with the meaning of knowledge. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect for God any dignity?﴾ [Nuh: 13]. The second: when the signs of treachery appear and its evidences are established, it becomes obligatory to throw back the covenant, lest persistence in it lead to ruin, and dropping certainty here is permitted out of necessity. As for when certainty is known, one is free from throwing back the covenant to them; the Prophet ﷺ marched toward the people of Makkah in the year of the conquest, when their breaking of the covenant had become well known, without throwing back their covenant to them. "Al-nabdh" means throwing and rejecting. Al-Azhari said: its meaning is that if you make a covenant with a people and you know from them a breach of the covenant, then do not strike them before announcing to them that you have annulled the covenant and the truce, so that they are equal with you in knowledge of the breach, and then strike them. Al-Nahhas said: This is among the miraculous features of what came in the Qur'an, which cannot be found in speech like it, despite its brevity and the abundance of its meanings. The meaning is: if you fear from a people with whom you have a covenant treachery, then throw back to them the covenant, that is, say to them: "I have thrown back to you your covenant, and I am going to fight you," so that they know that, and they are equal with you in knowledge, and do not fight them while there is a covenant between you and them and they trust you, for that would be treachery and betrayal. Then He clarified this by His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not love the treacherous﴾. I say: what al-Azhari and al-Nahhas mentioned, of throwing back the covenant while knowing of its breach, is refuted by what the Prophet ﷺ did at the conquest of Makkah, for when they breached it he did not notify them, but said: (O God, cut off news from them) and raided them. And this is also the meaning of the verse, because in cutting the covenant from them and breaking it with knowledge of it there is the occurrence of the breaking of their covenant and equality with them. As for without knowledge of their breaking the covenant, it is not lawful and not permissible. Al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud related from Sulaym ibn 'Amir who said: There was a covenant between Mu'awiyah and the Romans, and he was marching toward their lands so as to be close, so that when the covenant expired he would raid them. A man came to him on a horse or a mule, saying: "God is greatest, God is greatest, [fulfilment, not treachery]," so they looked and it was 'Amr ibn 'Anbasah. Mu'awiyah sent for him and asked him, and he said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: (Whoever has between himself and a people a covenant, let him not tie a knot or untie it until its term has ended or he throws back to them on equal terms). So Mu'awiyah turned back with the people. Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hadith that is good and sound. And "al-sawa'" means equality and moderation.

And the reciter said:

So strike the faces of the treacherous enemies until they answer you with equality.

Al-Kisa'i said: "al-sawa'" means justice. It may also mean the middle, and from it is His saying: ﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 55]. And from it is the saying of Hassan:

Woe to the companions of the Prophet and his kin, after the burial in the midst of the tomb.

Al-Farra' said: It is said "then throw back to them on equal terms" openly, not secretly.

The third: Muslim related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: (For every treacherous one there is a banner on the Day of Resurrection raised for him according to the measure of his treachery. Indeed, there is no more treacherous one than the leader of the general public). Our scholars, may God have mercy upon them, said: Treachery against the imam is greater and more abominable than in other cases, because of the harm in it, for if they betray and this is known of them and the covenant is not thrown back, the enemy will not trust them regarding any covenant or truce, so their strength increases and their harm grows, and that deters people from entering the religion, and requires blame upon the leaders of the Muslims. As for when the enemy has no covenant, it is fitting that one should devise against him by every stratagem and turn upon him every deception. On this is based his saying ﷺ: (War is deception). [In Kashf al-Khafa: the kha' with fatha is more famous and the dal is silent in all of them; they said the most eloquent is fatha with silent dal, and it is the dialect of the Prophet ﷺ.] The scholars differed on whether one may fight alongside a treacherous imam, on two opinions. Most of them held that one does not fight with him, unlike the treacherous and the wicked. Some held that one may fight with him. Both opinions are in our school.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 59:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that they have escaped﴾. That is, whoever escaped from the battle of Badr got ahead into life. Then He resumed, saying: "Indeed, they cannot escape Us" — that is, in this world, until Allah grants you victory over them. It was also said: it means in the Hereafter. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Ibn 'Amir, Hafs and Hamzah read "yahsabanna" (let them not suppose) with the ya', while the rest read it with the ta', so that the verb has a subject pronoun. "Those who disbelieve" is then the first object (maf'ul awwal), and "saba'u" (they escaped) is the second object (maf'ul thani).

As for the reading with the ya', a group of grammarians, including Abu Hatim, claimed that this is a grammatical error (lahn) which it is not permissible to recite with, and which is not appropriate for anyone who knows i'rab (grammatical inflection) or who has been taught it. Abu Hatim said: "Because 'yahsabanna' has not come with a single object, whereas it requires two objects."

Al-Nahhas said: "This is severe bias. The reading is permissible, and the meaning is: 'Let not those behind them who disbelieve suppose that they escaped,' so the pronoun refers back to what came before. However, the reading with the ta' is clearer."

Al-Mahdawi said: "Whoever reads with the ya' may take the pronoun in the verb to refer to the Prophet ﷺ, and 'those who disbelieve, they escaped' would serve as the two objects. It is also permissible for 'those who disbelieve' to be the subject, with the first object omitted; the meaning being: 'Let not those who disbelieve suppose themselves to have escaped.'"

Makki said: "It is also permissible to supply 'an' (that) after 'saba'u', so that it stands in place of the two objects, and the sense is: 'Let not those who disbelieve suppose that they escaped.' This is like ﴿Do the people suppose that they will be left alone?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2], where 'an' stands in place of the two objects."

Ibn 'Amir read "innahum la yu'jizun" with a fatha on the hamzah. Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd found this reading unlikely. Abu 'Ubayd said: "It is only permissible if the meaning is: 'And do not suppose that those who disbelieve, that they cannot escape Us (la yu'jizuni).'" Al-Nahhas said: "What Abu 'Ubayd mentioned is not permissible according to the Basran grammarians: one cannot say 'hasibtu Zaydan annahu kharij' (I supposed Zayd that he is going out) except with a kasrah on the alif, and it is not allowed because it occupies the position of the subject (mubtada'), as you say: 'hasibtu Zaydan [abuhu kharij]' (I supposed Zayd, his father is going out). If you open it, the meaning becomes 'I supposed Zayd's going out (kharujahu),' and this is impossible. Furthermore, there is the remoteness that there is no way to make sense of what he said, except by treating 'la' as superfluous, and there is no justification for attributing a particle in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to such lengthy argument without a proof that must be accepted."

"The reading is good on the understanding that the meaning is: 'Because they cannot escape Us' (li-annahum la yu'jizuni)."

Makki said: "So the meaning is: 'Let not the disbelievers suppose themselves to have got away because they cannot escape,' that is, they cannot slip away. Here 'anna' is in the accusative position by the omission of the lam, or in the genitive position by treating the lam as operative, given how often it is omitted with 'anna'; this is related from al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i."

The rest read "inna" with a kasrah, as a new independent clause (isti'naf), cut off from what precedes it. This is the preferred reading, because of the emphasis (ta'kid) it carries and because the community (al-jama'ah) follows it.

It is related from Ibn Muhaysin that he read "la yu'ajjizuni" with tashdid and a kasrah on the nun. Al-Nahhas said: "This is an error in two respects. First, 'a''jazahu' means he weakened him and weakened his affair. Second, it should have been with two nuns."

And the meaning of "a'jazahu" is that he preceded him and escaped from him, so that he was not able to reach him.

**First issue:** On the words ﴿And prepare against them﴾, Allah, glorified is He, commanded the believers to prepare strength against the enemies after He had stressed the precedence of taqwa (God-consciousness). Had Allah willed, He would have defeated them by speech, by spitting in their faces, and by a handful of dust, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did. But He willed to test some people by means of others, by His prior knowledge and His executed decree. Whatever you prepare for your friend of good or for your enemy of evil is included in your preparation. Ibn Abbas said: "The strength here is weapons and bows." In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Uqbah ibn Amir, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while on the pulpit, saying: 'And prepare against them whatever you can of strength. Indeed, strength is archery. Indeed, strength is archery. Indeed, strength is archery.'" This is a text narrated from Uqbah by Abu Ali Thumamah ibn Shufayy al-Hamdani, and there is no other narration from him in the Sahih. Another hadith on archery from Uqbah also: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Lands will be opened to you, and Allah will suffice you, so let none of you fail to amuse himself with his arrows.'" And he ﷺ said: "Everything a man amuses himself with is vain, except his shooting with his bow, his training of his horse, and his playing with his wife, for indeed it is part of the truth." The meaning of this, and Allah knows best, is that whatever a man amuses himself with that benefits him neither in this world nor in the next is vain, and turning away from it is better. As for these three matters, although one does them for amusement and enjoyment, they are truth because of their connection to what may be beneficial. Shooting with the bow and training the horse are both aids (ma'awin [[from j, k and z. It is the plural of ma'unah. In awb: ta'awun]]) to fighting. Playing with one's wife may lead to offspring who affirm the oneness of Allah and worship Him; therefore these three are of the truth. In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, on the authority of Uqbah ibn Amir, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah admits three persons into Paradise for one arrow: its maker, who seeks good in his crafting; the archer; and the one who hands him the arrows." The virtue of archery is great, its benefit to the Muslims is great, and its harm to the disbelievers is severe. The Prophet ﷺ said: "O children of Isma'il, shoot, for your father was an archer." Learning horsemanship (furusiyyah [[the art of horsemanship and cavalry skill]]) and the use of weapons is a communal obligation (fard kifayah [[an obligation which, if fulfilled by some, lifts it from the rest]]), and it may become an individual obligation (muta'ayyan).

**Second issue:** On the words ﴿and from the garrisoning (ribat) of horses﴾. Al-Hasan, Amr ibn Dinar and Abu Haywah read "wa min rubuṭ al-khayl" with a damma on the ra' and the ba', as the plural of ribat, like kitab and kutub. Abu Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd: "The ribat of horses is five or more, and its plural is rubuṭ. It is the horses that are tethered (tartabit), from which the verb is derived: rabaṭa yarbiṭu rabṭan, and irtabaṭa yartabiṭu irtibaṭan. The marbit of horses and their marabit are the tethering of them facing the enemy." The poet said:

"God commanded their tethering against His enemy, in war; indeed God is the best of granters of success."

Makhul ibn Abd Allah said:

"You blame me for tethering the fine horses and holding them back, while God has enjoined them upon His Prophet Muhammad."

Garrisoning horses is a great virtue and an honourable station. Urwah al-Bariqi had seventy horses kept ready for jihad. The preferred ones are the females, as said by Ikrimah and a group, and this is correct, for the belly of the female is a treasure and her back is honour. Gabriel's horse was female. The imams narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Horses are of three kinds: for one man it is a reward, for another a shield, and for another a burden," and the hadith continues. He did not specify males over females. The best of them is the one with the greatest reward and the greatest benefit. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked: "Which slaves are best?" He said: "The most expensive in price and the most precious to their owners." Al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Wahb al-Jushami, who had companionship with the Prophet, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Name yourselves with the names of the prophets, and the names most beloved to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are Abd Allah and Abd al-Rahman. Tether the horses, stroke their forelocks and their haunches, adorn them with necklaces, but do not hang upon them bowstrings [[awtar: plural of watr (with kasra), meaning blood-vengeance. The meaning: do not seek upon them the blood-debts and grudges you held in the Jahiliyyah. It is also said: the plural of the bowstring of a bow, for they used to hang them on the necks of animals to ward off the evil eye. This was one of the symbols of the Jahiliyyah, so it was disliked.]], and upon you is every kumayt [[kumayt (diminutive): one whose colour is between black and red, applying to both male and female. The aghar: one with white on his face. The muhajjal: one with white on his legs.]] that is aghar muhajjal, or ashqar aghar muhajjal, or adham aghar muhajjal." Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Qatadah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The best of horses is the adham [[black]] aqram [[with a white blaze]] arthām [[the arthам: one whose nose and upper lip are white]], then the aqram muhajjal [[the aqram: one with a blaze on his forehead, which is a slight whiteness on the face of the horse, short of a full white face]], tlq al-yamin [[i.e. free of it; it has no white on the legs]]. If it is not adham, then kumayt with this mark." Al-Darimi also narrated it from Abu Qatadah: a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I want to buy a horse; which one should I buy?" He said: "Buy an adham arthām muhajjal, tlq al-yad al-yumna, or one from the kumayt with this mark; you will gain and be safe." The Prophet ﷺ disliked the shikal among horses. The shikal: the horse has white on its right hind leg and its left forefoot, or on its right forefoot and its left hind leg. Muslim narrated it from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. It is mentioned that the horse on which al-Husayn ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, was killed was a shikal.

**Third issue:** If it is said: his saying ﴿and prepare against them whatever you can of strength﴾ would have sufficed, so why did He single out archery and horses for mention? It is said in reply: since horses were the foundation of wars and their burdens [[awzar al-harb: its loads of weapons, arms and equipment]], in whose forelocks good is tied, and they are the strongest of strength, the firmest of preparation, the fortresses of horsemen, and by them one charges in the battlefield, He singled them out for mention to honour them, and swore by their dust to ennoble them. So He said: ﴿By the chargers, panting﴾ [[see vol. 20, p. 153]] [al-'Adiyat: 1], and so on. And since arrows are among the most effective of what is used in war, and the most harmful to the enemy, and the nearest to taking lives, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ singled them out for mention and drew attention to them. A parallel to this in the revelation is ﴿Gabriel and Michael﴾ [[see vol. 2, p. 36]] [al-Baqarah: 98], and there are many like it.

**Fourth issue:** Some of our scholars have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of endowing (waqf) horses and weapons, and of establishing storehouses and custodians for them as preparation against enemies. The scholars differed [[in j, z and h: from Malik]] on the permissibility of endowing animals such as horses and camels, on two views: prohibition, which is the view of Abu Hanifah; and validity, which is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The latter is more correct, because of this verse, and because of the hadith of Ibn Umar concerning the horse upon which he rode in the way of Allah, and the Prophet's statement concerning Khalid: "As for Khalid, you are wronging Khalid, for he has endowed his armour and his equipment (i'tad [[the implements of war, whether weapons or animals and others]]) in the way of Allah," and the hadith continues. And what is narrated: a woman made a camel an endowment in the way of Allah, then her husband wished to perform Hajj, so she asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "Give it to him so that he may perform Hajj upon it, for Hajj is part of the way of Allah." Also, it is property that is used for a pious purpose, so it is permissible to endow it, like real estate. Al-Suhayli mentioned in connection with this verse the naming of the horses of the Prophet ﷺ and his weapons. Whoever wishes them will find them in the book al-A'lam [[this is the book al-Ta'rif wa'l-i'lam fima ubhima fi'l-Qur'an min al-asma' al-a'lam. It is a manuscript preserved at the Dar al-Kutub under numbers 232 and 439, tafsir]].

**Fifth issue:** His saying ﴿to terrify thereby the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾, meaning: you frighten with it the enemy of Allah and your enemy, from among the Jews, Quraysh and the disbelieving Arabs.

﴿And others besides them⦆: meaning Persia and Rome, as said by al-Suddi. It was also said: the jinn, and this is the choice of al-Tabari. It was also said: what is meant is every enemy whose enmity is not known. Al-Suhayli said: it was said they are the Qurayzah. It was also said: they are of the jinn, and other things were said. One should not say anything about them, because Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿and others besides them whom you do not know; Allah knows them﴾. So how can anyone claim knowledge of them, unless a hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is authentic concerning it, namely his saying concerning this verse: "They are the jinn." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, Satan does not harm anyone in a house in which there is a noble (ataq) horse." It is called ataq only because it has been freed from being a mixed-breed (hajjanah). This hadith was supported by al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah, from Ibn al-Mulayki, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It is also narrated that the jinn do not approach a house in which there is a horse, and that they flee from the neighing of horses.

**Sixth issue:** His saying ﴿and whatever you spend of anything﴾, meaning: give in charity. It was also said: you spend it on yourselves or on your horses.

﴿in the way of Allah will be repaid to you﴾, in the Hereafter: the good deed multiplied tenfold, up to seven hundred times [[from j, h and z]], and up to many more multiples.

﴿and you will not be wronged﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 61:

There are two issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾. He said "lahā" (to it) because al-salm (peace) is feminine. It is also possible that the feminine refers to the act (fa'lah). Al-junuh (inclination) means al-mayl (leaning). He says: if they lean, meaning those to whom their covenant has been thrown back, toward al-musalamah (reconciliation), that is al-sulh (settlement), then lean toward it. Jana'a al-rajul ila al-akhar means he inclined toward him. From this it is said that the ribs are jawanih (curved sides), because they lean over the hashwah (the intestines). Janahat al-ibil means when the camels' necks incline while walking. Dhu al-Rummah said:

When he dies upon the saddle, I revive his spirit
With your remembrance, and the white camels walking easily (al-marasil)

Janh (inclining)

And al-Nabighah said:

Janawih (birds) who are certain that a tribe,
When the two hosts meet, will be the first to prevail

Meaning birds. Janah al-layl means the night came and let its ropes (atnab) fall onto the earth. Al-silm and al-salam both mean al-sulh (settlement). Al-A'mash, Abu Bakr, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Mufaddal read "lil-silm" with a kasrah on the sin; the rest read it with a fatha. The meaning of this has already been fully discussed in "al-Baqarah" [see vol. 3, p. 22]. Al-salam may also come from al-taslim. The majority read "fajnah" with a fatha on the nun, which is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read "fajnuh" with a damma on the nun, which is the dialect of Qays. Ibn Jinni said: this dialect is the analogical one.

The second: This verse has been disputed as to whether it is abrogated (mansukhah) or not. Qatadah and Ikrimah said it was abrogated by ﴿So kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5] and ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. They said: Bara'ah (Surah al-Tawbah) abrogated every truce until they say, "There is no god but Allah." Ibn 'Abbas said: its abrogating verse is ﴿So do not weaken and call for peace while you are the superior, and Allah is with you﴾ [Muhammad: 35]. It was also said: it is not abrogated; rather it intends accepting the jizyah from the People of the Jizyah. The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made peace in the time of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and after him among the imams with many lands of the non-Arabs, on what they took from them, and left them in what they were in, while they were able to annihilate them. Likewise the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made peace with many people of the lands in exchange for wealth they would pay; among them Khaybar, whose people he returned to it after conquest on condition that they work and pay half. Ibn Ishaq said: Mujahid said this verse refers to Qurayzah, because the jizyah is accepted from them, whereas nothing is accepted from the polytheists. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of the verse is, if they call you to settlement, then respond to them, and there is no abrogation in it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: by this the answer differs. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿So do not weaken and call for peace while you are the superior, and Allah is with you﴾ [Muhammad: 35]. So when the Muslims are in honor, strength, protection, a great community and great firmness, there is no settlement, as he said:

So there is no settlement until horses are pierced by lances
And skulls are struck by white, polished swords

If the Muslims have an interest in settlement, for a benefit they obtain or a harm they repel, there is no harm in the Muslims initiating it when they are in need of it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made peace with the people of Khaybar on conditions which they broke, so he annulled their settlement. He also made peace with al-Damri [al-Damri: Makhshi ibn 'Amr al-Damri, of Banu Damrah ibn Bakr; this was at the Ghazwat al-Abwa'. Akeydir: Akeydir ibn 'Abd al-Malik, a man of Kindah. Dumah: Dumat al-Jandal, a city near Damascus], Ukaydir of Dumah, and the people of Najran. He also concluded a truce with Quraysh for ten years, until they broke his covenant. The caliphs and the companions continued to follow this path which we have laid out, acting by the ways we have explained.

Al-Qushayri said: when strength belongs to the Muslims, the truce should not reach a year. When strength belongs to the unbelievers, it is permissible to make a truce with them for ten years, and no more is allowed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made a truce with the people of Makkah for ten years.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: The scholars differed about the period that existed between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the people of Makkah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. 'Urwah said it was four years. Ibn Jurayj said it was three years. Ibn Ishaq said it was ten years. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said: it is not permissible to make a truce with polytheists for more than ten years, following what the Prophet (ﷺ) did in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. If the polytheists are given a truce for more than that, it is void, because the basic principle is the obligation to fight the polytheists until they believe or give the jizyah. Ibn Habib said on the authority of Malik (may Allah be pleased with him): it is permissible to make a truce with polytheists for a year, two years, three years, and for an indefinite period. Al-Muhallab said: the Prophet (ﷺ) only made this agreement, whose outward appearance is weakness for the Muslims, because Allah stopped the she-camel of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makkah when he set out toward it, and she knelt down. He said: (The one who stopped her is the one who stopped the elephant). As related by al-Bukhari from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah. It indicates the permissibility of settlement and truce with polytheists without wealth being taken from them, when the imam sees this as the right course. It is permissible, when the Muslims are in need, to conclude a settlement with wealth they give to the enemy, as the Prophet (ﷺ) made a truce with 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari and al-Harith ibn 'Awf [in the originals: "ibn Nawfal"; the correction is from the books of biography] al-Murri on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), on condition that he would give them a third of the produce of Madinah, and they would withdraw with those of Ghatafan who were with them and abandon Quraysh, and return with their people from them. This speech was a mere negotiation (muradah) [al-muradah: diplomacy and deception] and not a binding contract. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw that they had repented and were satisfied, he consulted Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, is this a matter you love, so that we do it for you, or something Allah has commanded you, so that we hear and obey, or a matter you do for us?" He said: "Rather, it is a matter I do for you, for the Arabs have shot at you from one bow." Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, we and these people were upon polytheism and worship of idols, not worshipping Allah nor knowing Him, and they never hoped to obtain from us a single date except by purchase or hospitality. Now that Allah has honored us with Islam, guided us to it, and strengthened us through you, shall we give them our wealth? By Allah, we will give them nothing but the sword, until Allah judges between us and them." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was pleased with that and said: (You and that). He said to 'Uyaynah and al-Harith: (Depart, for you have nothing from us but the sword). Sa'd took the document, in which there was no testimony that there is no god but Allah, and erased it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 62–63:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And if they intend to deceive you﴾, that is, by showing you peace while concealing treachery and betrayal, then incline to it; you are not responsible for their corrupt intentions.

(Indeed, Allah is sufficient for you) Allah is your sufficiency, that is, He takes upon Himself your sufficiency and protection. The poet said:

When war comes and the staffs are split, then you are sufficient, and al-Dahhak is a sharpened sword.

That is: you are sufficient, and al-Dahhak is a sword sufficient (for himself).

The words of the Most High: ﴿It is He who supported you with His help﴾, that is, He strengthened you with His victory, meaning on the Day of Badr.

(And with the believers) al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said: it was revealed concerning the Ansar.

(And He joined their hearts) that is, He united the hearts of the Aws and the Khazraj. The bringing together of hearts amid the intense tribal zealousness (ta'assub) among the Arabs was one of the signs and miracles of the Prophet ﷺ, because one of them would be struck with a slap and would fight over it until he obtained retaliation for it. They were the most fiercely zealous (hamiyyah) of Allah's creation, so Allah united them through faith, to the point that a man fought his father and his brother for the sake of religion. It was also said: He meant the bringing together of the Muhajirun and the Ansar. And the meaning is close.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 62–63:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And if they intend to deceive you﴾, that is, by showing you peace while concealing treachery and betrayal, then incline to it; you are not responsible for their corrupt intentions.

(Indeed, Allah is sufficient for you) Allah is your sufficiency, that is, He takes upon Himself your sufficiency and protection. The poet said:

When war comes and the staffs are split, then you are sufficient, and al-Dahhak is a sharpened sword.

That is: you are sufficient, and al-Dahhak is a sword sufficient (for himself).

The words of the Most High: ﴿It is He who supported you with His help﴾, that is, He strengthened you with His victory, meaning on the Day of Badr.

(And with the believers) al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said: it was revealed concerning the Ansar.

(And He joined their hearts) that is, He united the hearts of the Aws and the Khazraj. The bringing together of hearts amid the intense tribal zealousness (ta'assub) among the Arabs was one of the signs and miracles of the Prophet ﷺ, because one of them would be struck with a slap and would fight over it until he obtained retaliation for it. They were the most fiercely zealous (hamiyyah) of Allah's creation, so Allah united them through faith, to the point that a man fought his father and his brother for the sake of religion. It was also said: He meant the bringing together of the Muhajirun and the Ansar. And the meaning is close.

This is not a repetition, for He said earlier: ﴿And if they intend to deceive you, then sufficient for you is Allah﴾, and that was a particular sufficiency. But in His saying: ﴿O Prophet, sufficient for you is Allah﴾ He intended generality, meaning: Allah is sufficient for you in every state.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: It was revealed concerning the conversion of ʿUmar, for the Prophet ﷺ had become Muslim along with thirty-three men and six women, then ʿUmar became Muslim and they became forty. The verse is Meccan, but it was written, by the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, in a Medinan surah. Al-Qushayri mentioned this.

I say: What he mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning the conversion of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) has been contradicted in the biography (sirah). From ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, who said: "We were not able to pray at the Kaʿbah until ʿUmar became Muslim. When he became Muslim, he fought the Quraysh until he prayed at the Kaʿbah, and we prayed with him." ʿUmar's conversion occurred after those companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who had left for Abyssinia had departed. Ibn Ishaq said: The total of those Muslims who joined the land of Abyssinia and emigrated there, apart from their children whom they took with them as small children or who were born there, was eighty-three men, if ʿAmmar ibn Yasir was among them, and he was uncertain about this.

Al-Kalbi said: The verse was revealed at al-Baydaʾ during the Battle of Badr, before the fighting.

His Exalted saying: ﴿And those who follow you of the believers﴾. It has been said: the meaning is "Allah is sufficient for you, and the Emigrants and the Helpers are sufficient for you." It has also been said: the meaning is "Allah suffices you, and suffices those who follow you," as said by al-Shaʿbi and Ibn Zayd. The first view is from al-Hasan, and al-Nahhas and others chose it. So "man" (مَنِ) according to the first view is in the nominative position, in conjunction with the name of Allah the Exalted, meaning: indeed sufficient for you is Allah and your followers from among the believers. According to the second view, it is by an implied verb. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: (Allah suffices me in it, and the sons of Qaylah) [[He means al-Aws and al-Khazraj, the two tribes of the Helpers. Qaylah is an ancient name for their mother, namely Qaylah daughter of Kahil.]]. It has also been said: it is permissible that the meaning of "and those who follow you of the believers" is "Allah is sufficient for them," so the predicate is implied. It is also permissible that "man" is in the accusative position, meaning: Allah suffices you and suffices those who follow you. [[The wording of the original sources is confused here. What is in al-Nahhas's I'rab of the Qur'an is: (O Prophet, sufficient for you is Allah), a subject and predicate, meaning: Allah suffices you. It is said: "ahsabahu" when it sufficed him.

(And those who follow you) is in the accusative position, conjoined to the kaf (you) in interpretation, meaning: Allah the Mighty and Majestic suffices you and suffices those who follow you, as he said:

When the battle cry comes and the staves are split, / Sufficient for you is al-Dahhak, a keen sword.

It is also permissible that (those who follow you) is in the nominative position, and grammarians have three views on it. Abu Jaʿfar said: I heard ʿAli ibn Sulayman say: it is conjoined to the name of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning: sufficient for you is Allah and those who follow you. He said: similar to it is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: (Allah the Mighty and Majestic suffices me in it, and the sons of Qaylah). The second view: that the estimate is "and those who follow you of the believers likewise," as a subject and predicate, as al-Farazdaq said:

And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left / Of wealth nothing but a shaved or a stripped remnant.

The third view is the best: that it is by implication, meaning "and sufficient for you are those who follow you." Likewise the hadith is by implication. We have set aside the first view because it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he forbade saying: "What Allah wills and you will." The second: the poet is compelled, since the poem is in the nominative. And there may be other than this.]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 65–66:

﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden, and He knows that there is weakness in you. So if there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand, by the permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.﴾ (8:66)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight﴾ means: encourage them and spur them on. It is said: ḥāraḍa ʿalā al-amr (he urged upon the matter), wāẓaba, wāṣaba and akabba, all with one meaning. Al-ḥāriḍ is the one who has come close to destruction, and from this is the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿until you become ḥaraḍan﴾ [Yusuf: 85], meaning: melting away with grief, so that he draws close to destruction and becomes one of the perishing.[[See vol. 9, p. 249 onward.]]

﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ is a statement in the form of a report, which implicitly contains a promise conditioned on a condition, because its meaning is: if twenty of you who are steadfast endure, they will overcome two hundred. The words ʿishrūn (twenty), thalāthūn (thirty) and arbaʿūn (forty) are each a noun established in the form of the plural for this number, and this noun follows the pattern of Filasṭīn (Palestine).

If someone asks: why is the first letter of ʿishrīn (twenty) vowelled with a kasra, while the first letter of thalāthīn (thirty) and what follows up to tha­mānīn (eighty) is vowelled with a fatḥa, except for sittīn (sixty)? The answer according to Sibawayh is that ʿishrīn, from ʿashara (ten), is in the position of ithnān (two) from wāḥid (one), so the first letter of ʿishrīn is vowelled with a kasra just as ithnān is. The evidence for this is their saying sittūn and tisʿūn, just as it is said sittah and tisʿah.

Abu Dawud related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The verse ﴿If there are among you twenty steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ was revealed, and this was difficult for the Muslims, when Allah made it obligatory upon them that not one of them should flee from ten. Then the lightening came, and He said: ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden﴾." [Abu Tawbah recited up to His saying: "a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred."] He said: When Allah, exalted is He, lightened the number for them, their steadfastness was reduced by the degree to which it was lightened for them.

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: "Some people said that this was on the day of Badr and was abrogated. This is an error on the part of the one who said it. It has never been transmitted that the polytheists fought the Muslims on this basis. Rather, the Creator, mighty and majestic, made this obligatory upon them at first, and He attached it to the reason that you understand what you fight for, which is the reward, while they do not know what they fight for."

I say: The hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas indicates that this was an obligation. Then, when this was difficult for them, the obligation was reduced to the steadfastness of one against two, so He lightened it for them and made it obligatory upon them that a hundred should not flee from two hundred. Accordingly, on this view it is a lightening and not an abrogation. This is good. The judge Ibn al-Tayyib mentioned that if a ruling is abrogated in part, or part of its attributes, or its number is changed, it is permissible to say that it has been abrogated, because then it is no longer the first, but rather something other than it. He mentioned a difference of opinion on this matter.

There are five issues in this passage. The first concerns the word ﴿أَسْرَى﴾ (captives). It is the plural of ﴿أَسِير﴾ (asir), like ﴿قَتِيل﴾ (qatil) with ﴿قَتْلَى﴾ (qatla) and ﴿جَرِيح﴾ (jarih) with ﴿جَرْحَى﴾ (jarha). The plural of ﴿أَسِير﴾ is also said to be ﴿أُسَارَى﴾ (with a damma on the hamza) and ﴿أَسَارَى﴾ (with a fatha on the hamza), but these forms are not the most eloquent. They used to bind the captive with rawhide, which is called ﴿الْإِسَار﴾ (al-isar, the binding). So every person taken prisoner was called an asir, even if he was not actually bound. al-A'sha said:

"Poetry bound me in its house, / as the women who bind captives bind the donkey."

This was discussed earlier in Surat al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 21.]]. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "The ﴿أَسْرَى﴾ are those who are not tied when they are taken, while the ﴿أُسَارَى﴾ are those who are tied fast." Abu Hatim reported that he heard this from the Arabs.

The second issue is that this verse was revealed on the day of Badr, as a rebuke from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the Companions of His Prophet ﷺ. The meaning is: "It was not right for you to do this act, which made it necessary for the Prophet ﷺ to have captives before ﴿الْإِثْخَان﴾ (al-ithkhan)* ." Its gloss is: "al-ithkhan in a thing means to exaggerate and increase it; here it means exaggerating in killing the disbelievers." This is indicated by Allah's words: ﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾. The Prophet ﷺ did not order that the men be spared during the battle, nor did he ever desire the goods of this world. It was the majority of those who engaged in the fighting who did this. So the reproach and rebuke were directed at those who advised the Prophet ﷺ to accept ransom. This is the view of most of the exegetes, and it is the only view that can be upheld. The mention of the Prophet ﷺ in the verse came because he did not forbid it when he saw it from the 'arish (the shelter), and when Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah disliked it. But he, peace be upon him, was occupied by the sudden turn of events and the descent of victory, so he left off forbidding the sparing of the captives. For this reason, he and Abu Bakr wept when the verses were revealed. And Allah knows best.

Muslim narrated from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, whose beginning was mentioned earlier in Surat Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 193.]], and this is its completion. Abu Zamil said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "When they took the captives, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Abu Bakr and 'Umar: '(What do you think about these captives?)' Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, they are our cousins and kinsmen. I think you should take ransom from them, so that it will be a strength for us against the disbelievers, and perhaps Allah will guide them to Islam.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: '(What do you think, O son of al-Khattab?)' I said: 'No, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I do not hold the view that Abu Bakr holds. Rather, I think that you should let us take them so that we may strike their necks. Enable 'Ali to take 'Aqil and strike his neck, and enable me to take so-and-so (a relative of 'Umar) and I will strike his neck, for these are the leaders of disbelief and its chieftains.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined toward what Abu Bakr said and did not incline toward what I said. When the next day came, I went and found the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr sitting and weeping. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me why you and your companion are weeping. If I find a reason to weep, I will weep, and if I do not find one, I will feign weeping because of your weeping.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: '(I weep for what your companions proposed to me, taking ransom. Their punishment was shown to me, as near as this tree.)' (a tree that was close to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ). Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted slaughter in the land﴾ up to His words: ﴿So eat of what you have taken, lawful and good﴾ [al-Anfal: 69]. So Allah made the spoils lawful for them."

Yazid ibn Harun narrated: he told us, Yahya told us, Abu Mu'awiyah told us, from al-A'mash, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Abu 'Ubaydah, from 'Abd Allah, who said: "When the day of Badr came, the captives were brought, and al-'Abbas was among them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: '(What do you think about these captives?)' Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, they are your people and your family. Spare them, perhaps Allah will accept their repentance.' 'Umar said: 'They denied you, expelled you and fought you. Bring them forward and strike their necks.' 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah said: 'Look for a valley full of firewood and set it alight over them.' Al-'Abbas, who was listening, said: 'You have cut off your kinship ties.' He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered and did not answer them with anything. Some people said: 'He will take the view of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.' Some people said: 'He will take the view of 'Umar.' Some people said: 'He will take the view of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah.' Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out and said: '(Allah softens the hearts of some men until they are softer than milk, and hardens the hearts of other men until they are harder than stones. Your likeness, O Abu Bakr, is the likeness of Ibrahim, who said: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36]. And your likeness, O Abu Bakr, is the likeness of 'Isa, who said: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118] [See vol. 6, p. 377]. And your likeness, O 'Umar, is like the likeness of Nuh, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26] [See vol. 18, p. 312]. And your likeness, O 'Umar, is the likeness of Musa, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 88] [See vol. 8, p. 374]. You are in need, so let none of them escape except with ransom or the striking of the neck.'" 'Abd Allah said: "Except Suhayl ibn Bayda', for I heard him mention Islam." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fell silent. He said: "I never feared that stones would fall on me from the sky as I feared on that day." Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted slaughter in the land﴾ up to the end of the two verses.

In another narration: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "(A punishment almost befell us because of the opposition of Ibn al-Khattab. Had a punishment descended, none would have escaped except 'Umar.)"

Abu Dawud narrated from 'Umar, who said: "When the day of Badr came and he (meaning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ) took the ransom, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted slaughter in the land﴾ up to His words: ﴿for there would have touched you, for what you took, a great punishment﴾ [al-Anfal: 68]. Then He made the spoils lawful."

al-Qushayri mentioned that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is the first battle we have fought against the polytheists, so inflicting slaughter is more beloved to me." And ﴿al-ithkhan﴾ is the great number of killings, according to Mujahid and others, meaning one exaggerates in killing the polytheists. The Arabs say: "So-and-so exaggerated in this matter," meaning he went to extremes. Some said: "Until he is subdued and killed." al-Mufaddal recited:

"She prays at dawn, though her time is not in worship, / and you have exaggerated Pharaoh in his disbelief, disbelief."

It was also said: "﴿until he inflicts slaughter﴾" means "until he is firmly established." It was also said: al-ithkhan is strength and force. So Allah, glorified and exalted, made known that killing the captives who were ransomed at Badr was better than ransoming them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "This was on the day of Badr, when the Muslims were few. When they increased and their authority became strong, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed after this concerning the captives: ﴿Then either release them as a favour or ransom﴾ [Muhammad: 4] [See vol. 16, p. 226], as its explanation will come in Surat al-Qital, if Allah wills." It has also been said: they were rebuked because the matter of Badr had great weight and consequence in the killing, enslaving and taking of the chieftains, nobles and leaders of Quraysh, and of their wealth. All of this is of great consequence, so their duty was to await revelation and not to rush. When they rushed and did not wait, what befell them befell them. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: al-Tabari and others narrated with a chain of transmission that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the people: "(If you wish, take ransom for the captives, and seventy of you will be killed in the battle, equal to their number. And if you wish, they will be killed and you will be safe.)" They said: "We will take the ransom, and seventy of us will be martyred." 'Abd ibn Humayd also mentioned with his chain that Jibril, peace be upon him, descended to the Prophet ﷺ with this choice given to the people. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat Al 'Imran [See vol. 4, p. 193]. 'Abidah al-Salmani said: "They sought both good options, so seventy of them were killed at Uhud."

Here an objection arises, which is the fourth issue: it may be said, if there was a choice, how did the rebuke come with His words ﴿it would have touched you﴾? The answer: the rebuke came first, because of their eagerness to take ransom, and then the choice came after that. What indicates this is that al-Miqdad, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered the killing of 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, said: "My captive, O Messenger of Allah." And Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who took his brother captive, said: "Hold him tightly, for he has a wealthy mother." And there are other accounts of this sort and of their eagerness to take ransom. When the captives were gathered and driven to Madinah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ carried out the killing of al-Nadr, 'Uqbah and others, and began to deliberate about the rest. Then the choice came from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then consulted his Companions. 'Umar kept to his first opinion on killing, and Abu Bakr saw the benefit in the strength of the Muslims through the ransom money. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined toward the opinion of Abu Bakr. Both opinions were ijtihad after the choice was given. Nothing further was revealed on this matter as a reproach. [In MS j, k, h: "reproach"; in MS a, b: "reproaching him"; in MS ي: "faulting."] And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: "At Badr there were polytheist captives, and Allah revealed: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives until he has inflicted slaughter in the land﴾. They were polytheists on that day. They were ransomed and returned. Had they been Muslims, they would have stayed and not returned. The number of those killed among them was forty-four men, and an equal number were taken captive. The number of martyrs was small." 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "The number killed was seventy, and the captives were likewise seventy." Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Musayyab and others said the same. This is the correct view, as it is in Sahih Muslim: they killed seventy that day and took seventy captive. al-Bayhaqi mentioned: "They brought the captives, and over them was Shuqran, the freedman of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; they were forty-nine men who were counted, while they were seventy in origin, an agreed matter without doubt." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Malik only said 'they were polytheists' because the exegetes narrated that al-'Abbas said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'I am a Muslim.' And in another narration the captives said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'We believe in you.' Malik rejected all of this, and argued for its invalidity with what has been mentioned of their return, and in addition that they fought him at Uhud." Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "They differed about the time of al-'Abbas's Islam. It was said: he embraced Islam before the day of Badr, and for this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: '(Whoever meets al-'Abbas, let him not kill him, for he was taken out unwillingly.)' It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said on the day of Badr: '(Indeed some people from Banu Hashim and others have been taken out unwillingly, having no need to fight us. So whoever among you meets any of Banu Hashim, let him not kill him, and whoever meets Abu al-Bakhtari, let him not kill him, and whoever meets al-'Abbas, let him not kill him, for he was taken out under compulsion.)" He mentioned the hadith. And it is mentioned that he embraced Islam when he was captured on the day of Badr. It is also mentioned that he embraced Islam in the year of Khaybar, and he used to write to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with news of the polytheists. He loved to emigrate, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote to him: '(Remain in Makkah, for your staying there is more beneficial to us.)'

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 68:

There are two issues here.

The first: God's saying, ﴿Had it not been for a decree from God that had already gone forth﴾, concerning His not punishing a people until He has made clear to them what they should guard against. The scholars differed about "the decree of God that had already gone forth" in several opinions, the most sound of which is what preceded concerning the permission to take spoils of war, for these were forbidden to those before us. When the day of Badr came, people rushed to the spoils, and God, mighty and majestic, revealed, ﴿Had it not been for a decree from God that had already gone forth﴾, meaning the permission to take spoils.

Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related in his Musnad: Salam narrated to us from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When the day of Badr came, the people hastened to the spoils and took them, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Spoils are not lawful for any black-headed people other than you." So when the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions obtained spoils, they gathered them, and a fire came down from heaven and consumed them [[It is well known that this was in earlier nations, so consider this carefully.]]. Then God, exalted is He, revealed, ﴿Had it not been for a decree from God that had already gone forth﴾ up to the end of the two verses. Al-Tirmidhi also narrated it and said: a hasan sahih hadith. Mujahid and al-Hasan also said this.

From them (Ibn Abbas) and also Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the preceding decree is God's forgiveness of the people of Badr for whatever of their sins came before or after. Another group said: the preceding decree is God's pardon for them regarding this specific sin. The general sense is more sound, based on the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to Umar concerning the people of Badr: "What would make you know? Perhaps God looked upon the people of Badr and said, 'Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.'" Muslim transmitted it.

It was also said: the preceding decree is that He would not punish them while Muhammad (peace be upon him) was among them. It was said: the preceding decree is that He does not punish anyone for a sin committed in ignorance until he has been warned beforehand. Another group said: the preceding decree is among what God decreed of erasing minor sins through avoiding major sins. Al-Tabari held that all these meanings are included within the wording and that it encompasses them all, and he avoided specifying one meaning over another.

The second: Ibn al-Arabi said: The verse is evidence that if a servant ventures into what he believes to be forbidden, while in God's knowledge it is permissible for him, there is no punishment upon him. Such is the fasting person who says, "This is my day of nawb [[Nawb: what is from you a day and a night's journey; it was also said three days; and it was said two or three farsakhs.]], so I will break my fast now," or the woman who says, "This is my day of menstruation, so I will break my fast," and they do so, while nawb and menstruation do require breaking the fast. In the well-known position of the school, there is expiation for this, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifah said: there is no expiation upon him, and this is the other narration. The reasoning of the first narration is that the arising of permissibility does not establish an excuse against the penalty of prohibition when one violates it deliberately, just as if one had intercourse with a woman and then married her. The reasoning of the second narration is that the sanctity of the day is void in the sight of God, mighty and majestic, so the violation fell upon a place that has no sanctity in God's knowledge, and it is like one who intends intercourse with a woman who has been brought to him while he believes she is not his wife, and she turns out to be his wife. This is the more sound view. The first justification is not binding, because God's knowledge and our knowledge are equal in the matter of prohibition, whereas in our case our knowledge and God's knowledge differ, so reliance is upon God's knowledge, as He said: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from God that had already gone forth, a severe punishment would have touched you for what you took﴾.

Its apparent meaning requires that the entire spoil belong to those who seized it, and that they share in it equally. However, the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And know that whatever you obtain as spoil, a fifth of it belongs to Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], clarify that a fifth of it must be set aside and spent on the categories mentioned. The discussion of this has already been given in full.

There are three issues here. The first concerns the address in His words, ﴿O Prophet, say to those in your hands of the captives﴾. It is said that the address is to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions. It is also said that it is to him alone. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the captives in this verse are al-'Abbas and his companions. They said to the Prophet ﷺ: "We have believed in what you have brought, we testify that you are the Messenger of Allah, and we will advise you against your people." So this verse was revealed. The invalidity of this view has already been mentioned from the words of Malik.

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): the Prophet ﷺ set the ransom of the people of ignorance (jahiliyyah) at the Battle of Badr at four hundred.

From Ibn Ishaq: Quraysh sent to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the ransom of their captives, and each people ransomed its captive with what they agreed to. Al-'Abbas said: "O Messenger of Allah, I was already a Muslim." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah knows your Islam. If it is as you say, then Allah will reward you for it. But as for the outward of your affair, it was against us. So ransom yourself and your two nephews Nawfal ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib, and your ally 'Utbah ibn 'Amr, brother of Banu al-Harith ibn Fihr." He said: "That is not with me, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Then where is the wealth that you buried, you and Umm al-Fadl, when you said to her: 'If I am struck down on this journey of mine, then this wealth is for the children of al-Fadl, 'Abdullah and Qutham'?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I know indeed that you are the Messenger of Allah. This is something no one knew except me and Umm al-Fadl. So count for me, O Messenger of Allah, what you took from me: twenty ounces of wealth that I had with me." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No, that is something Allah gave us from you." So he ransomed himself, his two nephews and his ally, and Allah revealed concerning him: "O Prophet, say to those in your hands of the captives," the verse.

Ibn Ishaq said: The captive who was ransomed the most was al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, because he was a wealthy man, and he ransomed himself for one hundred ounces of gold.

In al-Bukhari: Musa ibn 'Uqbah said, Ibn Shihab said: Anas ibn Malik told me that some men of the Ansar asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, permit us to leave the ransom of our nephew al-'Abbas." He said: "No, by Allah, you will not leave a single dirham."

Al-Naqqash and others mentioned that the ransom of each of the captives was forty ounces, except al-'Abbas, for the Prophet ﷺ said: "Double the ransom for al-'Abbas." He charged him with ransoming his two nephews 'Aqil ibn Abi Talib and Nawfal ibn al-Harith, so he paid on their behalf eighty ounces, and on his own behalf eighty ounces. And twenty ounces were taken from him at the time of the battle. That was because he was one of the ten who guaranteed the feeding of the people of Badr, and the turn came to him on the day of Badr, and they fought before he had fed them, and the twenty ounces remained with him, so they were taken from him at the time of the battle. Thus there were taken from him that day one hundred and eighty ounces.

Al-'Abbas said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You have left me, as long as I live, to beg Quraysh with my hand." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Where is the gold that you left with your wife Umm al-Fadl?" Al-'Abbas said: "What gold?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "You said to her: 'I do not know what may befall me in this venture of mine. If some harm comes to me, then it is for you and your child.'" He said: "O son of my brother, who told you this?" He said: "Allah told me." Al-'Abbas said: "I testify that you are truthful, and I never knew you to be the Messenger of Allah until today. I know that no one informed you of this except the Knower of hidden things. I testify that there is no god but Allah and that you are His servant and Messenger, and I have disbelieved in what is other than Him." He then ordered his two nephews, and they both embraced Islam. Concerning them was revealed: "O Prophet, say to those in your hands of the captives."

The one who captured al-'Abbas was Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn 'Amr, brother of Banu Salamah, and he was a short man, while al-'Abbas was large and tall. When he brought him to the Prophet ﷺ, he said to him: "Indeed an angel helped you against him."

The second issue concerns His words, ﴿If Allah knows any good in your hearts﴾, meaning Islam. ﴿He will give you better than what has been taken from you﴾, meaning from the ransom. It is said: in this world. It is also said: in the Hereafter.

In Sahih Muslim: when wealth from Bahrain came to the Prophet ﷺ, al-'Abbas said to him: "I ransomed myself and I ransomed 'Aqil." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Take." So he spread out his garment and took as much as he could carry. (Abridged.)

Outside the Sahih: al-'Abbas said to him: "This is better than what was taken from me, and I still hope that Allah will forgive me." Al-'Abbas said: "He also gave me Zamzam, and I would not love to have for it all the wealth of the people of Makkah."

Al-Tabari traced to al-'Abbas that he said: "It was concerning me that it was revealed, when I informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of my Islam, and I asked him to reckon for me the twenty ounces that were taken from me before the ransom, but he refused, and said: 'That is for...' Then Allah replaced that for me with twenty slaves, all of whom trade with my wealth."

In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), she said: When the people of Makkah sent for the ransom of their captives, Zaynab sent for the ransom of Abu al-'As with wealth, and she sent with it a necklace of hers that had been with Khadijah, which she had given to Abu al-'As when she entered upon him with it. She said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw it, he was greatly moved by it and said: "If you see fit to release her captive and return to her what is hers?" They said: "Yes." The Prophet ﷺ had taken a pledge from him, or promised him, that he would let Zaynab go to him.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Zayd ibn Harithah and a man of the Ansar and said: "Wait in the valley of Yajaj [[Yajaj (kayasma', yansuru, yadribu): a place in Makkah.]] until Zaynab passes by you, and accompany her until you bring her." Ibn Ishaq said: That was a month after Badr.

'Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr said: I was told by Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that she said: When Abu al-'As came to Makkah he said to me: "Prepare yourself, and join your father." She said: I went out preparing myself, and Hind bint 'Utbah met me and said: "O daughter of Muhammad, has it not reached me that you intend to join your father?" I said to her: "I did not intend that." She said: "O cousin, do not do it. I am a wealthy woman, and I have goods that you need. If you want a good, I will sell it to you, or if you want a loan of provisions, I will lend it to you, for what passes between men does not pass between women." She said: By Allah, I did not think she said that except to do it, so I feared her and concealed it, and I said: "I do not intend that." When Zaynab finished her preparations, she set out, and her father-in-law Kinanah ibn al-Rabi' led her out by day. The people of Makkah heard of it, and Habbar ibn al-Aswad and Nafi' ibn 'Abd al-Qays al-Fihri set out in pursuit of her. Habbar was the first to reach her, and he terrified her with the spear while she was in her howdah. Kinanah knelt down, scattered his arrows, then took his bow and said: "By Allah, no man comes near me but I will put an arrow in him." Abu Sufyan came with the nobles of Quraysh and said: "O man, hold back your arrows from us until we speak with you." Abu Sufyan stood over him and said: "You have done nothing right. You went out with the woman in the sight of the people, and you know our calamity that befell us at Badr. The Arabs will think and speak that this is a weakness on our part, and that your going out with his daughter in the sight of the people from among us is weakness. Return with the woman, keep her for some days, then send her away secretly [[i.e., take her away in concealment.]] gently at night, and join her to her father. By my life, we have no need to hold her back from her father, and we have no revenge now for what was done to us." He did so, and when two or three days had passed he sent her away, and she set out until she came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

They mentioned that she had miscarried what was in her belly, because of the terror that befell her when Habbar ibn Umm Dirham terrified her.

The third issue: Ibn al-'Arabi said: "When those among the polytheists were taken captive, some of them spoke of Islam, but they did not carry out a resolve in it, nor did they acknowledge it with a firm acknowledgment. It seems that they wanted to draw near to the Muslims and not to be distant from the polytheists. Our scholars said: If the disbeliever speaks of faith in his heart and with his tongue, but does not carry out a resolve in it, he is not a believer. And if such a thing is found in a believer, he is a disbeliever, except for the whisperings that he cannot ward off, for Allah has pardoned them and dropped them. Allah has made the reality clear to His Messenger ﷺ, and said: ﴿But if they intend your betrayal﴾, meaning, if this statement from them was treachery and deceit, ﴿then they have already betrayed Allah before﴾, with their disbelief and their scheming against you and their fighting against you. And if this statement from them was good, and Allah knows it, then He accepts that from them and compensates them with better than what has left them, and forgives them what preceded of their disbelief, their treachery and their scheming."

The plural of khiyanah (betrayal) is khaya'in, and it should have been said khawa'in, since it is from the waw-root, but they differentiated it from the plural of khai'nah. It is said: khā'in, khawwān, khawanah and khānah.

**Ninth issue? No, this is the first of seven issues.** There are seven issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾. He concluded the surah by mentioning allegiance (*muwalah*, mutual alliance and loyalty), so that each group would know its *wali* (protector and ally), the one it seeks help from. The meanings of *hijrah* (emigration) and *jihad* (striving in the way of Allah) have already been explained, linguistically and in meaning.[[See vol. 3, p. 49.]]

(And those who gave shelter and gave help) is in coordination with it (*ma'tuf 'alayhi*). These are the Ansar (the Helpers), who had settled in the abode and in faith before them (the Emigrants). The Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muhajirun (the Emigrants) joined them.

(Those) is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (*marfu' bil-ibtida'*).

(Some of them) is a second subject, and (allies of one another) is its predicate. The whole is the predicate of *inna* (indeed). Ibn 'Abbas said: "*Awliya' ba'd*" (allies of one another) refers to inheritance. They used to inherit from one another through emigration, and one who had believed but had not emigrated did not inherit from one who had emigrated. Allah abrogated this with His saying: ﴿And those related by blood are closer...﴾ (Q. 8:75). Abu Dawud transmitted this. Thus inheritance passed to the blood-relatives among the believers, and people of two different religions do not inherit from one another at all. Then came the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him: "Give the shares to their rightful owners," as explained earlier in the verses on inheritance. It has also been said: there is no abrogation here, and its meaning concerns support and assistance, as was discussed earlier in *al-Nisa'*.[[See vol. 5, p. 80.]]

(And those who believed) is a new inchoative subject, and its predicate is: ﴿You have no duty of protection toward them at all until they emigrate﴾. Yahya ibn Wthhab, al-A'mash and Hamzah read *min wilayatihim* with a kasra on the waw (*wiliyatihim*). It has been said this is a dialect. It has also been said it derives from *waliytu al-shay'* (I took charge of the thing); one says *waliyyun bayyinu al-wilayah* (a clear guardian) and *wali bayyinu al-wilayah* (a clear protector). The fatha (*wilayatihim*) is clearer and better in this sense, because it means support and kinship. The word *wilayah* may also be used in the sense of authority (*imarah*).

**The second issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they seek your help in religion﴾. He means: if these believers who have not emigrated from the land of war call upon you for help with manpower or wealth to rescue them, then help them, for that is an obligation upon you, so do not abandon them. Except against a people between you and whom there is a covenant; then do not help them against those people, and do not break the covenant until its term is complete.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Except when they are captives, and weak, for then the alliance with them remains in force and support for them is obligatory, to the point that not one eye of ours should blink without going out to rescue them, if our numbers can bear that, or spending all our wealth to extract them, so that no dirham is left for anyone. Thus Malik and all the scholars said. *Inna li-Llah wa-inna ilayhi raji'un* (Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return), over what has befallen creation in abandoning their brothers in the captivity of the enemy, while in their hands are treasures of wealth, surplus of means, power, numbers, strength and vigor.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible to read *fa-'alaykumu al-nasr* (then upon you is the help) in the accusative as an incitement (*al-ighra'*).

**The third issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved, some of them are allies of others﴾. Allah severed the alliance between the disbelievers and the believers. He made the believers allies of one another, and the disbelievers allies of one another; they support one another by their religion and deal with one another according to their beliefs.

Our scholars said concerning a disbelieving woman who has a Muslim brother: he does not marry her off, since there is no *wilayah* (guardianship) between them; her co-religionists marry her off. This was reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Ibn 'Umar, and one report from 'Ali, and it is the view of the people of Madinah.
